hello-print.title: Hello, print()
objectives: Run a Python program that prints text
Write string literals with single and double quotes
Control print's separator and line ending with sep and end
Write comments
hello-print.article:
# Your First Program: print()

## Intuition
A Python program is a text file of instructions that run from the top line to the bottom line.
The first instruction most people learn is `print`, which shows text on the screen (the
*standard output*). Everything you print here is checked by the tests, character by character.

## Precise explanation
```python
# A comment starts with # and is ignored by Python.
print("Hello, world!")        # text in double quotes is a *string*
print('Single quotes work too')
print("Python", "is", "fun")  # several values are joined with a space: Python is fun
print("2026", "10", "24", sep="-")   # sep replaces the space: 2026-10-24
print()                        # an empty line
print("Loading", end="...")   # end replaces the newline normally printed at the end
print("done")                  # continues on the same line: Loading...done
```
* A **string** is text between matching quotes. Use double quotes when the text contains a
  single quote (`"It's"`) and single quotes when it contains double quotes (`'She said "hi"'`).
* `print(a, b, c)` prints its arguments separated by `sep` (default `" "`) and then prints
  `end` (default `"\n"`, a newline).
* Python runs lines in order; a typo such as `Print(...)` stops the program with a `NameError`.

## Worked example
```python
print("Score", "10", sep=": ", end="!\n")
```
prints `Score: 10!` followed by a newline.

## Common mistakes
* Missing quotes: `print(Hello)` makes Python look for a variable called `Hello`.
* Mismatched quotes: `print("Hi')` is a `SyntaxError`.
* Extra spaces: `print("a ", "b")` prints `a  b` (two spaces) because `sep` adds one more.
* Forgetting that `end=""` removes the newline, so the next print continues on the same line.

## Why this matters
Every later program reports results through `print` or through return values. Getting output
exactly right is also how automatic graders and command-line tools communicate.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: An Informal Introduction to Python](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S040`)
- [The Python Tutorial: Input and Output](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S041`)
hello-print.statement:
## Task

Write a program that prints **exactly** these six lines (no extra spaces):

```
Hello, world!
Python is fun
2026-10-24
                         <- this line is empty
Loading...done
She said "hi"
```

**Requirements**
* Line 2 must come from one `print` call with three arguments: `"Python"`, `"is"`, `"fun"`.
* Line 3 must come from one `print` call with the arguments `"2026"`, `"10"`, `"24"` and `sep`.
* Line 5 must come from two `print` calls, the first using `end`.
* Line 6 contains double quotes, so write it with single quotes around it.

The tests run your file and compare everything it prints.
hello-print.starter:
# Print six lines. The first one is done for you.
print("Hello, world!")
# TODO: line 2 - print three words with one print call
# TODO: line 3 - use sep="-"
# TODO: line 4 - an empty line
# TODO: line 5 - two print calls, the first with end="..."
# TODO: line 6 - She said "hi"
hello-print.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-01 Hello, print().

Each `print` call writes its arguments joined by `sep` and then writes `end`. Changing `sep`
produces the date, an empty call produces the blank line, and `end="..."` replaces the newline
so that `done` continues the fifth line. Single quotes let the last string contain double quotes.
"""
# Line 1: a plain string
print("Hello, world!")
# Line 2: three arguments joined by the default separator " "
print("Python", "is", "fun")
# Line 3: a custom separator
print("2026", "10", "24", sep="-")
# Line 4: an empty line
print()
# Line 5: end="..." keeps the next print on the same line
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")
# Line 6: single quotes around text that contains double quotes
print('She said "hi"')
hello-print.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each `print` call writes its arguments joined by `sep` and then writes `end`. Changing `sep`
produces the date, an empty call produces the blank line, and `end="..."` replaces the newline
so that `done` continues the fifth line. Single quotes let the last string contain double quotes.
hints: `print("Python", "is", "fun")` already puts one space between the words.
`print()` with no arguments prints an empty line; `sep="-"` changes the separator.
`print("Loading", end="...")` then `print("done")`; finally `print('She said "hi"')`.

failureFeedback.advice: Compare your output with the six expected lines; look for extra spaces or missing lines.
Use one print with three arguments; print adds the spaces for you.
Pass `sep="-"` so the parts are joined by dashes, not spaces.
Line 4 must be empty: call `print()` with no arguments.
The first call needs `end="..."` so `done` continues the same line.
Wrap the last string in single quotes so it can contain double quotes.

variables.title: Variables and f-strings

Choose readable snake_case names
Do simple arithmetic with + - * /
Insert values into text with f-strings
variables.article:
# Variables and f-strings

## Intuition
A variable is a name tag attached to a value. `age = 19` means "from now on, `age` refers to
19". You can later move the tag to a different value: `age = 20`.

## Precise explanation
```python
name = "Ada"          # a string
age = 19              # a whole number (int)
height_m = 1.68       # a decimal number (float)
is_student = True     # a truth value (bool): True or False
next_age = age + 1    # the right side is computed first, then stored: 20
```
* `=` is **assignment**, not "equals". The right-hand side is evaluated, then the name on the
  left is bound to the result.
* Names may contain letters, digits and `_`, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive
  (`Age` and `age` are different). Python style uses `snake_case`.
* Python works as a calculator: `+ - * /` add, subtract, multiply and divide. `/` always gives
  a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. (More operators come in PY-05.)
* An **f-string** inserts values into text: `f"Name: {name}"` → `Name: Ada`. Any expression can
  go inside the braces: `f"{age + 1}"` → `20`.

## Worked example
```python
price = 4
count = 3
total = price * count
print(f"{count} items cost {total}")   # 3 items cost 12
count = 5                              # reassignment
print(f"{count} items cost {total}")   # 5 items cost 12 — total was computed earlier!
```

## Common mistakes
* Using a variable before assigning it → `NameError`.
* Expecting `total` to update automatically when `count` changes; it stores a value, not a formula.
* Forgetting the `f` before the quotes: `"Name: {name}"` prints the braces literally.
* Writing `"Age: " + age` — you cannot add a string and an int (see PY-03).

## Why this matters
Every model, dataset and hyperparameter in later topics lives in a variable. Clear names such as
`learning_rate` instead of `x` make code readable.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: An Informal Introduction to Python](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S040`)
- [The Python Tutorial: Input and Output](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S041`)

variables.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-02 Variables and f-strings.

Four assignments create the variables with the requested types; `next_age` is computed from
`age`, so changing `age` and re-running the program would update it. Each f-string inserts one
variable into a fixed label.
"""
name = "Ada"
age = 19
height_m = 1.68
is_student = True
next_age = age + 1

print(f"Name: {name}")
print(f"Age next year: {next_age}")
print(f"Height: {height_m} m")
print(f"Student: {is_student}")

## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Four assignments create the variables with the requested types; `next_age` is computed from
`age`, so changing `age` and re-running the program would update it. Each f-string inserts one

`True` has a capital T and no quotes; `next_age = age + 1`.

Use `1.68` (a float), not `"1.68"`.
Use the keyword `True` (capital T, no quotes).
Compute `next_age = age + 1` after creating `age`.

types-conversion.title: Types and Conversion
objectives: Recognise int, float, str and bool values
Inspect a value with type()
Convert between types with int(), float(), str() and round()
types-conversion.article:
# Types and Conversion

## Intuition
`"3"` and `3` look alike on screen but are different kinds of value: one is text, the other a
number. Python must know the **type** of a value to know what operations mean: `"3" + "3"` is
`"33"`, while `3 + 3` is `6`.

## Precise explanation
| Type | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `0`, `-7`, `2026` | whole numbers, any size |
| `float` | `3.5`, `0.1`, `2.0` | decimals, stored approximately |
| `str` | `"hi"`, `"19.99"` | text |
| `bool` | `True`, `False` | truth values |

* `type(x)` returns the type; `type(x).__name__` is its name as text, e.g. `"float"`.
* Conversions create a **new** value: `int("3")` → `3`, `float("19.99")` → `19.99`,
  `str(3)` → `"3"`, `int(3.9)` → `3` (truncates toward zero), `bool(0)` → `False`.
* `round(x, 2)` rounds to two decimal places.
* Mixing types: `int + float` gives a float; `str + int` is a `TypeError` — convert first.

## Worked example
```python
quantity_text = "3"
quantity = int(quantity_text)   # 3
label = str(quantity) + " items" # "3 items"
print(type(quantity).__name__)  # int
print(0.1 + 0.2)                # 0.30000000000000004  (floats are approximate)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))      # 0.3
```

## Common mistakes
* `int("19.99")` raises `ValueError`; use `float("19.99")` first.
* Comparing floats exactly; `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False`. Round or compare with a tolerance.
* Expecting `int(2.7)` to round to 3 — it truncates to 2.

## Why this matters
Data read from files, forms and the keyboard always arrives as text. Converting it correctly is
the first step of every data pipeline, and dtype mistakes are a common source of ML bugs.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: An Informal Introduction to Python](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S040`)
- [Built-in Functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S048`)
- [Built-in Types](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S049`)
types-conversion.statement:
## Task

The starter defines three text values that came from a form:

```python
price_text = "19.99"
quantity_text = "3"
discount_text = "0.1"
```

Create:
* `price` — `price_text` as a `float`
* `quantity` — `quantity_text` as an `int`
* `discount` — `discount_text` as a `float`
* `total` — `price * quantity * (1 - discount)`
* `total_rounded` — `total` rounded to 2 decimal places
* `label` — the text `"3 items"`, built with `str(quantity) + " items"`

Then print exactly:
```
Total: 53.97
price is float
quantity is int
3 items
```
Use `type(...).__name__` for lines 2 and 3.
types-conversion.starter:
price_text = "19.99"
quantity_text = "3"
discount_text = "0.1"

# TODO: convert the three texts, compute total, total_rounded and label
# TODO: print the four lines
types-conversion.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-03 Types and Conversion.

Each text is converted with the function for its target type. The total is computed with
floats, then rounded only for display, so `total` keeps full precision. `str(quantity)` turns
the number back into text before it is joined with `" items"`.
"""
price_text = "19.99"
quantity_text = "3"
discount_text = "0.1"

price = float(price_text)
quantity = int(quantity_text)
discount = float(discount_text)
total = price * quantity * (1 - discount)
total_rounded = round(total, 2)
label = str(quantity) + " items"

print(f"Total: {total_rounded}")
print(f"price is {type(price).__name__}")
print(f"quantity is {type(quantity).__name__}")
print(label)
types-conversion.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each text is converted with the function for its target type. The total is computed with
floats, then rounded only for display, so `total` keeps full precision. `str(quantity)` turns
the number back into text before it is joined with `" items"`.
hints: `price = float(price_text)` and `quantity = int(quantity_text)`.
`total_rounded = round(total, 2)`; print it with an f-string.
`print(f"price is {type(price).__name__}")` prints the type's name.

failureFeedback.advice: Use `float(price_text)`; `int` cannot parse `"19.99"`.
Use `int(quantity_text)` so quantity is a whole number.
Multiply by `(1 - discount)` and round only `total_rounded`, not `total`.
Convert with `str(quantity)` before adding `" items"`.
Print `total_rounded`, then the two type names from `type(x).__name__`, then the label.

input-output.article:
# Reading Input

## Intuition
`print` sends text out; `input` brings text in. When a program reaches `input()` it waits for
one line from the keyboard (or from whatever is connected to *standard input*, such as a file or
an automatic grader) and gives it to you as a string.

## Precise explanation
```python
name = input()                 # one line, without the trailing newline, always a str
year = int(input())            # convert when you need a number
city = input("City? ")         # an optional prompt is printed first (not used in graded tasks)
```
* `input()` returns a `str`, even if the user typed digits. `input() + 1` is a `TypeError`.
* `text.strip()` removes spaces, tabs and newlines from both ends. `int()` and `float()`
  already ignore surrounding whitespace, but names and words do not.
* Each call reads the **next** line. If there is no line left, Python raises `EOFError`.

## Worked example
Input:
```
  Grace
1990
```
```python
name = input().strip()     # "Grace"
birth_year = int(input())  # 1990
print(f"Hello, {name}! In 2030 you will turn {2030 - birth_year}.")
```
Output: `Hello, Grace! In 2030 you will turn 40.`

## Common mistakes
* Forgetting `int(...)`, then subtracting a string.
* Printing a prompt in graded tasks: the prompt becomes part of your output and breaks exact
  comparisons. Tests in this site supply input directly, so call `input()` with no prompt.
* Calling `input()` more times than there are lines.

## Why this matters
Reading and validating outside data is where most real programs start: command-line tools,
web forms (FA-01 later) and dataset files all deliver text you must parse.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: Input and Output](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S041`)
- [Built-in Functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S048`)


"""

arithmetic-operators.article:
# Arithmetic Operators

## Intuition
Converting 3725 seconds into hours, minutes and seconds is a division with remainders: how many
whole hours fit, and what is left over? Python has an operator for each part.

## Precise explanation
| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `+ - *` | add, subtract, multiply | `7 * 2 == 14` |
| `/` | true division (always float) | `7 / 2 == 3.5` |
| `//` | floor division (round down) | `7 // 2 == 3`, `-7 // 2 == -4` |
| `%` | remainder (modulo) | `7 % 2 == 1` |
| `**` | power | `2 ** 10 == 1024` |

* For non-negative `a` and positive `b`: `a == (a // b) * b + a % b`.
* **Precedence**: `**` first, then `* / // %`, then `+ -`; use parentheses to be explicit:
  `2 + 3 * 4 == 14`, `(2 + 3) * 4 == 20`, `-2 ** 2 == -4`.
* **Augmented assignment**: `x += 5` means `x = x + 5` (also `-=`, `*=`, `//=`, ...).
* **Format specs** inside f-strings: `f"{5:02d}"` → `05` (at least 2 digits, zero-padded);
  `f"{62.0833:.2f}"` → `62.08` (two decimals).

## Worked example
`3725` seconds: hours = `3725 // 3600` = 1; remaining = `3725 % 3600` = 125;
minutes = `125 // 60` = 2; seconds = `125 % 60` = 5 → `1:02:05`.

## Common mistakes
* Using `/` where you want a whole number: `3725 / 3600` is `1.034...`.
* Forgetting zero-padding, producing `1:2:5`.
* Writing `x ^ 2` for a power — `^` is bitwise XOR in Python; use `x ** 2`.

## Why this matters
Integer division and remainders appear in batching (`n // batch_size` full batches), image
indexing (row = `i // width`, column = `i % width`) and time-series resampling.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: An Informal Introduction to Python](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S040`)
- [Built-in Types](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S049`)
arithmetic-operators.statement:
## Task

Read one non-negative integer: a number of seconds. Print two lines:

1. The duration as `H:MM:SS` — hours without padding, minutes and seconds with two digits.
2. The duration in minutes with exactly two decimals, followed by ` minutes`.

**Example**
```
input:  3725
output: 1:02:05
        62.08 minutes
```
Hours may exceed 24 (`90000` → `25:00:00`).
arithmetic-operators.starter:
total = int(input())
# TODO: compute hours, minutes and seconds with // and %
# TODO: print H:MM:SS and the minutes with two decimals
arithmetic-operators.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-05 Arithmetic Operators.

Floor division gives the number of whole hours; the remainder holds what is left, which is split
again into minutes and seconds. `:02d` pads minutes and seconds to two digits and `:.2f` shows
the true-division result with two decimals.
"""
total = int(input())
hours = total // 3600
rest = total % 3600
minutes = rest // 60
seconds = rest % 60
print(f"{hours}:{minutes:02d}:{seconds:02d}")
print(f"{total / 60:.2f} minutes")
arithmetic-operators.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Floor division gives the number of whole hours; the remainder holds what is left, which is split
again into minutes and seconds. `:02d` pads minutes and seconds to two digits and `:.2f` shows
the true-division result with two decimals.
hints: `hours = total // 3600` and `rest = total % 3600`.
`minutes = rest // 60`, `seconds = rest % 60`.
`print(f"{hours}:{minutes:02d}:{seconds:02d}")` and `print(f"{total / 60:.2f} minutes")`.

failureFeedback.advice: Pad minutes and seconds with `:02d`.
Use `:.2f` so zero is printed as `0.00`.
Take the remainder after removing hours before computing minutes.
Do not wrap hours at 24; just use `total // 3600`.
Minutes use true division `/`, then `:.2f` formatting.

string-basics.article:
# Strings: Indexing, Slicing and Methods

## Intuition
A string is a row of characters with numbered positions, starting at 0. You can point at one
position, cut out a piece, or ask the string to produce a changed copy of itself.

## Precise explanation
```
 P   y   t   h   o   n
 0   1   2   3   4   5     positive index
-6  -5  -4  -3  -2  -1     negative index (counts from the end)
```
* `word[0]` → `"P"`, `word[-1]` → `"n"`. An index past the end raises `IndexError`.
* **Slicing** `word[start:stop]` takes positions `start` up to but **not including** `stop`:
  `word[0:3]` → `"Pyt"`; omitted ends mean "from the start"/"to the end": `word[:3]`, `word[3:]`.
  Slices never raise errors: `"ab"[:3]` → `"ab"`.
* A third number is the step: `word[::2]` → `"Pto"`, `word[::-1]` → `"nohtyP"` (reversed).
* `len(word)` → 6. `"th" in word` → `True` (substring test).
* Methods return **new** strings: `word.upper()`, `word.lower()`, `"  x ".strip()`,
  `"a-b".replace("-", "+")`, `"py".title()`. Strings are immutable: `word[0] = "J"` is an error.

## Worked example
`word = "Python"` → `len(word)` 6, `word[0]` P, `word[-1]` n, `word[:3]` Pyt,
`word[::-1]` nohtyP, `word.upper()` PYTHON, `"th" in word` True.

## Common mistakes
* Off-by-one: the last character is `word[len(word) - 1]`, not `word[len(word)]`.
* Expecting `word.upper()` to change `word`; store the result if you need it.
* Confusing `word[1:3]` (2 characters) with "characters 1 to 3 inclusive".

## Why this matters
Text cleaning in NLP, parsing HTTP requests and file names, and reading model output all rely on
slicing and string methods.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: An Informal Introduction to Python](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S040`)
- [Built-in Types](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S049`)
string-basics.statement:
## Task

Read one word (strip surrounding spaces). Print exactly these seven lines for it:

```
Length: <number of characters>
First: <first character>
Last: <last character>
First three: <first three characters, or the whole word if shorter>
Reversed: <the word backwards>
Upper: <the word in upper case>
Contains 'th': <True or False>
```

**Example** for `Python`:
```
Length: 6
First: P
Last: n
First three: Pyt
Reversed: nohtyP
Upper: PYTHON
Contains 'th': True
```

conditionals.article:
# Conditionals

## Intuition
Programs make decisions: *if* the score is at least 90, the grade is A; *otherwise, if* it is at
least 80, B; and so on. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block
whose condition is true.

## Precise explanation
```python
if score < 0 or score > 100:
    print("Invalid score")
elif score >= 90:
    print("A")
elif score >= 80:
    print("B")
else:
    print("F")
```
* Comparisons produce bools: `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.
* `and` is true only if both sides are; `or` if at least one is; `not` flips a bool.
* Chained comparison: `0 <= score <= 100` means `0 <= score and score <= 100`.
* The **indented** lines (4 spaces) form the block. `elif` and `else` are optional; at most one
  branch runs.
* `=` assigns, `==` compares. `if score = 90:` is a `SyntaxError`.

## Worked example
`score = 85`: `85 < 0 or 85 > 100` is False → `85 >= 90` False → `85 >= 80` True → prints `B`;
the remaining branches are skipped.

## Common mistakes
* Wrong order: testing `score >= 60` before `score >= 90` gives every passing score a D.
* Writing `if 0 <= score and <= 100` — each side of `and` must be a full comparison.
* Forgetting the colon after the condition, or mixing tabs and spaces.

## Why this matters
Thresholds turn model scores into decisions (spam / not spam), and branches handle edge cases
such as empty data, which you will meet in every later topic.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: More Control Flow Tools](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S042`)
- [Built-in Types](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S049`)
conditionals.statement:
## Task

Read one integer score. Print two lines.

Line 1 — the grade:
| Score | Output |
|---|---|
| below 0 or above 100 | `Invalid score` |
| 90–100 | `A` |
| 80–89 | `B` |
| 70–79 | `C` |
| 60–69 | `D` |
| 0–59 | `F` |

Line 2 — `Pass` if the score is valid and at least 60, `Fail` if it is valid and below 60, and
`Check the input` if it is invalid.
conditionals.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Invalid scores are handled first so that later branches only see 0–100. The bands are tested from
highest to lowest, so each `elif` implicitly knows the score is below the previous threshold.
The second decision reuses a chained comparison for validity.
hints: Test the invalid case first: `if score < 0 or score > 100:`.
Then go from the highest band down with `elif score >= 90:`, `elif score >= 80:` ...
For line 2 use a second if/elif/else; `0 <= score <= 100` checks validity.

failureFeedback.advice: Use `>=` so that exactly 90 is an A and 89 is a B.
Check the bands from highest to lowest with elif.
Handle scores above 100 before the A band.
Negative scores are invalid, not F.
60 passes; 59 fails.

while-loops.article:
# While Loops

## Intuition
Sometimes you do not know in advance how many times to repeat something: "keep reading numbers
until the user types `done`". A `while` loop repeats its block for as long as its condition is
true.

## Precise explanation
```python
count = 0
while count < 3:      # checked before every repetition
    print(count)
    count += 1        # without this the loop never ends
```
* `while True:` loops forever until a `break` statement leaves it — a common pattern when the
  stopping condition is discovered *inside* the loop.
* `continue` skips the rest of the current repetition.
* A **sentinel** is a special input that means "stop", such as `done`.
* `None` represents "no value yet". Test it with `is None`.

```python
largest = None
while True:
    line = input().strip()
    if line == "done":
        break
    x = int(line)
    if largest is None or x > largest:
        largest = x
```

## Worked example
Lines `4`, `9`, `2`, `done`: count 1→2→3, total 4→13→15, largest 4→9→9. Output:
`count=3 total=15 max=9`.

## Common mistakes
* Infinite loops: the condition never becomes false and there is no `break`.
* Converting the sentinel: `int("done")` raises `ValueError`; check for it first.
* Starting `largest = 0`, which is wrong when every number is negative.

## Why this matters
Training loops run "until converged", agents loop "until the goal is reached or the step budget
runs out" (AG-05 later), and servers loop over incoming requests.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: More Control Flow Tools](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S042`)
while-loops.statement:
## Task

Read integers, one per line, until a line equal to `done` (ignore surrounding spaces). Then print
one line:

```
count=<how many numbers> total=<their sum> max=<the largest>
```
If `done` is the first line, print `count=0 total=0 max=None`. Numbers may be negative.
while-loops.starter:
count = 0
total = 0
largest = None
# TODO: loop, reading lines until "done"; update count, total and largest
print(f"count={count} total={total} max={largest}")
while-loops.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-08 While Loops: Read Until Done.

The loop has no natural end, so `while True` with a `break` on the sentinel is clearest. Three
accumulators are updated per number; starting the maximum at `None` makes the first number win
regardless of sign, and lets the empty case print `None`.
"""
count = 0
total = 0
largest = None
while True:
    line = input().strip()
    if line == "done":
        break
    x = int(line)
    count += 1
    total += x
    if largest is None or x > largest:
        largest = x
print(f"count={count} total={total} max={largest}")
while-loops.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The loop has no natural end, so `while True` with a `break` on the sentinel is clearest. Three
accumulators are updated per number; starting the maximum at `None` makes the first number win
regardless of sign, and lets the empty case print `None`.
hints: Use `while True:` and read `line = input().strip()` at the top of the loop.
`if line == "done": break` must come before `int(line)`.
Update the maximum with `if largest is None or x > largest: largest = x`.

failureFeedback.advice: Start `largest` at `None`, not 0, so negative maxima work.
Strip each line before comparing it with `done`.
Break as soon as you see `done`; ignore anything after it.
If `done` comes first, print the initial values: 0, 0 and None.

for-loops-range.article:
# For Loops and range

## Intuition
When you know what to repeat over — the numbers 1 to n, or the letters of a word — a `for` loop
is simpler than `while`: it hands you each item in turn and stops by itself.

## Precise explanation
```python
for i in range(5):        # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4   (stop is excluded)
    print(i)
for i in range(1, 6):     # 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    ...
for i in range(10, 0, -3):  # 10, 7, 4, 1  (step may be negative)
    ...
for ch in "abc":          # 'a', 'b', 'c'
    ...
```
* `range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, `range(start, stop, step)` produce integers from `start`
  up to but not including `stop`. `range(0)` and `range(1, 1)` are empty.
* `break` and `continue` work as in while loops.
* Loops can be nested; the inner loop runs completely for each outer repetition.

## Worked example
Sum of multiples of 3 or 5 up to 10:
```python
total = 0
for i in range(1, 11):
    if i % 3 == 0 or i % 5 == 0:
        total += i          # 3 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 10 = 33
```

## Common mistakes
* `range(1, n)` stops at `n - 1`; use `range(1, n + 1)` to include n.
* Testing `% 3` before `% 15` in FizzBuzz, so 15 prints `Fizz` instead of `FizzBuzz`.
* Changing the loop variable inside the loop and expecting it to affect the next repetition.

## Why this matters
Epoch loops in training, sweeps over hyperparameters, and iteration over pixels, tokens and
episodes are all `for` loops.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: More Control Flow Tools](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S042`)
for-loops-range.statement:
## Task

Read an integer `n` (0 ≤ n ≤ 1000). For each `i` from 1 to `n` print one line:
* `FizzBuzz` if `i` is divisible by both 3 and 5,
* `Fizz` if divisible by 3 only,
* `Buzz` if divisible by 5 only,
* otherwise the number itself.

Finally print `sum=<sum of all i from 1 to n divisible by 3 or 5>`.

**Example** for `n = 5`:
```
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
sum=8
```
for-loops-range.starter:
n = int(input())
total = 0
# TODO: loop from 1 to n, print FizzBuzz lines and add multiples of 3 or 5 to total
print(f"sum={total}")
for-loops-range.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

`range(1, n + 1)` visits every number once. The combined case is tested first because a number
divisible by 15 also passes the single tests. The sum is a separate condition inside the same
loop, so no second pass is needed.
hints: `for i in range(1, n + 1):` includes n.
Check `i % 15 == 0` (or `i % 3 == 0 and i % 5 == 0`) before the single cases.
Add to `total` inside `if i % 3 == 0 or i % 5 == 0:`.

failureFeedback.advice: Test divisibility by both 3 and 5 before testing 3 alone.
Use `range(1, n + 1)` so n itself is included.
With n = 0 the loop runs zero times; only the sum line is printed.
Add i to the total when it is divisible by 3 **or** 5.

greeting-formatter.article:
# Functions, Strings and f-strings

## Intuition
A function is a named recipe: you give it ingredients (arguments) and it hands back a result
(the return value). Most bugs in beginner code come from mixing up *printing* something with
*returning* it. Printing shows text to a human; returning gives a value to the rest of the
program — and to the automatic tests.

## Precise explanation
```python
def greet(name="World"):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
```
* `def` creates a function object and binds it to the name `greet`.
* `name="World"` is a **default argument**: if the caller passes nothing, `name` is `"World"`.
* An **f-string** (`f"..."`) evaluates every `{expression}` inside it and inserts the result.
* `return` ends the function and sends the value back to the caller. A function with no
  `return` returns `None`.

Useful string methods: `s.strip()` removes leading/trailing whitespace; `s.title()`
capitalises each word; `s.lower()` / `s.upper()` change case. Strings are **immutable** — each
method returns a *new* string and leaves the original unchanged.

## Worked example
```python
>>> raw = "   ada lovelace  "
>>> clean = raw.strip()        # 'ada lovelace'
>>> clean.title()              # 'Ada Lovelace'
>>> f"Hello, {clean.title()}!"
'Hello, Ada Lovelace!'
>>> raw                        # unchanged
'   ada lovelace  '
```

## Common mistakes
* Using `print(...)` inside the function and forgetting `return` → the caller receives `None`.
* Writing `raw.strip()` on its own line and expecting `raw` to change (strings are immutable).
* Forgetting the `f` prefix, which produces the literal text `{name}`.
* Using a mutable default such as `def f(x=[])` — the same list is shared between calls.

## Why this matters
Every later exercise — from a NumPy helper to an agent tool — is a function whose *return
value* is checked. Clean input normalisation (strip, lower) is also the first step of every
text-processing pipeline in NLP.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
- [Learn Python - Interactive Course](https://aqemery.github.io/learn-python/) — aqemery (GitHub user) (`S005`)
greeting-formatter.statement:

**Requirements**

2. If the cleaned name is empty, use `"World"`.
3. Convert the name to title case (`str.title()`).
4. Return exactly `"Hello, <Name>!"`. Do not print anything.

**Constraints:** `name` is a `str` of length 0–100.

**Return format:** a `str`.

**Examples**
```python
greet()                    # 'Hello, World!'   — default argument used
greet("  ada lovelace ")   # 'Hello, Ada Lovelace!' — stripped, then title-cased
greet("   ")               # 'Hello, World!'   — only spaces → empty after strip
```

    """Return 'Hello, <Name>!' with the name stripped and title-cased."""

greeting-formatter.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-10 Greeting Formatter.

The function normalises its input first (strip), handles the empty case by falling back to the
default, and only then formats. Doing validation before formatting keeps each step simple and
means the f-string always receives a clean, non-empty name. `str.title()` is applied inside the
f-string so the stored value stays as the user typed it (minus whitespace).
"""
def greet(name="World"):
    name = name.strip()
    if not name:
        name = "World"
    return f"Hello, {name.title()}!"

The function normalises its input first (strip), handles the empty case by falling back to the
default, and only then formats. Doing validation before formatting keeps each step simple and
means the f-string always receives a clean, non-empty name. `str.title()` is applied inside the
f-string so the stored value stays as the user typed it (minus whitespace).

Build the answer with `f"Hello, {name.title()}!"` and `return` it.

`.title()` also lowercases the remaining letters — use it rather than `.capitalize()` on the first letter only.

Handle the empty-input edge case
Return a tuple of results
sum-and-mean.article:
# The Accumulator Pattern

## Intuition
To add up a column of numbers by hand you keep a running total and update it once per number.
In code this is the **accumulator pattern**: start a variable at a neutral value, then update it
inside a loop.

## Precise explanation
```python
total = 0            # neutral element for addition
for x in nums:
    total += x       # same as total = total + x
```
The mean (arithmetic average) of $n$ numbers is

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.$$

It is undefined when $n = 0$, so code must decide what to do with an empty list. Here we return
`None` for the mean (the sum of an empty list is still `0`).

A function can return several values as a **tuple**: `return total, mean` returns
`(total, mean)`, which the caller can unpack: `t, m = sum_and_mean(data)`.

Python also provides `sum(nums)` and `statistics.mean(nums)`; the latter raises
`StatisticsError` on empty input. Writing the loop yourself once makes clear what those helpers do.

## Worked example
For `[2, 4, 9]`: total goes 0 → 2 → 6 → 15; n = 3; mean = 15 / 3 = 5.0.

## Common mistakes
* Dividing by `len(nums)` without checking for zero → `ZeroDivisionError`.
* Initialising `total = nums[0]` → crashes on an empty list and double-counts if you then loop
  over all items.
* Using `//` (floor division) instead of `/` → `7 // 2 == 3`, not `3.5`.

## Why this matters
Means appear everywhere: average loss per batch, average reward per episode, feature
standardisation. The empty-input edge case is the classic source of crashes in data pipelines.

## Library implementation

Python's built-in `sum(nums)` performs the same accumulation, and `statistics.fmean(nums)`
computes the mean (it raises `StatisticsError` for empty data instead of returning `None`).
You will import modules properly in PY-15; the comparison below already uses them.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
- [statistics — Mathematical statistics functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S003`)
sum-and-mean.statement:
## Task

Write `sum_and_mean(nums)` returning a tuple `(total, mean)`.

**Requirements**
* `total` is the sum of the numbers (an `int` if all inputs are ints).
* `mean` is `total / len(nums)` as a `float`.
* For an empty list return `(0, None)`.
* Use a loop (do not call `sum` or `statistics`). Do not modify the input list.

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ `len(nums)` ≤ 10⁵; elements are ints or floats.

**Examples**
```python
sum_and_mean([2, 4, 9])     # (15, 5.0)
sum_and_mean([])            # (0, None)   — mean undefined for empty data
sum_and_mean([-1.5, 1.5])   # (0.0, 0.0)
```
sum-and-mean.starter:
def sum_and_mean(nums):
    """Return (total, mean) of nums; mean is None for an empty list."""
    total = 0
    # TODO: loop and accumulate, then compute the mean safely
    return total, None
sum-and-mean.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-11 Sum and Mean of a List.

One pass over the data maintains two accumulators: the running total and the count. Counting
inside the loop means the function would also work for any iterable (not only lists). The empty
case is detected via `count == 0` before division, avoiding `ZeroDivisionError`.
"""
def sum_and_mean(nums):
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += 1
    if count == 0:
        return 0, None
    return total, total / count
sum-and-mean.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

One pass over the data maintains two accumulators: the running total and the count. Counting
inside the loop means the function would also work for any iterable (not only lists). The empty
case is detected via `count == 0` before division, avoiding `ZeroDivisionError`.
hints: Loop with `for x in nums:` and update `total += x`.
Check `if len(nums) == 0:` (or `if not nums:`) before dividing.
Use true division `/` so the mean is a float.

failureFeedback.advice: Return `(0, None)` before dividing; dividing by zero raises an error.
Use `/` not `//`.
Floats are compared with a tolerance of 1e-9; make sure you return numbers, not strings.
With one element the mean equals that element as a float.

filter-evens.article:
# Filtering with List Comprehensions

## Intuition
Filtering means keeping the items that pass a test. In Python the most readable filter is a
**list comprehension**: "give me `x` for each `x` in `nums` if `x` is even".

## Precise explanation
`a % b` is the remainder of `a` divided by `b`. An integer `x` is even exactly when
`x % 2 == 0`. In Python `%` always returns a result with the sign of the divisor, so
`-4 % 2 == 0` and `-3 % 2 == 1`: the test works for negative numbers too.

```python
[x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
```
is equivalent to
```python
out = []
for x in nums:
    if x % 2 == 0:
        out.append(x)
```
Both keep the original order and build a **new** list.

## Worked example
`nums = [5, -4, 0, 7, 12]` → test each: 5%2=1 ✗, -4%2=0 ✓, 0%2=0 ✓, 7%2=1 ✗, 12%2=0 ✓ →
`[-4, 0, 12]`.

## Common mistakes
* Testing `x % 2 == 1` for "odd" and then negating incorrectly; just test `== 0`.
* Removing items from a list while looping over it — skips elements. Build a new list instead.
* Forgetting that `0` is even.

## Why this matters
Boolean filtering is the same idea as NumPy masks (`a[a % 2 == 0]`) and pandas row selection
(`df[df.score > 50]`), which you will use constantly.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)

**Constraints:** `nums` is a list of 0–10⁵ integers (may be negative). Do not modify `nums`.

**Examples**
```python
evens([5, -4, 0, 7, 12])   # [-4, 0, 12]  — 0 and negatives handled
evens([1, 3, 5])           # []           — nothing passes the test
```

A conditional list comprehension iterates once, keeps elements whose remainder modulo 2 is zero,
and returns a new list, so the input is untouched and order is preserved. Python's `%` makes
the test correct for negative numbers.
"""
def evens(nums):
    return [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]

vowel-counter.article:
# Counting with Dictionaries

## Intuition
Counting how often each vowel appears is like tallying votes: one box per candidate, add a mark
for each vote. A **dictionary** maps keys (the candidates) to values (the tallies).

## Precise explanation
* Iterating over a string yields its characters: `for ch in "hey": ...` gives `'h'`, `'e'`, `'y'`.
* `ch in "aeiou"` tests membership (works for strings, lists, sets, dict keys).
* Initialise all counters so missing vowels report 0:
  `counts = {v: 0 for v in "aeiou"}` (a **dict comprehension**).
* Lower-case once (`text.lower()`) so `'A'` and `'a'` are counted together.

```python
counts = {v: 0 for v in "aeiou"}
for ch in text.lower():
    if ch in counts:
        counts[ch] += 1
```

## Worked example
`"Banana Split!"` → lower: `"banana split!"` → a appears 3 times, i once →
`{'a': 3, 'e': 0, 'i': 1, 'o': 0, 'u': 0}`; total = 4.

## Common mistakes
* Forgetting to lowercase, so capital vowels are missed.
* Writing `counts[ch] += 1` for a key that doesn't exist → `KeyError`. Pre-fill keys or use
  `dict.get(ch, 0) + 1`.
* Counting `'y'` — this problem defines vowels as `a e i o u` only.

## Why this matters
Frequency counting is the foundation of bag-of-words models, n-gram language models and
histograms. `collections.Counter` does this for you; knowing the manual version helps you read it.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
vowel-counter.statement:
## Task

Write `count_vowels(text)` returning `(total, counts)` where `counts` is a dict with exactly the
keys `'a','e','i','o','u'` mapped to how many times each occurs in `text` (case-insensitive), and
`total` is the sum of those counts.

**Constraints:** `text` is a `str` of length 0–10⁵. Only the five ASCII vowels count.

**Examples**
```python
count_vowels("Banana Split!")
# (4, {'a': 3, 'e': 0, 'i': 1, 'o': 0, 'u': 0})
count_vowels("rhythm")
# (0, {'a': 0, 'e': 0, 'i': 0, 'o': 0, 'u': 0})   — 'y' is not a vowel here
```
vowel-counter.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Pre-filling the dictionary guarantees all five keys appear even when a vowel is absent. Lowering
the text once makes the comparison case-insensitive. Membership in a dict is an O(1) lookup, so
the whole function is a single linear pass.
hints: Create `counts = {v: 0 for v in 'aeiou'}` so every key exists.
Loop over `text.lower()` and test `if ch in counts`.
`total = sum(counts.values())`.

failureFeedback.advice: Lower-case the text before counting.
All five vowel keys must be present, even with count 0.
'y' is not counted in this problem.
`total` must equal the sum of the dictionary values.

fibonacci-sequence.title: Fibonacci Sequence
objectives: Maintain state across loop iterations
Use tuple assignment
Handle small-n boundary cases
fibonacci-sequence.article:
# Loop State and Tuple Assignment

## Intuition
Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … To generate them
you only need to remember the *last two* values — a sliding window of state.

## Precise explanation
$F_0 = 0,\; F_1 = 1,\; F_k = F_{k-1} + F_{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$.

**Tuple assignment** evaluates the whole right-hand side first, then assigns:
```python
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
    out.append(a)
    a, b = b, a + b    # new a = old b, new b = old a + old b
```
Without tuple assignment you would need a temporary variable (`t = a + b; a = b; b = t`).
Writing `a = b` then `b = a + b` is a bug: `a` has already changed.

`_` is a conventional name for a loop variable you don't use.

## Worked example (n = 6)
| step | append a | (a, b) after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | (1, 1) |
| 2 | 1 | (1, 2) |
| 3 | 1 | (2, 3) |
| 4 | 2 | (3, 5) |
| 5 | 3 | (5, 8) |
| 6 | 5 | (8, 13) |

Result: `[0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5]`.

## Common mistakes
* Naive recursion `fib(k-1) + fib(k-2)` — exponential time; n = 40 takes seconds.
* Special-casing n = 1 and n = 2 with hard-coded lists and getting n = 0 wrong.
* Sequential (not simultaneous) assignment, as described above.

## Why this matters
Carrying a small amount of state through a loop is the core of running averages, momentum in
optimizers (DL-14) and discounted returns in RL (RL-01).

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
fibonacci-sequence.statement:
## Task

Write `fibonacci(n)` returning a list of the first `n` Fibonacci numbers, starting `0, 1, ...`.

**Requirements:** iterative (O(n) time); `n = 0` returns `[]`; a negative `n` also returns `[]` (raising errors for bad input comes later, in PY-19).

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴.

**Examples**
```python
fibonacci(6)   # [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5]
fibonacci(1)   # [0]
fibonacci(0)   # []
```
fibonacci-sequence.starter:
def fibonacci(n):
    """Return the first n Fibonacci numbers [0, 1, 1, 2, ...]."""
    out = []
    # TODO
    return out
fibonacci-sequence.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-14 Fibonacci Sequence.

Two variables hold the current and next Fibonacci numbers. Simultaneous tuple assignment advances
the window by one step. Because the loop runs exactly n times, the n = 0 and n = 1 cases need no
special handling.
"""
def fibonacci(n):
    out = []
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(a)
        a, b = b, a + b
    return out
fibonacci-sequence.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Two variables hold the current and next Fibonacci numbers. Simultaneous tuple assignment advances
the window by one step. Because the loop runs exactly n times, the n = 0 and n = 1 cases need no
special handling.
hints: Keep two variables `a, b = 0, 1`.
Each iteration: append `a`, then `a, b = b, a + b`.
Loop exactly `n` times with `for _ in range(n)`; `range(n)` is empty when n ≤ 0, so no special case is needed.

Avoid recursion; an O(n) loop finishes instantly.
A negative n should give an empty list; `range(n)` already does this.

standard-library.article:
# Importing the Standard Library

## Intuition
Python ships with a large **standard library**: modules of tested code for maths, randomness,
counting, queues and combinations. Importing a module is like taking a toolbox off the shelf.
You already know how to write many of these tools as loops; now you can choose the shorter,
well-tested version and know what it does for you.

## Precise explanation
```python
import math                       # use as math.sqrt(...)
from collections import Counter   # use the name directly: Counter(...)
import itertools as it            # an alias: it.combinations(...)
```
* `import` runs the module once and binds its name. `dir(math)` lists what it contains and
  `help(math.ceil)` shows documentation.
* Avoid `from math import *`: it hides where names come from.

| Module / function | What it gives you | The loop it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `math.sqrt`, `math.hypot`, `math.ceil`, `math.pi` | exact, fast numeric functions | `x ** 0.5`, `-(-a // b)` |
| `random.Random(seed)` | an independent random generator with its own seed | — |
| `collections.Counter(text)` | counts of each item; `.most_common()` | a dict of counts (PY-13) |
| `collections.defaultdict(list)` | a dict that creates missing values | `d.setdefault(k, [])` |
| `collections.deque` | a queue with fast `append` and `popleft` | `list.pop(0)` (slow) |
| `heapq.nsmallest(k, nums)` | the k smallest items without sorting everything | `sorted(nums)[:k]` |
| `itertools.combinations(items, 2)` | every unordered pair, in order | two nested `for` loops |

**Reproducible randomness.** `rng = random.Random(42)` creates a generator; calling
`rng.random()` gives floats in `[0, 1)` and the sequence is the same every time for the same seed.
Python documents that `random()` output is reproducible across versions; other methods such as
`randint` may change between versions, so graded tasks build integers from `random()`:
`int(rng.random() * 6) + 1` is a die roll from 1 to 6.

## Worked example
```python
from collections import Counter
Counter("banana").most_common(1)      # [('a', 3)]
import heapq
heapq.nsmallest(2, [5, 1, 4, 1])      # [1, 1]
import itertools
list(itertools.combinations("abc", 2))  # [('a','b'), ('a','c'), ('b','c')]
```

## Common mistakes
* Naming your own file `random.py` or `math.py`: `import random` then imports *your* file.
* Using the global `random.random()` in code that must be reproducible; create `Random(seed)`.
* Expecting `Counter.most_common` to break ties alphabetically — it keeps first-seen order, so
  sort yourself when ties must be deterministic.
* Forgetting that `itertools.combinations` returns an iterator; wrap it in `list(...)`.

## Why this matters
Later topics use `collections.Counter` for word counts, `deque` for breadth-first search,
`heapq` for planners and top-k results, and `itertools` for Shapley value subsets.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: Modules](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/modules.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S045`)
- [The Python Tutorial: Brief Tour of the Standard Library](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/stdlib.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S047`)
- [math — Mathematical functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S050`)
- [collections — Container datatypes](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S051`)
- [heapq — Heap queue algorithm](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S052`)
- [itertools — Functions creating iterators for efficient looping](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S053`)
- [random — Generate pseudo-random numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S004`)
standard-library.statement:
## Task

Implement six small functions, each using the named module:

1. `hypotenuse(a, b)` → length of the hypotenuse, using `math.hypot` (or `math.sqrt`).
2. `pages_needed(items, per_page)` → how many pages are needed to show `items` items,
   using `math.ceil`. `pages_needed(0, 10) == 0`.
3. `most_common_letter(text)` → the most frequent **letter** (case-insensitive, ignore
   non-letters, use `collections.Counter`); break ties by alphabetical order; return `None` if
   there are no letters.
4. `dice_rolls(seed, n)` → a list of `n` die rolls from `rng = random.Random(seed)`, each
   `int(rng.random() * 6) + 1`.
5. `smallest_k(nums, k)` → the `k` smallest numbers in ascending order, using `heapq.nsmallest`.
6. `all_pairs(items)` → a list of all unordered pairs (as tuples) in input order, using
   `itertools.combinations`.

**Examples**
```python
hypotenuse(3, 4)                 # 5.0
pages_needed(21, 10)             # 3
most_common_letter("Hello, World")  # 'l'
smallest_k([5, 1, 4, 1], 2)      # [1, 1]
all_pairs(["a", "b", "c"])       # [('a', 'b'), ('a', 'c'), ('b', 'c')]
```
standard-library.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each function delegates the core work to a standard-library tool: `math.hypot` and `math.ceil`
for numerics, `Counter` for counting (with an explicit alphabetical tie-break, which
`most_common` does not provide), a seeded `random.Random` for reproducible rolls, `heapq` for a
partial sort and `itertools.combinations` for pairs.
hints: `math.ceil(items / per_page)` rounds up; `Counter(ch for ch in text.lower() if ch.isalpha())` counts letters.
For ties, find the highest count, then return `min` of the letters that have it.
`[int(rng.random() * 6) + 1 for _ in range(n)]`, `heapq.nsmallest(k, nums)`, `list(itertools.combinations(items, 2))`.

failureFeedback.advice: Use `math.ceil(items / per_page)`; integer `//` rounds down.
Lowercase first, keep only `ch.isalpha()`, break ties with `min`, and return None when nothing is left.
Create `random.Random(seed)` inside the function and use only `rng.random()`.
`heapq.nsmallest(k, nums)` already returns ascending order.
Convert the combinations iterator to a list of tuples.

Use a set for fast membership
Preserve first-occurrence order
unique-words.article:
# Sets, Order and Normalisation

## Intuition
A **set** remembers *whether* you have seen something, not *when*. To list unique words in the
order they first appeared, combine a set (fast "seen?" checks) with a list (keeps order).

## Precise explanation
* `set()` stores unique hashable items; `x in s` is on average O(1).
* Converting a list to a set loses order: `list(set(words))` may come back in any order.
* Pattern:
```python
seen, out = set(), []
for w in words:
    if w not in seen:
        seen.add(w)
        out.append(w)
```
* Normalisation: two tokens should count as the same word if they differ only in case or in
  surrounding punctuation. `w.strip(string.punctuation).lower()` removes punctuation from both
  ends only (so the apostrophe in "don't" survives).
* `str.split()` with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty strings.

## Worked example
`"The cat saw the CAT, then the dog."` → split → `The, cat, saw, the, CAT,, then, the, dog.` →
normalise → `the, cat, saw, the, cat, then, the, dog` → unique in order →
`['the', 'cat', 'saw', 'then', 'dog']`.

## Common mistakes
* `sorted(set(words))` — alphabetical, not first-occurrence order.
* `split(" ")` — produces empty strings for double spaces.
* Stripping *all* punctuation characters with `replace`, which turns "don't" into "dont".
* Keeping tokens that become empty after stripping (e.g. a lone "—").

## Why this matters
Building a vocabulary (word → index) for NLP models is exactly this operation; the order
determines each word's index, so it must be deterministic.

## Library implementation

Since Python 3.7 dictionaries keep insertion order, so `list(dict.fromkeys(words))` removes
duplicates while keeping first occurrences — a common one-line idiom once the words are
normalised. The set-plus-list loop makes the idea explicit; the test checks both agree.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
unique-words.statement:
## Task

Write `unique_words(sentence)` that returns the list of distinct words in order of first
appearance.

**Rules**
1. Split on whitespace with `str.split()`.
2. Normalise each token: strip characters in `string.punctuation` from both ends, then lowercase.
3. Discard tokens that are empty after stripping.
4. Keep the first occurrence of each normalised word.

**Constraints:** `len(sentence)` ≤ 10⁵.

**Examples**
```python
unique_words("The cat saw the CAT, then the dog.")
# ['the', 'cat', 'saw', 'then', 'dog']
unique_words("Don't stop -- don't!")
# ["don't", 'stop']   — inner apostrophe kept; '--' becomes empty and is dropped
```
unique-words.starter:

def unique_words(sentence):
    """Return distinct normalised words in first-occurrence order."""
    # TODO
    return []
unique-words.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-16 Unique Words in Order.

Each token is normalised by stripping punctuation from its ends and lowercasing. The set gives
constant-time duplicate checks while the list records first-occurrence order. Empty tokens
(pure punctuation) are skipped by the `if word` condition.
"""
import string


def unique_words(sentence):
    seen = set()
    out = []
    for token in sentence.split():
        word = token.strip(string.punctuation).lower()
        if word and word not in seen:
            seen.add(word)
            out.append(word)
    return out
unique-words.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each token is normalised by stripping punctuation from its ends and lowercasing. The set gives
constant-time duplicate checks while the list records first-occurrence order. Empty tokens
(pure punctuation) are skipped by the `if word` condition.
hints: `token.strip(string.punctuation).lower()` normalises one token.
Skip a token if it is empty after normalising.
Use a `seen` set alongside an output list to keep order.

failureFeedback.advice: Don't sort; keep first-occurrence order.
Strip punctuation only from the ends (str.strip), and drop empty tokens.
Use `split()` with no argument to handle tabs/newlines/multiple spaces.
Tokens that are empty after stripping must not be added.

functions-as-values.article:
# Functions as Values

## Intuition
In Python a function is a value like a number or a list. You can store it in a variable, pass
it to another function ("sort these words *using this rule*"), or build a new function from old
ones. This is how sorting keys, callbacks, tool registries and decorators work.

## Precise explanation
**Passing and returning functions**
```python
def apply_twice(f, x):
    return f(f(x))

def make_adder(n):
    def add(x):          # a nested function "remembers" n: a closure
        return x + n
    return add

apply_twice(make_adder(3), 10)   # 16
```
**lambda** creates a small unnamed function from one expression:
`square = lambda x: x * x`. It is most useful as a `key`:
`sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w))` sorts by length, then alphabetically.

**Flexible parameters**
```python
def report(name, *scores, sep=", ", **extra):
    # scores is a tuple of extra positional arguments
    # sep is keyword-only because it comes after *scores
    # extra is a dict of extra keyword arguments
```
`report("ada", 90, 85, sep="/", club="ai")` → `scores == (90, 85)`,
`extra == {"club": "ai"}`. Calling with `*list` or `**dict` unpacks them into arguments.

**Decorators** wrap a function to add behaviour. `@count_calls` above `def f` means
`f = count_calls(f)`.
```python
import functools

def count_calls(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)        # keep func's name and docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        wrapper.calls += 1
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    wrapper.calls = 0
    return wrapper
```

## Worked example
`pipeline(str.strip, str.lower)("  Hi ")` applies `strip` then `lower` → `"hi"`.

## Common mistakes
* Calling instead of passing: `sorted(words, key=len())` is an error; pass `len`.
* Mutable default arguments: `def f(x, seen=[])` shares one list across calls.
* Forgetting to `return` the wrapper (or the wrapped function's result) in a decorator.
* Putting a keyword-only parameter before `*args` and expecting it to collect a positional value.

## Why this matters
`key=` functions sort model results, callbacks drive training loops, and agent tool registries
(AG-01) register Python functions with a decorator and call them with `**arguments`.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial: More Control Flow Tools](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S042`)
- [Built-in Functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S048`)
- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
functions-as-values.statement:
## Task

Implement:

1. `pipeline(*funcs)` → returns a new function `run(x)` that applies each function in `funcs` in
   order and returns the final value. With no functions, `run(x)` returns `x`.
2. `sort_words(words)` → a new list sorted by length, then alphabetically (use `sorted` with a
   `lambda` key).
3. `format_record(name, *scores, sep=", ", **extra)` → a string:
   `"<name>: <scores joined by sep>"`, followed — if `extra` is not empty — by `" | "` and the
   extra items as `key=value`, sorted by key and joined by `", "`.
   With no scores the part after the colon is empty: `"ada: "`.
4. `count_calls(func)` → a decorator. The returned wrapper calls `func` with the same
   arguments, returns its result, has an attribute `calls` counting how many times it was
   called, and keeps `func`'s `__name__` (use `functools.wraps`).

**Examples**
```python
pipeline(str.strip, str.upper)("  hi ")             # 'HI'
sort_words(["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi"])        # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'pear', 'apple']
format_record("ada", 90, 85)                       # 'ada: 90, 85'
format_record("bob", 70, sep="/", year=2, club="ai")  # 'bob: 70 | club=ai, year=2'
```
functions-as-values.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

`pipeline` returns a closure that remembers `funcs`. The sort key is a tuple, so ties in length
fall back to alphabetical order. `format_record` treats `*scores` as a tuple and `**extra` as a
dict, sorting the latter so the output is deterministic. The decorator stores its counter on the
wrapper itself and forwards every argument with `*args, **kwargs`.
hints: Inside `run`, loop `for f in funcs: x = f(x)`, then return x.
`key=lambda w: (len(w), w)`; build the score text with `sep.join(str(s) for s in scores)`.
For extras: `", ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(extra.items()))`. For the decorator, copy the pattern from the lesson.

failureFeedback.advice: Apply the functions left to right, feeding each result into the next.
Use `sorted` (it returns a new list) with a tuple key `(len(w), w)`.
Sort `extra.items()` by key and join scores with the given `sep`.
Initialise `wrapper.calls = 0` and increment it inside the wrapper; return func's result.
Decorate the wrapper with `@functools.wraps(func)`.

gradebook-aggregate.title: Gradebook Aggregation
objectives: Group records with dict.setdefault / defaultdict
Sort with a key function and tie-breaking

gradebook-aggregate.article:
# Grouping and Sorting Records

## Intuition
Given a pile of (student, score) slips, you sort them into one stack per student, compute each
stack's average, then rank students. That is **group → aggregate → sort**, the same recipe as
SQL `GROUP BY` and pandas `groupby` (PD-08).

## Precise explanation
**Grouping** with a dict of lists:
```python
groups = {}
for name, score in records:
    groups.setdefault(name, []).append(score)
```
`setdefault(key, default)` returns the existing value or inserts `default` first.
`collections.defaultdict(list)` does the same automatically.

**Sorting with a key**: `sorted(items, key=f)` sorts by `f(item)`. To sort by average
descending and break ties by name ascending, use a tuple key with a negated number:
```python
sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))
```
Tuples compare element by element, so the name is consulted only when averages are equal.

**Rounding**: `round(x, 2)` rounds to 2 decimals (using round-half-to-even on the exact binary
value). Round only for the final output, never in intermediate steps.

## Worked example
records = [("ann", 90), ("bob", 70), ("ann", 80), ("cy", 85)]
groups: ann → [90, 80], bob → [70], cy → [85]; averages 85.0, 70.0, 85.0.
Sorted: (-85, "ann"), (-85, "cy"), (-70, "bob") → ann, cy, bob.

## Common mistakes
* `sorted(..., reverse=True)` with a tuple key reverses the name tie-break too.
* Rounding each score before averaging.
* Overwriting `groups[name] = [score]` instead of appending.

## Why this matters
Grouped statistics drive per-class metrics, per-client summaries in federated learning and
leaderboards; deterministic tie-breaking keeps outputs reproducible.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
gradebook-aggregate.statement:
## Task

Write `gradebook(records)` where `records` is a list of `(name, score)` tuples.

Return a list of `(name, average, count)` tuples:
* `average` = mean score rounded to 2 decimals (`round(x, 2)`), `count` = number of scores;
* sorted by average **descending**, ties broken by name **ascending**.

Ignore records whose score is not in `[0, 100]` (they do not count).

**Constraints:** ≤ 10⁵ records; names are non-empty strings; scores are ints/floats.

**Examples**
```python
gradebook([("ann", 90), ("bob", 70), ("ann", 80), ("cy", 85)])
# [('ann', 85.0, 2), ('cy', 85.0, 1), ('bob', 70.0, 1)]  — tie on 85 broken by name
gradebook([("x", 101), ("x", 50)])
# [('x', 50.0, 1)]  — 101 is out of range and ignored
```
gradebook-aggregate.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Invalid scores are filtered while grouping, so names that only have invalid scores never appear.
Averages are computed from raw scores and rounded once. The tuple sort key `(-average, name)`
gives descending averages with ascending-name tie-breaks in a single stable sort.
hints: Skip a record unless `0 <= score <= 100`.
`groups.setdefault(name, []).append(score)` groups scores.

factorial-validated.title: Validated Factorial
objectives: Raise exceptions for invalid input
Use isinstance checks correctly
Compute a product iteratively
factorial-validated.article:
# Validating Input and Raising Exceptions

## Intuition
A function has a *contract*: what it accepts and what it promises to return. When a caller
breaks the contract (e.g. asks for the factorial of −3), the function should fail **loudly**
with a clear error rather than return a wrong answer silently.

## Precise explanation
The factorial of a non-negative integer $n$ is $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdots n$, with $0! = 1$ (the
empty product).

```python
result = 1
for k in range(2, n + 1):
    result *= k
```
Python integers have arbitrary precision, so `factorial(50)` is exact.

**Raising exceptions**
* `TypeError` — the argument has the wrong *type* (e.g. `2.5`, `"5"`).
* `ValueError` — right type, unacceptable *value* (e.g. `-3`).
```python
if not isinstance(n, int) or isinstance(n, bool):
    raise TypeError("n must be an int")
if n < 0:
    raise ValueError("n must be >= 0")
```
`bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python (`True == 1`), so it must be excluded explicitly if you
want to reject it.

## Worked example
`factorial(5)`: result 1 → ×2 = 2 → ×3 = 6 → ×4 = 24 → ×5 = 120.

## Common mistakes
* Returning `-1` or `None` for bad input — the caller may not notice.
* `range(1, n)` — stops at n−1 (off-by-one).
* Recursion without a base case for 0 → infinite recursion.
* Accepting `5.0` because `5.0 == 5`; the contract asks for an `int`.

## Why this matters
ML code fails in confusing ways deep inside a pipeline when inputs are invalid. Early, specific
exceptions turn a mysterious NaN three steps later into an obvious message. Factorials also
power combinatorics (binomial coefficients, MA-07).

## Library implementation

`math.factorial(n)` computes the same value (and also raises `ValueError` for negative
numbers and `TypeError` for floats). It is implemented in C and uses a faster
divide-and-conquer product for large `n`, but the result is identical.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
factorial-validated.statement:
## Task

Write `factorial(n)`.

**Requirements**
* Return $n!$ as an `int` for integers $n \ge 0$ (with $0! = 1$). Use a loop, not `math.factorial`.
* Raise `TypeError` if `n` is not an `int`, or is a `bool`.
* Raise `ValueError` if `n < 0`.

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ n ≤ 1000 for valid input.

**Examples**
```python
factorial(5)     # 120
factorial(0)     # 1      — empty product
factorial(-2)    # raises ValueError
factorial(3.0)   # raises TypeError — floats are rejected even if whole
```

factorial-validated.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-19 Validated Factorial.

Type validation comes before value validation so that comparing `n < 0` is never attempted on,
say, a string. `bool` is rejected explicitly because it is a subclass of `int`. The loop starts
at 2 because multiplying by 1 changes nothing; for n = 0 or 1 the loop body never runs and the
empty product 1 is returned.
"""
def factorial(n):
    if isinstance(n, bool) or not isinstance(n, int):
        raise TypeError("n must be an int")
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be non-negative")
    result = 1
    for k in range(2, n + 1):
        result *= k
    return result

matrix-transpose.title: Matrix Transpose with Validation

Validate rectangular shape
Reason about rows and columns by index
matrix-transpose.article:
# Nested Lists and the Transpose

## Intuition
A matrix stored as a list of rows is like a spreadsheet. The **transpose** flips it over its
diagonal: rows become columns. Row 0 of the result is column 0 of the original.

## Precise explanation
For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the transpose $A^\top$ is $n \times m$ with
$(A^\top)_{ji} = A_{ij}$.

As a nested comprehension (outer loop over output rows = input columns):
```python
[[matrix[i][j] for i in range(m)] for j in range(n)]
```
Equivalently with `zip`: `[list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)]`. `zip(*matrix)` unpacks the rows
as separate arguments and groups the i-th elements together. **Warning:** `zip` silently stops
at the shortest row, so it hides ragged input — validate first.

A matrix is **rectangular** when every row has the same length. A "ragged" list of lists is not a
matrix.

Edge cases: an empty matrix `[]` transposes to `[]`. A matrix of empty rows `[[], []]` has
shape 2×0; its transpose is 0×2, which as a list of rows is `[]`.

## Worked example
```
[[1, 2, 3],        [[1, 4],
 [4, 5, 6]]   →     [2, 5],
                    [3, 6]]
```
Shape (2, 3) → (3, 2).

## Common mistakes
* Swapping loop order in the comprehension, which returns a copy instead of the transpose.
* `[[0]*m]*n` to pre-allocate — every row is the **same** list object; writing one cell changes
  all rows.
* Mutating the input in place.

## Why this matters
Transposes are everywhere in ML: $X^\top X$ in least squares (ML-09), switching between
"samples × features" and "features × samples", attention's $QK^\top$ (LM-07). Shape validation
is the habit that prevents silent broadcasting bugs in NumPy.

## Library implementation

The idiomatic transpose of a rectangular list of lists is `[list(row) for row in zip(*matrix)]`:
`zip(*matrix)` passes every row as a separate argument and yields one tuple per column. It does
not validate ragged input (it silently stops at the shortest row), which is why the exercise asks
for explicit checks. In NP-01 and later, NumPy's `array.T` does the same for arrays.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
- [Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/) — Marc Peter Deisenroth, A. Aldo Faisal, Cheng Soon Ong (Cambridge University Press) (`S009`)
matrix-transpose.statement:
## Task

Write `transpose(matrix)` for a list of lists of numbers.

**Requirements**
* Return a new list of lists equal to the transpose. Do not modify the input.
* If rows have different lengths, raise `ValueError("ragged matrix")`.
* `[]` and any matrix whose rows are all empty return `[]`.
* Do not use NumPy.

**Constraints:** up to 500×500.

**Examples**
```python
transpose([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])   # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
transpose([[7]])                    # [[7]]
transpose([[1, 2], [3]])            # raises ValueError — ragged
```

    # TODO: validate row lengths, then build the transpose

matrix-transpose.solution:
r"""Reference solution for PY-20 Matrix Transpose with Validation.

Validation runs first so the comprehension can assume a rectangle. The outer comprehension loops
over column indices of the input (rows of the output), the inner one collects that column from
every row. When rows are empty, `n == 0` and the result is `[]`, which correctly represents a
0-row matrix. New lists are built, so the input is untouched.
"""
def transpose(matrix):
    if not matrix:
        return []
    n = len(matrix[0])
    for row in matrix:
        if len(row) != n:
            raise ValueError("ragged matrix")
    return [[row[j] for row in matrix] for j in range(n)]

safe-divide.title: Safe Division with Exceptions
objectives: Catch specific exceptions with try/except
Distinguish recoverable and unrecoverable errors
Process a batch while recording failures
safe-divide.article:
# Handling Exceptions Deliberately

## Intuition
Some errors are expected and recoverable (dividing by zero in a ratio where "undefined" is a
fine answer); others signal a bug (passing a string where a number belongs). Good code catches
the first kind *specifically* and lets the second kind surface.

## Precise explanation
```python
try:
    result = a / b
except ZeroDivisionError:
    result = None
```
* Code in `try` runs; if an exception is raised, Python looks for a matching `except`.
* Catch the **narrowest** exception you can handle. A bare `except:` or `except Exception:`
  also swallows typos (`NameError`) and type bugs, hiding real problems.
* `else:` runs only if no exception occurred; `finally:` always runs.
* Division by zero: `1 / 0` raises `ZeroDivisionError`, and so does `1.0 / 0.0` in plain Python
  (NumPy instead returns `inf` with a warning).

**Batch processing pattern:** process each item, store the result or a marker, and keep a list
of the indices that failed — one bad record should not abort a whole dataset.

## Worked example
`divide_pairs([(6, 3), (1, 0), (5, 2)])` → results `[2.0, None, 2.5]`, failed indices `[1]`.

## Common mistakes
* `except:` with no type → hides `TypeError` from `safe_divide("6", 3)`.
* Checking `if b == 0` only — fine for numbers, but the exercise asks you to practise exceptions.
* Returning the error message string as the result, mixing types in the output list.

## Why this matters
Data loaders, tool-calling agents (AG-15) and federated clients that drop out (FL topics) all
need the same skill: recover from expected failures, record them, continue.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
safe-divide.statement:
## Task

Implement two functions.

1. `safe_divide(a, b)` → `a / b` as a float, or `None` if `b` is zero. Catch **only**
   `ZeroDivisionError`; any other error (e.g. `TypeError` for strings) must propagate.
2. `divide_pairs(pairs)` → `(results, failed)` where `results[i] = safe_divide(*pairs[i])` and
   `failed` is the sorted list of indices whose result is `None`.

**Constraints:** numbers are ints or floats; `len(pairs)` ≤ 10⁵.

**Examples**
```python
safe_divide(7, 2)          # 3.5
safe_divide(1, 0)          # None
safe_divide("6", 3)        # raises TypeError (not caught)
divide_pairs([(6, 3), (1, 0), (5, 2)])   # ([2.0, None, 2.5], [1])
```

guessing-game-feedback.title: Guessing Game Feedback

Model game state deterministically
Validate inputs and limits
guessing-game-feedback.article:
# Deterministic Game Loops

## Intuition
An interactive guessing game ("too low", "too high", "correct!") is really a loop over guesses
with a stopping condition. If we pass the guesses in as a list instead of calling `input()`, the
game becomes **deterministic** and testable — the same idea used to test agents with scripted
model outputs (AG-06).

## Precise explanation
* Loop over guesses; compare each to the target; produce one feedback string per guess.
* **Early termination:** `break` leaves the loop as soon as the guess is correct; later guesses
  are ignored.
* **Attempt limit:** stop after `max_attempts` guesses even if not solved.
* The final status depends on *how* the loop ended. Python's `for ... else` runs the `else`
  block only if the loop was **not** broken — handy, but a boolean flag is often clearer.

State summary returned as a dict:
```python
{"feedback": [...], "attempts": k, "won": True/False}
```

## Worked example
target = 42, guesses = [50, 25, 42, 10]:
50 → "too high", 25 → "too low", 42 → "correct" → stop. attempts = 3, won = True;
the guess 10 is never examined.

## Common mistakes
* Forgetting to `break`, so guesses after the correct one add feedback.
* Counting attempts with `len(guesses)` instead of guesses actually used.
* Off-by-one with the attempt limit (`>` vs `>=`).
* Using `input()` — untestable and blocks automated runners.

## Why this matters
Every agent, simulator and RL environment is a loop of "observe, act, check if done, stop at a
step budget". This is the smallest version of that loop.

## References

- [The Python Tutorial (Python 3.15.1 docs)](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) — Python Software Foundation (`S001`)
guessing-game-feedback.statement:
## Task

Write `guess_feedback(target, guesses, max_attempts=7)` returning a dict
`{"feedback": list[str], "attempts": int, "won": bool}`.

**Rules**
* Process guesses in order, at most `max_attempts` of them.
* For each processed guess append `"too low"`, `"too high"` or `"correct"`.
* Stop immediately after `"correct"`.
* `attempts` = number of guesses processed; `won` = whether `"correct"` occurred.
* Raise `ValueError` if `max_attempts < 1`.

**Constraints:** ints; `len(guesses)` ≤ 1000.

**Examples**
```python
guess_feedback(42, [50, 25, 42, 10])
# {'feedback': ['too high', 'too low', 'correct'], 'attempts': 3, 'won': True}
guess_feedback(5, [1, 2, 3], max_attempts=2)
# {'feedback': ['too low', 'too low'], 'attempts': 2, 'won': False}   — limit reached
```
guessing-game-feedback.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Slicing `guesses[:max_attempts]` enforces the attempt budget up front. Each guess produces one
feedback string; on a correct guess the flag is set and the loop breaks, so later guesses are
never processed. Because exactly one string is appended per processed guess, `attempts` is just
the length of the feedback list.
hints: Loop over `guesses[:max_attempts]`.
Compare with `<`, `>`, `==` and append the right string.
Set `won = True` and `break` on a correct guess; attempts = len(feedback).

failureFeedback.advice: Stop the loop with `break` after a correct guess.
Check your attempt-limit comparison: max_attempts guesses are allowed, not max_attempts-1.
Only the first max_attempts guesses may be processed.
Validate max_attempts before looping.
