histogram-bins.article:
# Histograms

## Intuition
A histogram groups numbers into bins (intervals) and counts how many fall in each — a quick
picture of a distribution's shape: where it peaks, how wide it is, whether it is skewed.

## Precise explanation
With range $[\text{lo}, \text{hi}]$ and $k$ bins, width $w = (\text{hi}-\text{lo})/k$ and edges
$e_j = \text{lo} + j w$ for $j = 0..k$. Bin $j$ is the half-open interval $[e_j, e_{j+1})$,
**except the last bin, which is closed** $[e_{k-1}, e_k]$ so the maximum value is counted.
This is the same convention NumPy's `np.histogram` uses.

Index of value $x$: $j = \lfloor (x - \text{lo})/w \rfloor$, then clamp $j = k$ to $k-1$.
Values below lo or above hi are ignored.

If lo/hi are not given, use the data's min and max. If they are equal, the width is zero; a
common convention (used here) is to widen the range to $[\text{lo}-0.5, \text{hi}+0.5]$.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="280" height="150" viewBox="0 0 280 150" role="img" aria-label="Histogram with four bins of heights 2, 5, 3 and 1">
<title>Four-bin histogram</title>
<line x1="20" y1="130" x2="270" y2="130" stroke="#333"/>
<rect x="30" y="90" width="55" height="40" fill="#9ecae1" stroke="#3182bd"/>
<rect x="90" y="30" width="55" height="100" fill="#9ecae1" stroke="#3182bd"/>
<rect x="150" y="70" width="55" height="60" fill="#9ecae1" stroke="#3182bd"/>
<rect x="210" y="110" width="55" height="20" fill="#9ecae1" stroke="#3182bd"/>
<text x="52" y="85" font-size="12">2</text><text x="112" y="25" font-size="12">5</text><text x="172" y="65" font-size="12">3</text><text x="232" y="105" font-size="12">1</text>
</svg>

*Figure (original): counts per bin; the last bin includes its right edge.*

## Worked example
data `[1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, 2 bins over [1, 5]: width 2, edges [1, 3, 5].
Bin 0 = [1, 3): 1, 2, 2 → 3. Bin 1 = [3, 5]: 3, 4, 5 → 3.

## Common mistakes
* Dropping the maximum value because every bin is half-open.
* Floating-point edges such as 0.1 + 0.2; compute edges as `lo + j*w`.
* Too few/too many bins hiding the shape.

## Why this matters
Histograms are the first look at any feature, the basis of intensity histograms in images
(CV-09), and the binning used in calibration plots.

## Library implementation

`np.histogram(data, bins=k, range=(lo, hi))` uses the same rule: equal-width bins, each
half-open `[a, b)` except the last, which also includes `hi`; when `lo == hi` it widens the range
by 0.5 on each side, exactly as this exercise specifies. It returns `(counts, edges)` — the
opposite order to your function.

## References

- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
histogram-bins.statement:
## Task

Write `histogram(data, bins, lo=None, hi=None)` returning `(edges, counts)`.

* `edges` has `bins + 1` floats; `counts` has `bins` ints.
* Default `lo = min(data)`, `hi = max(data)`; if `lo == hi`, use `lo - 0.5` and `hi + 0.5`.
* Bins are `[e_j, e_{j+1})` except the last, which includes `hi`. Ignore values outside `[lo, hi]`.
* Raise `ValueError` if `bins < 1`, if `data` is empty and `lo`/`hi` are not both given, or if
  `lo > hi`.

**Examples**
```python
histogram([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)
# ([1.0, 3.0, 5.0], [3, 3])
histogram([0, 10, 11], 2, lo=0, hi=10)
# ([0.0, 5.0, 10.0], [1, 1])   — 11 is outside and ignored; 10 lands in the last bin
```

histogram-bins.solution:
r"""Reference solution for ST-04 Histogram with Equal-Width Bins.

Defaults and degenerate ranges are resolved before computing the width. Edges are computed by
multiplication (and the last edge pinned to hi to avoid rounding drift). Each in-range value's
bin index is the floor of its scaled position; the value equal to hi would land in a non-existent
bin `bins`, so it is clamped into the last, closed bin.
"""
def histogram(data, bins, lo=None, hi=None):
    if bins < 1:
        raise ValueError("bins must be >= 1")
    if lo is None or hi is None:
        if not data:
            raise ValueError("empty data needs explicit lo and hi")
        lo = min(data) if lo is None else lo
        hi = max(data) if hi is None else hi
    if lo > hi:
        raise ValueError("lo must be <= hi")
    if lo == hi:
        lo, hi = lo - 0.5, hi + 0.5
    lo, hi = float(lo), float(hi)
    w = (hi - lo) / bins
    edges = [lo + j * w for j in range(bins + 1)]
    edges[-1] = hi
    counts = [0] * bins
    for x in data:
        if x < lo or x > hi:
            continue
        j = int((x - lo) / w)
        if j >= bins:
            j = bins - 1
        counts[j] += 1
    return edges, counts

z-scores.article:
# z-scores

## Intuition
A z-score answers "how many standard deviations is this value from the mean?" It puts values on
a common, unit-free scale, so a test score and a height can be compared.

## Precise explanation
$$z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar x}{s}$$
where $s$ is the standard deviation (population by default here). Standardized data has mean 0
and standard deviation 1. If all values are equal, $s = 0$ and z-scores are undefined.

**Outlier rule of thumb:** flag values with $|z| > 3$ (or 2.5, 2…). It is a heuristic: in small
samples a single extreme value inflates $s$ and can hide itself (*masking*), which is why robust
alternatives use the median and IQR.

## Worked example
data `[2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]`: mean 5, sd 2 → z = `[-1.5, -0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0, 0, 1, 2]`.

## Common mistakes
* Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation.
* Using the sample sd in one place and the population sd elsewhere.
* Not guarding against zero standard deviation.

## Why this matters
Standardization is the default preprocessing for gradient-based models and distance-based models
(k-NN, k-means) so that no feature dominates just because of its units.

## References

- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
z-scores.statement:
## Task

  Raise `ValueError` for empty data or zero standard deviation.
* `outliers(data, threshold=3.0)` → sorted list of **indices** whose population z-score has
  `abs(z) > threshold`.

**Examples**
```python
z_scores([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])   # [-1.5, -0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
outliers([10, 11, 9, 10, 50], threshold=1.5)   # [4]
```

z-scores.solution:
r"""Reference solution for ST-05 Standardize to z-scores.

The mean and standard deviation are computed once and every value is shifted and scaled. A zero
spread makes standardization meaningless, so it is rejected. `outliers` reuses `z_scores` and
returns indices so the caller can locate the original records.
"""
import math


def z_scores(data, sample=False):
    n = len(data)
    if n == 0 or (sample and n < 2):
        raise ValueError("not enough data")
    m = sum(data) / n
    var = sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in data) / (n - 1 if sample else n)
    sd = math.sqrt(var)
    if sd == 0:
        raise ValueError("standard deviation is zero")
    return [(x - m) / sd for x in data]


def outliers(data, threshold=3.0):
    return [i for i, z in enumerate(z_scores(data)) if abs(z) > threshold]

Compute exact probabilities with fractions.Fraction

Test two events for independence
probability-basics.article:
# Probability by Counting Outcomes

## Intuition
Roll two fair dice. There are 36 equally likely outcomes. The probability of an event such as
"the total is 7" is simply the fraction of outcomes in which it happens: 6 of 36, so 1/6.
When outcomes are equally likely, probability is counting.

## Precise explanation
* **Sample space** $\Omega$: the list of all outcomes, e.g. pairs `(d1, d2)`.
* **Event**: a set of outcomes — in code, a predicate function `lambda o: o[0] + o[1] == 7`.
* With equally likely outcomes, $P(A) = \dfrac{|A|}{|\Omega|}$.
* **Complement**: $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$.
* **Union** (inclusion–exclusion): $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ — outcomes in both
  would otherwise be counted twice.
* **Independence**: $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$.

`fractions.Fraction(6, 36)` stores the exact value `Fraction(1, 6)`, so equality tests like
independence are exact; with floats, `0.1 * 3 == 0.3` is False.

## Worked example
$A$ = "first die is even" (18 outcomes), $B$ = "total is 7" (6 outcomes),
$A \cap B$ = {(2,5), (4,3), (6,1)} (3 outcomes). $P(A)P(B) = \frac12 \cdot \frac16 = \frac1{12}
= \frac{3}{36} = P(A \cap B)$, so they are independent. $P(A \cup B) = \frac{18 + 6 - 3}{36} = \frac{21}{36}$.

## Common mistakes
* Assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (the *totals* 2..12 are not).
* Adding $P(A) + P(B)$ for overlapping events.
* Confusing independent with mutually exclusive: exclusive events with non-zero probability are
  never independent.

## Why this matters
Probability is the language of classification ("70% spam"), of ST-07 and Naive
Bayes, and of every simulation in this topic.

## Library implementation

The nested comprehension in `two_dice` is what `itertools.product(range(1, 7), repeat=2)`
generates, and `Fraction` is the standard library's exact rational type. There is no library
function for "probability of a predicate" — counting is the method. The test below confirms
the `itertools` version gives the same space.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [fractions — Rational numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/fractions.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S058`)
probability-basics.statement:
## Task

Implement:

1. `two_dice()` → list of all 36 outcomes `(d1, d2)` with `d1, d2` in 1..6, ordered by `d1`
   then `d2`.
2. `probability(space, event)` → `Fraction` of outcomes where `event(outcome)` is true. Raise
   `ValueError` for an empty space.
3. `complement(space, event)` → probability that the event does **not** happen.
4. `union(space, a, b)` → $P(A \cup B)$ computed by inclusion–exclusion (call `probability`
   three times).
5. `independent(space, a, b)` → `True` if $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$ exactly.

**Examples**
```python
space = two_dice()
probability(space, lambda o: sum(o) == 7)          # Fraction(1, 6)
union(space, lambda o: o[0] == 6, lambda o: o[1] == 6)   # Fraction(11, 36)
independent(space, lambda o: o[0] % 2 == 0, lambda o: sum(o) == 7)   # True
```

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Events are predicates, so intersections are built by combining predicates with `and`. Every
probability is an exact `Fraction`, which makes the independence test an exact equality, and the
union follows the inclusion–exclusion formula rather than counting directly.
hints: `[(d1, d2) for d1 in range(1, 7) for d2 in range(1, 7)]` builds the space in the right order.
`Fraction(sum(1 for o in space if event(o)), len(space))` is the probability.
The intersection event is `lambda o: a(o) and b(o)`.

Return `Fraction(count, len(space))`, not a float.
Subtract the probability of both events, which inclusion–exclusion counts twice.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A) * P(B) using Fractions.
Raise ValueError when the sample space is empty.

conditional-bayes.entryPoint: conditional(space, a, b); posterior(prior, sensitivity, false_positive_rate); update(prior, sensitivity, false_positive_rate, results)
objectives: Compute P(A | B) by restricting the sample space

conditional-bayes.article:
# Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule

## Intuition
Knowing something changes the odds. Among two-dice rolls, $P(\text{total} = 8)$ is 5/36, but if
you are told the first die shows 6, only the 6 outcomes starting with 6 remain and one of them
totals 8: the probability becomes 1/6. Conditioning means *shrinking the sample space* to the
outcomes consistent with what you know.

## Precise explanation
$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) > 0.$$
**Bayes' rule** reverses a conditional:
$$P(D \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+)}, \qquad
  P(+) = P(+ \mid D)P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)P(\neg D).$$
For a medical test: $P(D)$ is the **prior** (how common the disease is), $P(+ \mid D)$ the
**sensitivity**, $P(+ \mid \neg D)$ the **false-positive rate**, and $P(D \mid +)$ the
**posterior**. For a negative result use $P(- \mid D) = 1 - \text{sensitivity}$ and
$P(- \mid \neg D) = 1 - \text{false-positive rate}$.

**Sequential updating**: after one result, the posterior becomes the prior for the next
(assuming results are independent given the true state).

## Worked example
Prior 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 5%:
$P(+) = 0.9 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99 = 0.0585$, so $P(D \mid +) = 0.009 / 0.0585 \approx 0.154$.
A positive test raises the probability from 1% to only about 15% because healthy people vastly
outnumber sick ones — the **base-rate effect**.

## Common mistakes
* Confusing $P(+ \mid D)$ (90%) with $P(D \mid +)$ (15%).
* Forgetting the false positives in the denominator.
* Dividing by $P(B) = 0$.

## Why this matters
Naive Bayes text classification (NL-14) is Bayes' rule applied to words, and
reasoning about precision versus recall (ML-06) is reasoning about base rates.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
conditional-bayes.statement:
## Task

Implement:

1. `conditional(space, a, b)` → $P(A \mid B)$ as a `Fraction`, counting outcomes in a list of
   equally likely outcomes; raise `ValueError` if no outcome satisfies `b`.
2. `posterior(prior, sensitivity, false_positive_rate)` → $P(D \mid +)$ as a float.
3. `update(prior, sensitivity, false_positive_rate, results)` → the probability of $D$ after
   applying Bayes' rule once per result in `results` (a list of booleans: `True` = positive,
   `False` = negative), in order. An empty list returns the prior.

**Examples**
```python
dice = [(a, b) for a in range(1, 7) for b in range(1, 7)]
conditional(dice, lambda o: sum(o) == 8, lambda o: o[0] == 6)   # Fraction(1, 6)
posterior(0.01, 0.9, 0.05)                                     # ≈ 0.1538
update(0.01, 0.9, 0.05, [True, True])                          # ≈ 0.7660
```
conditional-bayes.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Conditioning keeps only the outcomes where `b` holds and counts `a` among them, which equals
$P(A\cap B)/P(B)$. The posterior divides the true-positive mass by all positive mass. `update`
reuses the same formula with likelihoods chosen by each result, feeding each posterior forward as
the next prior.
hints: Count outcomes where `b` holds, and among those where `a` also holds; divide.
`evidence = sensitivity * prior + false_positive_rate * (1 - prior)`; posterior = numerator / evidence.
For a negative result use `1 - sensitivity` and `1 - false_positive_rate` as the likelihoods.

failureFeedback.advice: Restrict to outcomes where `b` holds, then count `a` among them.
Raise ValueError when no outcome satisfies the condition.
The denominator must include false positives from the healthy group: `fpr * (1 - prior)`.
Use each posterior as the prior for the next result.
For a negative result the likelihoods are `1 - sensitivity` and `1 - false_positive_rate`.

binomial-pmf.article:
# The Binomial Distribution

## Intuition
Flip a biased coin $n$ times. The number of heads is random; the binomial distribution says how
likely each count is. Every count $k$ can happen in $\binom{n}{k}$ orders, each with the same
probability.

## Precise explanation
For $n$ independent trials with success probability $p$:
$$P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k},\qquad k = 0,\dots,n.$$
Cumulative: $P(X \le k) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} P(X=j)$. Tail: $P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k-1)$.
Mean $np$, variance $np(1-p)$. Values of $k$ outside $0..n$ have probability 0.

`math.comb(n, k)` gives the binomial coefficient (you implemented it in MA-07).
In Python `0 ** 0 == 1`, which correctly handles $p = 0$ or $p = 1$ at the boundaries.

## Worked example
$n = 4$, $p = 0.5$: $P(X=2) = 6 \cdot 0.5^4 = 0.375$.
$P(X \ge 3) = P(3) + P(4) = 4/16 + 1/16 = 0.3125$.

## Common mistakes
* Forgetting the $\binom{n}{k}$ factor (computing one specific sequence).
* Computing $P(X\ge k)$ as $1 - P(X \le k)$ (off by one).
* Not validating $0 \le p \le 1$.

## Why this matters
Accuracy on a test set of $n$ examples is a binomial proportion; A/B tests, dropout masks
(DL-21) and client participation (FL-08) are Bernoulli processes.

## Library implementation

`scipy.stats.binom(n, p)` provides `.pmf(k)`, `.cdf(k)` and `.sf(k - 1)` (the survival function,
$P(X \ge k)$), computed in a numerically careful way for large `n`. The comparison runs only when
SciPy is installed.

## References

- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
binomial-pmf.statement:

* `binom_cdf(k, n, p)` → $P(X \le k)$ (0.0 if `k < 0`, 1.0 if `k >= n`).
* `prob_at_least(k, n, p)` → $P(X \ge k)$.

Raise `ValueError` if `n < 0` or `p` is outside `[0, 1]`.

**Examples**
```python

prob_at_least(3, 4, 0.5)  # 0.3125
binom_cdf(10, 10, 0.3)    # 1.0
```

and the upper tail uses the complement rule with k − 1 because P(X ≥ k) excludes k − 1 and below.

normal-distribution.article:
# The Normal Distribution

## Intuition
Heights, measurement errors and averages of many small effects pile up in a symmetric bell
shape. The **normal distribution** $\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ describes that bell: $\mu$ is its
centre and $\sigma$ its width. Because it is continuous, we ask for the probability of an
*interval*, which is the area under the curve.

## Precise explanation
**Density (pdf)**
$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$
**Cumulative probability (cdf)**, using the error function `math.erf`:
$$F(x) = P(X \le x) = \tfrac12\left[1 + \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma\sqrt2}\right)\right].$$
* $P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$. A single point has probability 0; $f(x)$ is a density, not a
  probability, and can exceed 1 when $\sigma$ is small.
* Standardising with $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ (ST-05) turns any normal into $\mathcal N(0, 1)$.
* **68–95–99.7 rule**: about 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73% of the mass lies within 1, 2 and 3
  standard deviations of the mean.
* **Normal approximation to the binomial** (ST-08): for large $n$,
  $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ is close to $\mathcal N(np,\, np(1-p))$, and
  $P(X \le k) \approx F(k + 0.5)$ — the $+0.5$ **continuity correction** accounts for replacing
  bars at integers with a smooth curve.

## Worked example
$\mathcal N(170, 10^2)$: $P(X \le 180) = F(180) = \frac12[1 + \operatorname{erf}(1/\sqrt2)] \approx 0.8413$;
$P(160 \le X \le 180) \approx 0.8413 - 0.1587 = 0.6827$.

## Common mistakes
* Passing the variance where the standard deviation is expected.
* Treating $f(x)$ as $P(X = x)$.
* Forgetting the $\sqrt2$ inside the erf.

## Why this matters
Confidence intervals (ST-12), the t-test (ST-18), weight
initialisation and Gaussian noise for privacy all use the normal distribution.

## Library implementation

`statistics.NormalDist(mu, sigma)` provides `.pdf(x)`, `.cdf(x)` and `.inv_cdf(p)` (the
quantile function you will use for confidence intervals), plus arithmetic on independent normal
variables. `scipy.stats.norm` offers the same functions vectorised over arrays. The tests compare
your functions with `NormalDist`, and with SciPy if it is installed.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [statistics — Mathematical statistics functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S003`)
- [math — Mathematical functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S050`)
normal-distribution.statement:
## Task

Implement with `math` only:

1. `normal_pdf(x, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)` and 2. `normal_cdf(x, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)` from the formulas
   above; raise `ValueError` if `sigma <= 0`.
3. `prob_between(a, b, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)` → $F(b) - F(a)$ (raise `ValueError` if `b < a`).
4. `empirical_rule()` → `{1: p1, 2: p2, 3: p3}`, the probabilities of lying within 1, 2, 3
   standard deviations of the mean.
5. `binomial_cdf_approx(k, n, p)` → normal approximation of $P(X \le k)$ for
   $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ with the continuity correction.

**Examples**
```python
normal_cdf(0)                    # 0.5
prob_between(160, 180, 170, 10)  # ≈ 0.6827
empirical_rule()[2]              # ≈ 0.9545
binomial_cdf_approx(55, 100, 0.5)  # ≈ 0.8643
```
normal-distribution.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The density and cdf are direct translations of their formulas; the cdf relies on `math.erf`,
which the standard library computes accurately. Interval probabilities are differences of the
cdf, the empirical rule reuses that on the standard normal, and the binomial approximation plugs
the binomial mean and standard deviation into the normal cdf at $k + 0.5$.
hints: pdf: `math.exp(-((x - mu) ** 2) / (2 * sigma ** 2)) / (sigma * math.sqrt(2 * math.pi))`.
cdf: `0.5 * (1 + math.erf((x - mu) / (sigma * math.sqrt(2))))`.
The empirical rule is `prob_between(-k, k)` for k = 1, 2, 3.

failureFeedback.advice: Divide by `sigma * sqrt(2*pi)` and square `(x - mu)` inside the exponent.
Use `0.5 * (1 + math.erf((x - mu) / (sigma * math.sqrt(2))))`.
Return a dict keyed by 1, 2 and 3 with `prob_between(-k, k)`.
Raise ValueError when sigma <= 0.
Use mean n*p, standard deviation sqrt(n*p*(1-p)) and evaluate at k + 0.5.

dice-lln.article:
# Simulation and the Law of Large Numbers

## Intuition
The expected sum of two fair dice is 7. Roll them 10 times and the average may be 6.2 or 8.1;
roll them 100 000 times and it will be very close to 7. The **law of large numbers** says sample
averages settle down to the expected value as the sample grows.

## Precise explanation
For i.i.d. $X_i$ with mean $\mu$, the running mean $\bar X_n = \frac1n\sum_{i\le n} X_i$
converges to $\mu$. Its typical error shrinks like $\sigma/\sqrt n$: 100× more rolls ≈ 10× less
error.

**Reproducible randomness.** `random.Random(seed)` creates an independent generator. Python only
guarantees the sequence of `rng.random()` (floats in $[0, 1)$) across versions, so we derive die
faces from it:
$$\text{face} = \lfloor 6u \rfloor + 1,\quad u = \text{rng.random()}.$$
Since $0 \le u < 1$, faces are 1..6 with equal probability.

## Worked example
If the first four `rng.random()` values were 0.10, 0.95, 0.50, 0.33, the faces are 1, 6, 4, 2;
the first two-dice roll sums to 7, the second to 6; running means 7.0, 6.5.

## Common mistakes
* Using the global `random.seed`, which other code can disturb.
* `int(u * 6)` without `+ 1` (faces 0..5) or `round(u * 6)` (faces 0..6 with uneven odds).
* Expecting the running mean to equal exactly 7.

## Why this matters
Monte Carlo simulation estimates quantities that are hard to compute exactly — expected returns
in RL (RL-11), bootstrap confidence intervals (ST-13), dropout's expected behaviour.

## References

- [random — Generate pseudo-random numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S004`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
dice-lln.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `roll(rng)` → one die face `int(rng.random() * 6) + 1`, using **only** `rng.random()`.
* `simulate_two_dice(n, seed)` → dict with keys
  * `"sums"`: list of `n` sums, each `roll(rng) + roll(rng)` (first die drawn first),
  * `"running_mean"`: list where element i is the mean of `sums[:i+1]`,
  * `"freq"`: dict mapping each sum 2..12 to its count (all 11 keys present),
  using `rng = random.Random(seed)`. Raise `ValueError` if `n < 1`.

**Examples**
```python
r = simulate_two_dice(5, seed=0)
len(r["sums"]) == 5 and all(2 <= s <= 12 for s in r["sums"])    # True
abs(simulate_two_dice(100000, seed=1)["running_mean"][-1] - 7) < 0.05   # True (LLN)
```
dice-lln.solution:
r"""Reference solution for ST-10 Dice Simulation and the Law of Large Numbers.

A private generator seeded once makes the whole simulation reproducible. Each die face comes from
a single `rng.random()` call (the only output Python guarantees across versions). One loop records
the sum, updates the frequency table and the running mean.
"""
import random


def roll(rng):
    return int(rng.random() * 6) + 1


def simulate_two_dice(n, seed):
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 1")
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    sums, running = [], []
    freq = {s: 0 for s in range(2, 13)}
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        s = roll(rng) + roll(rng)
        sums.append(s)
        freq[s] += 1
        total += s
        running.append(total / (i + 1))
    return {"sums": sums, "running_mean": running, "freq": freq}

covariance-correlation.article:
# Covariance and Correlation

## Intuition
Do two variables move together? If above-average $x$ tends to come with above-average $y$, the
products of their deviations are mostly positive — positive covariance. Correlation rescales
covariance to $[-1, 1]$ so it no longer depends on units.

## Precise explanation
$$\operatorname{cov}(x,y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\quad(\text{sample}),$$
$$r = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2}\,\sqrt{\sum (y_i-\bar y)^2}}.$$
The $n$ vs $n-1$ factor cancels in $r$. $r = \pm 1$ means a perfect line; $r = 0$ means no
*linear* relationship — $y = x^2$ on symmetric $x$ has $r = 0$ despite perfect dependence.
$r$ is the cosine of the angle between the centred vectors (compare MA-04).

`statistics.covariance` and `statistics.correlation` (Python 3.10+) implement these.

## Worked example
x = [1, 2, 3, 4], y = [2, 4, 5, 8]: means 2.5 and 4.75; deviation products
(−1.5)(−2.75)+(−0.5)(−0.75)+(0.5)(0.25)+(1.5)(3.25) = 9.5; sample cov = 9.5/3 ≈ 3.167;
Σdx² = 5, Σdy² = 18.75, r = 9.5/√93.75 ≈ 0.981.

## Common mistakes
* Interpreting correlation as causation.
* Ignoring that one outlier can create or destroy a strong r.
* Dividing by zero when one variable is constant (r is undefined).

## Why this matters
Correlated features cause unstable linear-model coefficients (ridge regression helps, ML-20),
and correlation matrices are a standard first exploratory step.

## Library implementation

Python 3.10+ provides `statistics.covariance(x, y)` (sample, $n-1$) and
`statistics.correlation(x, y)` (Pearson). NumPy's `np.cov` and `np.corrcoef` return full
matrices for several variables at once.

## References

- [statistics — Mathematical statistics functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S003`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)

**Examples**

```python
pearson([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 4, 5, 8])      # 0.9811...

```

sampling-distribution.article:
# Sampling Distributions and Standard Error

## Intuition
Take a random sample of 30 students and compute their mean height. Take another sample and the
mean changes a little. The **sampling distribution** is the distribution of that mean over all
possible samples. It is narrower than the population — averages vary less than individuals — and
it gets narrower as the sample grows.

## Precise explanation
* If individual values have standard deviation $\sigma$, the mean of $n$ independent values has
  standard deviation $\sigma / \sqrt n$. Quadrupling $n$ halves it.
* We rarely know $\sigma$, so we estimate it with the sample standard deviation $s$ (dividing by
  $n-1$, ST-01): the **standard error** is $\mathrm{SE} = s / \sqrt n$.
* **Central limit theorem (CLT)**: for large $n$ the sampling distribution of the mean is
  approximately normal (ST-09), even when the data are not. It says nothing
  about small samples or heavy outliers, and it assumes independent draws.
* **Normal-approximation 95% interval**: $\bar x \pm z\,\mathrm{SE}$ with $z \approx 1.96$
  (`NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)`). "95%" describes the *procedure*: about 95% of intervals built
  this way contain the true mean.

**Simulating sampling with replacement** (reproducibly): with `rng = random.Random(seed)`, draw
an index `int(rng.random() * len(population))` for each of the $n$ values.

## Worked example
Population of die faces 1..6: $\sigma = \sqrt{35/12} \approx 1.708$. For $n = 25$, the means of many
samples have standard deviation about $1.708/5 \approx 0.342$, and their histogram is close to a
bell even though each face is uniform.

## Common mistakes
* Using $\sigma$ of the data as the uncertainty of the mean (forgetting $\sqrt n$).
* Dividing by $n$ instead of $n - 1$ when estimating $s$.
* Saying "there is a 95% probability the true mean is in *this* interval".

## Why this matters
Standard errors are the denominator of the t-statistic (ST-18), and the bootstrap
(ST-13) estimates the same sampling distribution by resampling your data.

## Library implementation

`statistics.stdev(sample) / math.sqrt(len(sample))` gives the same standard error, and
`random.Random(seed).choices(population, k=n)` draws with replacement in one call (its exact
sequence is not guaranteed across Python versions, which is why the graded version builds
indices from `random()`). `scipy.stats.sem` computes the standard error for arrays.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [statistics — Mathematical statistics functions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S003`)
- [random — Generate pseudo-random numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S004`)

   `population[int(rng.random() * len(population))]`, and record their mean.
2. `standard_error(sample)` → $s / \sqrt n$ with the $n-1$ sample standard deviation; raise
   `ValueError` if the sample has fewer than 2 values.
3. `mean_ci95(sample)` → `(low, high)` = mean ∓ z · SE with `z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)`.

**Example**
```python

len(means)                 # 2000
# their standard deviation is close to 1.708 / 5 ≈ 0.342
standard_error([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])   # ≈ 0.7559
```

bootstrap-ci.article:
# The Bootstrap

## Intuition
We have one sample but want to know how much a statistic (e.g. the mean) would vary if we could
collect new samples. The bootstrap pretends the sample *is* the population and draws many
"new" samples from it, with replacement, recomputing the statistic each time. The spread of those
recomputed values estimates the statistic's uncertainty.

## Precise explanation
1. For $b = 1..B$: draw $n$ indices uniformly with replacement, form the resample, compute
   $\hat\theta^*_b$.
2. **Percentile interval** at level $1-\alpha$: the $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ percentiles of
   $\{\hat\theta^*_b\}$.

Index recipe used here (stable across Python versions): `int(rng.random() * n)`, drawn in order
for each position of each resample.

**Interpretation:** a 95% CI procedure captures the true parameter in about 95% of repeated
studies. It is *not* "a 95% probability that the parameter is in this particular interval" (that
is a Bayesian statement).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D[original sample n] --> R1[resample 1] --> T1[stat*]
  D --> R2[resample 2] --> T2[stat*]
  D --> RB[resample B] --> TB[stat*]
  T1 & T2 & TB --> P[percentiles α/2, 1−α/2] --> CI[interval]
```

## Worked example
For data [2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9] (mean 5.17) the reference solution with `seed=0`,
B = 2000 gives a 95% bootstrap CI for the mean of about [3.50, 7.00]; other seeds or B give
slightly different endpoints.

## Common mistakes
* Resampling *without* replacement (that just permutes the data).
* Resamples of a different size than the original.
* Very small B (e.g. 50) — noisy interval endpoints.

## Why this matters
Bootstrapping gives error bars for any metric — accuracy, F1, AUC — without formulas, and it is
the idea behind bagging and random forests.

## Library implementation

`scipy.stats.bootstrap((data,), np.mean, method="percentile")` computes percentile bootstrap
intervals (and better "BCa" intervals by default). Because it uses NumPy's random generator, its
resamples differ from yours, so the two intervals agree only approximately; the comparison checks
that they overlap closely and runs only when SciPy is installed.

## References

- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [random — Generate pseudo-random numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S004`)

import math

import random

def _ref(data, n_boot, alpha, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(data)
    b = sorted(sum(data[int(rng.random() * n)] for _ in range(n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot))
    def pct(q):
        r = q / 100 * (len(b) - 1); i = math.floor(r); f = r - i
        return b[i] + f * (b[i + 1] - b[i]) if i + 1 < len(b) else b[i]
    return pct(100 * alpha / 2), pct(100 * (1 - alpha / 2))

scipy-stats-intro.article:
# Introducing scipy.stats

## Intuition
In ST-08 and ST-09 you wrote the probability formulas yourself. In
practice you reach for `scipy.stats`: one object per distribution that knows its density,
cumulative probability, quantiles, mean and spread, tested by thousands of users. Knowing the
formulas lets you check the library; knowing the library saves you from re-deriving them.

## Precise explanation
`scipy.stats` provides distribution families. Calling a family with its parameters returns a
**frozen** distribution:

```python
from scipy import stats
heights = stats.norm(loc=170, scale=10)   # normal, mean 170, standard deviation 10
coins = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.5)          # number of heads in 10 fair flips
```

| Method | Continuous (`norm`) | Discrete (`binom`) |
|---|---|---|
| density | `pdf(x)` — probability density | `pmf(k)` — P(X = k) |
| `cdf(x)` | P(X ≤ x) | P(X ≤ k) |
| `ppf(q)` | the x with cdf(x) = q (inverse cdf, the quantile) | smallest k with cdf(k) ≥ q |
| `sf(x)` | 1 − cdf(x), the upper tail, computed accurately | same |
| `mean()`, `std()` | μ, σ | np, √(np(1−p)) |

`loc` and `scale` are SciPy's general names for shift and stretch; for the normal they are μ and σ.
Results are NumPy floats; wrap them in `float()` when you need plain Python numbers.

## Worked example
```python
stats.norm(170, 10).cdf(180)     # 0.8413...: 84% of heights are below 180
stats.norm(170, 10).ppf(0.975)   # 189.6: 97.5% are below this
stats.binom(10, 0.5).pmf(5)      # 0.24609375 = C(10,5) / 2**10
stats.binom(10, 0.5).ppf(0.5)    # 5.0: the median number of heads
```

## What the library does inside
`norm.cdf` evaluates the same error-function formula as ST-09, using special
functions that stay accurate far in the tails; `binom.pmf` evaluates C(n, k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ from
ST-08 in log space so large n does not overflow. `ppf` inverts the cdf numerically.

## Common mistakes
* Passing the variance as `scale`: `scale` is the standard deviation.
* Calling `pdf` on a discrete distribution: discrete ones have `pmf`.
* Using `1 - cdf(x)` for tiny tail probabilities: `sf(x)` keeps precision.
* Forgetting that `ppf` of a discrete distribution returns a float (`5.0`), not an `int`.

## Why this matters
Every test in the next steps turns a statistic into a p-value through one of these objects, and
machine-learning code uses them to sample noise, set priors and compute confidence intervals.

## References

- [Statistical functions (scipy.stats)](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html) — SciPy developers (`S101`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)

chi-square-scipy.article:
# Chi-Square Test with SciPy

## Intuition
A chi-square statistic says how far observed counts are from expected counts. On its own, 13.4
means little. The **p-value** turns it into a probability: if the hypothesised probabilities were
right, how often would random counts look at least this far off?

## Precise explanation
`scipy.stats.chisquare(f_obs, f_exp)` returns the statistic $\chi^2 = \sum (O_i - E_i)^2 / E_i$
and its p-value with $k - 1$ degrees of freedom:

```python
from scipy import stats
result = stats.chisquare([5, 8, 9, 8, 10, 20], f_exp=[10] * 6)
result.statistic   # 13.4
result.pvalue      # 0.0199
```

`f_exp` must be **counts** with the same total as `f_obs` (multiply probabilities by the total);
omitting it means "all categories equally likely". The p-value is the chi-square distribution's
upper tail, `stats.chi2(df).sf(statistic)`. With significance level α, reject the null hypothesis
when p < α. A p-value is **not** the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

## Worked example
For the die above, p ≈ 0.020. At α = 0.05 we reject fairness; at α = 0.01 we do not. The
evidence is the same; the decision depends on how strict the threshold is.

## What the library does inside
`chisquare` computes the same sum as your function in ST-16, which follows as an
optional deep dive, then calls the chi-square survival function instead of reading a table of
critical values. It also checks that observed and expected totals agree.

## Common mistakes
* Passing probabilities as `f_exp`: SciPy expects expected counts.
* Using proportions instead of counts for `f_obs`; the test needs the sample size.
* Rejecting when p > α, or reading 1 − p as the probability the hypothesis is false.
* Testing categories with expected counts below about 5, where the approximation is poor.

## Why this matters
Chi-square tests check whether class frequencies drifted between training and production data,
whether a random-number generator is uniform, and whether a feature's categories relate to labels.

## References

- [Statistical functions (scipy.stats)](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html) — SciPy developers (`S101`)
- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)

chi-square-gof.article:
# Chi-Square Goodness of Fit

## Intuition
Is a die fair? Roll it 60 times; a fair die should show each face about 10 times. The chi-square
statistic adds up how far each observed count is from its expected count, scaled by the expected
count, so that a gap of 5 matters more when you expected 10 than when you expected 1000.

## Precise explanation
With observed counts $O_i$ over $k$ categories, total $N = \sum O_i$, and hypothesised
probabilities $p_i$ (summing to 1), expected counts are $E_i = N p_i$ and
$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i},\qquad \text{df} = k - 1.$$
Under the null hypothesis (the probabilities are right), $\chi^2$ approximately follows a
chi-square distribution with df degrees of freedom. Reject at level α if $\chi^2$ exceeds the
critical value (e.g. 11.070 for df = 5, α = 0.05 — from standard tables).

Rule of thumb: every $E_i$ should be at least 5 for the approximation to be reliable.

## Worked example
Die rolled 60 times: O = [5, 8, 9, 8, 10, 20], E = 10 each.
χ² = (25 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 0 + 100)/10 = 13.4, df = 5 > 11.07 → reject fairness at 5%.

## Common mistakes
* Using proportions instead of counts.
* Dividing by $O_i$ instead of $E_i$.
* df = k instead of k − 1.

## Why this matters
Chi-square tests check categorical feature/label dependence (feature selection), detect drift in
class frequencies, and test random-number generators.

## Library implementation

`scipy.stats.chisquare(observed, f_exp=expected)` returns the same statistic together with a
p-value from the chi-square distribution with `len(observed) - 1` degrees of freedom, so you do not
need a critical-value table. The comparison runs only when SciPy is installed.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)

welch-t-scipy.article:
# Welch's t-test with SciPy

## Intuition
Two groups have different averages. Is the gap larger than the noise in each group would
produce? The t-statistic measures the gap in units of its standard error; the p-value asks how
often chance alone would give a t at least that extreme.

## Precise explanation
```python
from scipy import stats
result = stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False)       # Welch's test
result.statistic, result.pvalue, result.df
```

`equal_var=False` selects **Welch's** test: each group keeps its own variance, and the degrees of
freedom come from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula (usually not an integer). The default,
`equal_var=True`, is Student's test, which pools the variances and can be badly wrong when the
spreads or sizes differ — so always ask for Welch unless you have a reason not to.

`alternative` states the question:

| `alternative` | Null hypothesis rejected when … |
|---|---|
| `"two-sided"` | the means differ in either direction |
| `"greater"` | mean(x) > mean(y) |
| `"less"` | mean(x) < mean(y) |

A one-sided p-value is half the two-sided one when the difference points the hypothesised way.

## Worked example
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and y = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]: t = −2, df = 8, two-sided p ≈ 0.081. Not
significant at α = 0.05; with `alternative="less"`, p ≈ 0.040 and it is. Decide the alternative
**before** looking at the data — switching afterwards halves p dishonestly.

## What the library does inside
SciPy computes the same standard error, t and degrees of freedom as ST-18 (the optional
deep dive after this step), then reads the p-value from the t distribution's tails with `stats.t`.

## Common mistakes
* Leaving `equal_var=True` (Student's test) when group variances differ.
* Reporting only "p < 0.05" without the size of the difference.
* Picking the one-sided alternative after seeing which mean is larger.
* Using it on paired measurements (before/after on the same people): that is `ttest_rel`.

## Why this matters
Comparing two model variants across random seeds, or an A/B test of two page designs, ends with
exactly this test — and the mean difference tells you whether the effect is worth acting on.

## References

- [Statistical functions (scipy.stats)](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html) — SciPy developers (`S101`)
- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)

welch-t.article:
# Comparing Two Means: Welch's t

## Intuition
Model A scores 0.82 on average across runs, model B 0.79. Is A really better, or is the gap just
noise? The t-statistic compares the difference in means to how much that difference would wobble
by chance (its standard error).

## Precise explanation
With sample means $\bar x, \bar y$, sample variances $s_x^2, s_y^2$ (n−1 denominators), sizes
$n_x, n_y$:
$$t = \frac{\bar x - \bar y}{\sqrt{s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y}}.$$
Welch's test does **not** assume equal variances. Its approximate degrees of freedom
(Welch–Satterthwaite):
$$\nu = \frac{\left(s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y\right)^2}{\dfrac{(s_x^2/n_x)^2}{n_x-1} + \dfrac{(s_y^2/n_y)^2}{n_y-1}}.$$
Large $|t|$ (compared with a t-distribution with ν df; roughly $|t| > 2$ for moderate ν at 5%)
suggests a real difference. ν is usually not an integer.

## Worked example
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (mean 3, s² 2.5), y = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] (mean 5, s² 2.5):
SE = √(0.5 + 0.5) = 1, t = −2, ν = 1/(0.0625 + 0.0625) = 8.

## Common mistakes
* Using population variances.
* Pooling variances (Student's t) when spreads clearly differ.
* Reading "not significant" as "no difference".

## Why this matters
Comparing models across random seeds or cross-validation folds (ML-17) calls for exactly this
kind of test — with care about non-independence of folds.

## Library implementation

`scipy.stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False)` performs Welch's test: its `statistic` is your
t, and recent SciPy versions also expose the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom as `.df`, plus
a p-value. The comparison runs only when SciPy is installed.

## References

- [OpenIntro Statistics](https://www.openintro.org/book/os/) — OpenIntro (`S011`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)

welch-t.solution:
r"""Reference solution for ST-18 Welch's t-statistic by Hand.

Each group's squared standard error of the mean is its sample variance over its size. Their sum
is the variance of the difference in means; t divides the observed difference by its square
root. The Welch–Satterthwaite formula combines the two contributions into an effective df.
"""
import math


def _mean_var(a):
    n = len(a)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("each sample needs at least two values")
    m = sum(a) / n
    return m, sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in a) / (n - 1), n


def welch_t(x, y):
    mx, sx2, nx = _mean_var(x)
    my, sy2, ny = _mean_var(y)
    vx, vy = sx2 / nx, sy2 / ny
    if vx + vy == 0:
        raise ValueError("both samples have zero variance")
    t = (mx - my) / math.sqrt(vx + vy)
    df = (vx + vy) ** 2 / (vx ** 2 / (nx - 1) + vy ** 2 / (ny - 1))
    return t, df

permutation-test-scipy.article:
# Permutation Test with SciPy

## Intuition
If the group labels did not matter, shuffling them should not change the difference in means
much. A permutation test shuffles the labels many times and asks how often a shuffled difference
is at least as extreme as the real one. No normal distribution is assumed.

## Precise explanation
```python
from scipy import stats

def mean_diff(a, b, axis):
    return a.mean(axis=axis) - b.mean(axis=axis)

result = stats.permutation_test((x, y), mean_diff, permutation_type="independent",
                                n_resamples=9999, alternative="two-sided", random_state=0)
result.statistic, result.pvalue
```

* `data` is a tuple of samples; `permutation_type="independent"` reassigns values between groups.
* The statistic receives the samples as arrays (NumPy arrays, the subject of the next topic)
  and an `axis` keyword. `a.mean(axis=axis)` averages along that axis, which lets SciPy evaluate
  many shuffles in one call (`vectorized=True` is assumed when the function accepts `axis`).
* When `n_resamples` is at least the number of distinct relabellings, SciPy enumerates all of
  them and the p-value is **exact**; otherwise it samples randomly, so pass a seed as
  `random_state`.
* `alternative` works as in ST-17.

## Worked example
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], y = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7.5]: the observed difference is −2.1. There are only
C(10, 5) = 252 ways to split ten values into two groups of five, so with `n_resamples=9999` SciPy
checks all of them; 32 of 252 splits give a difference at least 2.1 in size, p = 0.127.

## What the library does inside
It is the loop from ST-20 (the optional deep dive after this step) — shuffle,
recompute, count — written with arrays so that thousands of shuffles are computed at once, plus
exact enumeration for small samples.

## Common mistakes
* Writing a statistic without the `axis` argument, so it silently averages over the wrong axis.
* Leaving out `random_state` and getting a different p-value every run.
* Using `permutation_type="samples"` (paired data) for two independent groups.

## Why this matters
Resampling tests let you compare model metrics, A/B groups or feature effects without assuming
normal errors — and SciPy's version is fast enough to run inside an evaluation pipeline.

## References

- [Statistical functions (scipy.stats)](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html) — SciPy developers (`S101`)
- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)

permutation-test-scipy.localPrelude:
import itertools

def brute_force_p(x, y):
    """Exact two-sided p-value: the share of all splits with |difference| at least the observed."""
    values, k = list(x) + list(y), len(x)
    observed = abs(sum(x) / len(x) - sum(y) / len(y))
    hits = total = 0
    for chosen in itertools.combinations(range(len(values)), k):
        a = [values[i] for i in chosen]
        b = [values[i] for i in range(len(values)) if i not in chosen]
        total += 1
        hits += abs(sum(a) / len(a) - sum(b) / len(b)) >= observed - 1e-12
    return hits / total

permutation-test.article:
# Permutation Tests

## Intuition
If the group labels "A" and "B" don't matter (the null hypothesis), then shuffling the labels
should produce differences in means just as large as the one we observed, fairly often. If
almost no shuffle produces a difference as extreme as the real one, the labels probably *do*
matter.

## Precise explanation
1. Observed statistic $d_\text{obs} = \bar x - \bar y$.
2. Pool all values. For $b = 1..B$: shuffle the pool, call the first $n_x$ values "x" and the
   rest "y", compute $d_b$.
3. Two-sided p-value with the standard +1 correction (counts the observed arrangement, never 0):
$$p = \frac{1 + \#\{b: |d_b| \ge |d_\text{obs}|\}}{B + 1}.$$

**Fisher–Yates shuffle** (uniform over permutations) using only `rng.random()`:
```text
for i from n-1 down to 1:
    j = int(rng.random() * (i + 1))   # 0 <= j <= i
    swap items[i], items[j]
```
Floating-point noise can make $|d_b|$ differ from $|d_\text{obs}|$ in the last bits even for
identical arrangements; compare with a small tolerance (`>= abs_obs - 1e-12`).

## Worked example
x = [5, 6, 7], y = [1, 2, 3]: $d_\text{obs} = 4$. Only the 2 of the 20 equally likely splits
(x and y swapped) are as extreme, so the exact p-value is 2/20 = 0.1; a Monte Carlo estimate
with many shuffles is close to 0.1.

## Common mistakes
* Shuffling `x` and `y` separately (labels never move).
* Biased shuffles such as `j = int(rng.random() * n)` for every i.
* Reporting p = 0.

## Why this matters
Permutation tests make almost no distributional assumptions; they also underlie permutation
feature importance (XA-08), where shuffling a feature breaks its link with the target.

## References

- [Think Stats (3rd edition)](https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-stats-3e/) — Allen B. Downey (`S010`)
- [random — Generate pseudo-random numbers](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html) — Python Software Foundation (`S004`)
permutation-test.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `fisher_yates(items, rng)` → a **new** shuffled list using exactly the recipe above
  (input unchanged).
* `permutation_test(x, y, n_perm=5000, seed=0)` → dict `{"observed": d_obs, "p_value": p}`.
  Use `rng = random.Random(seed)`; each permutation shuffles the pooled list `x + y` with
  `fisher_yates` (starting from the original pool each time). Count `abs(d_b) >= abs(d_obs) - 1e-12`.
  Raise `ValueError` if either group is empty or `n_perm < 1`.

**Examples**
```python
r = permutation_test([5, 6, 7], [1, 2, 3], n_perm=4000, seed=0)
r["observed"]                      # 4.0
abs(r["p_value"] - 0.1) < 0.02     # True
permutation_test([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], n_perm=100)["p_value"]   # 1.0
```
permutation-test.solution:
r"""Reference solution for ST-20 Permutation Test for a Mean Difference by Hand.

The Fisher–Yates loop picks each position's element uniformly from the not-yet-fixed prefix,
giving every permutation equal probability. Each permutation reassigns labels at random; the
fraction of shuffles at least as extreme as the observed difference (plus the observed
arrangement itself) is the p-value.
"""
import random


def fisher_yates(items, rng):
    a = list(items)
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, 0, -1):
        j = int(rng.random() * (i + 1))
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    return a


def permutation_test(x, y, n_perm=5000, seed=0):
    if not x or not y:
        raise ValueError("both groups must be non-empty")
    if n_perm < 1:
        raise ValueError("n_perm must be >= 1")
    nx = len(x)
    d_obs = sum(x) / nx - sum(y) / len(y)
    pool = list(x) + list(y)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    hits = 0
    for _ in range(n_perm):
        p = fisher_yates(pool, rng)
        d = sum(p[:nx]) / nx - sum(p[nx:]) / (len(p) - nx)
        if abs(d) >= abs(d_obs) - 1e-12:
            hits += 1
    return {"observed": d_obs, "p_value": (hits + 1) / (n_perm + 1)}

giving every permutation equal probability. Each permutation reassigns labels at random; the
fraction of shuffles at least as extreme as the observed difference (plus the observed

array-info.article:
# The ndarray

## Intuition
A NumPy array is a rectangular grid of numbers that all share one type. Because every element
has the same size and the grid is regular, NumPy can store the data in one contiguous block and
run fast compiled loops over it.

## Precise explanation
* `np.array(rows, dtype=float)` builds an array; `dtype` fixes the element type
  (`float64`, `int64`, `bool`, …).
* `a.shape` — tuple of lengths per axis; `a.ndim` — number of axes (`len(a.shape)`);
  `a.size` — total elements (product of the shape); `a.dtype` — element type.
* A 1-D array has shape `(n,)` (note the comma); a 2-D array `(rows, cols)`.
* Ragged nested lists (rows of different lengths) cannot form a numeric grid. Since NumPy 1.24
  `np.array([[1, 2], [3]])` raises `ValueError` unless you explicitly ask for `dtype=object`.

```python
>>> a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], dtype=float)
>>> a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, a.dtype
((2, 3), 2, 6, dtype('float64'))
```

## Worked example
`np.array([7, 8, 9])` → shape `(3,)`, ndim 1, size 3, dtype int64 (on most 64-bit platforms).
`np.array([[7], [8], [9]])` → shape `(3, 1)` — a column, ndim 2.

## Common mistakes
* Confusing `(3,)` and `(3, 1)` — they broadcast differently (NP-07).
* Expecting `len(a)` to be the total size (it is the length of the first axis).
* Mixing ints and strings in one list → NumPy picks a string dtype.

## Why this matters
Every ML dataset is an array of shape `(n_samples, n_features)`; knowing its shape and dtype is
the first debugging step for almost every error message in later topics.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Scientific Python Lectures](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/) — Scientific Python developers (`S006`)

  `dtype` is `str(a.dtype)`.

**Examples**
```python

describe(a)   # {'shape': (2, 3), 'ndim': 2, 'size': 6, 'dtype': 'float64'}

```

vectorized-math.article:
# Vectorised Arithmetic and ufuncs

## Intuition
In MA-04 you wrote a loop that multiplies matching elements and adds them up. NumPy
lets you write the *whole* operation at once: `a * b` multiplies every pair of elements, and
`.sum()` adds them. The loop still happens, but inside fast compiled code, typically tens to
hundreds of times faster than a Python loop on large arrays.

## Precise explanation
* Arithmetic operators on arrays of the same shape work **element-wise**:
  `a + b`, `a * b`, `a ** 2`, `a / 2`, `-a`. Mixing an array and a number applies the number to
  every element: `c * 9 / 5 + 32`.
* **Universal functions (ufuncs)** are element-wise functions: `np.exp`, `np.log`, `np.sqrt`,
  `np.abs`, `np.maximum(a, b)`. `math.exp` only accepts single numbers; `np.exp` accepts arrays.
* Reductions collapse an array: `a.sum()`, `a.mean()`, `a.max()`.
* `np.where(cond, x, y)` picks from `x` where `cond` is true and from `y` elsewhere. Both `x` and
  `y` are computed for every element, so they must not overflow.
* Comparing floats: use `np.allclose(a, b)` (tolerance) instead of `==`.

**Stable vectorised sigmoid.** MA-03 branched on the sign of one number. For
arrays, compute `e = np.exp(-np.abs(x))` (never larger than 1), then
`np.where(x >= 0, 1 / (1 + e), e / (1 + e))`.

## Worked example
```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]); b = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])
a * b            # array([ 4., 10., 18.])
(a * b).sum()    # 32.0 — the dot product
np.sqrt(np.mean(a ** 2))   # root-mean-square ≈ 2.160
```

## Common mistakes
* Using `math.exp(array)` → `TypeError`; use `np.exp`.
* Python lists do not vectorise: `[1, 2] * 2` is `[1, 2, 1, 2]`. Convert with `np.asarray`.
* Integer arrays: `np.array([1, 2]) / 2` is float, but in-place `a /= 2` on an int array fails;
  create float arrays with `dtype=float`.
* Shape mismatches such as `(3,) * (4,)` raise `ValueError` — check shapes first.

## Why this matters
Every later topic expresses its maths as array expressions; checking them against a slow,
obviously-correct loop is the standard way to test numerical code.

## Library implementation

NumPy also has a dedicated function for this step: `np.dot(a, b)` (or `a @ b`, introduced in
NP-06) computes the dot product directly, and is what you would normally write.
The element-wise form `(a * b).sum()` shows what `np.dot` does. `scipy.special.expit` is a
library sigmoid for arrays. The tests compare your functions with these.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Universal functions (ufunc) basics (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.ufuncs.html) — NumPy Developers (`S081`)
vectorized-math.statement:
## Task

Implement (inputs may be lists or arrays; convert with `np.asarray(x, dtype=float)`):

1. `dot_loop(a, b)` — the dot product with a Python loop (raise `ValueError` if lengths differ).
2. `dot_vectorized(a, b)` — the same with `*` and `.sum()` (same `ValueError`); return a `float`.
3. `fahrenheit(celsius)` — `celsius * 9 / 5 + 32` as an array.
4. `rms(x)` — root-mean-square $\sqrt{\frac1n\sum x_i^2}$ as a `float`.
5. `sigmoid(x)` — stable element-wise sigmoid returning an array of the same shape; must not
   produce warnings or `nan` for inputs like `[-1000, 0, 1000]`.

**Examples**
```python
dot_vectorized([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])   # 32.0
fahrenheit([0, 100])                    # array([ 32., 212.])
sigmoid([-1000, 0, 1000])               # array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
```
vectorized-math.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Converting inputs to float arrays makes every operator element-wise. The dot product becomes one
multiplication and one reduction; RMS chains a power, a mean and a square root. The sigmoid only
exponentiates non-positive numbers, so both branches given to `np.where` are finite everywhere.

slicing-subgrid.article:
# Slicing, Views and Copies

## Intuition
Slicing cuts a rectangle out of a grid. In NumPy that rectangle is usually a **view**: a window
onto the same memory. Changing the view changes the original — powerful, but surprising.

## Precise explanation
* `a[r0:r1, c0:c1]` selects rows `r0..r1-1` and columns `c0..c1-1`.
* Steps: `a[::2, ::2]` takes every other row and column.
* Basic slicing returns a **view** (`np.shares_memory(view, a)` is True). Use `.copy()` to get
  independent data.
* Out-of-range slice ends are silently clipped (`a[0:100]` on 5 rows gives 5 rows) — validate if
  you need exact sizes.
* Negative indices count from the end: `a[-1]` is the last row; `a[1:-1, 1:-1]` is the interior.

## Worked example
```python
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
a[1:3, 1:3]     # [[ 5,  6], [ 9, 10]]
a[::2, ::2]     # [[ 0,  2], [ 8, 10]]
a.sum() - a[1:-1, 1:-1].sum()   # border sum = 120 - 30 = 90
```

## Common mistakes
* `a[1:3][1:3]` — slices rows twice instead of rows then columns.
* Modifying a crop and accidentally editing the source image.
* Off-by-one: stop indices are exclusive.

## Why this matters
Cropping image patches (CV), selecting time windows and mini-batches are all slicing; view
semantics explain many "my data changed by itself" bugs.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Scientific Python Lectures](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/) — Scientific Python developers (`S006`)
slicing-subgrid.statement:
## Task

Implement for a 2-D array `a`:
* `crop(a, top, left, h, w)` → a **copy** of the `h × w` block starting at `(top, left)`;
  raise `ValueError` if the block does not fit inside `a` or `h`, `w` < 1 or top/left < 0.
* `every_other(a)` → `a[::2, ::2]` (a view is fine).
* `border_sum(a)` → sum of the elements on the outer border (for 1 or 2 rows/cols every element
  is on the border).

**Examples**
```python
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
crop(a, 1, 1, 2, 2)   # array([[ 5,  6], [ 9, 10]])
every_other(a)        # array([[ 0,  2], [ 8, 10]])
border_sum(a)         # 90
```
slicing-subgrid.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

`crop` validates bounds (slicing would silently clip) and returns a copy so callers can modify it
safely. `every_other` uses steps. `border_sum` subtracts the interior from the total; for arrays
with fewer than three rows or columns the interior slice is empty and sums to 0.
hints: Check `top + h <= a.shape[0]` and `left + w <= a.shape[1]`.
`a[top:top+h, left:left+w].copy()`.
Border = total − interior `a[1:-1, 1:-1].sum()` (the interior is empty for small arrays).

failureFeedback.advice: Return `.copy()` of the slice so modifying the crop doesn't modify the input.
Slicing silently clips; check the bounds yourself.
For 1×1 or 2×2 arrays the interior is empty, so the border is everything.
Use a[top:top+h, left:left+w] (one bracket, comma between axes).

boolean-mask.article:
# Boolean Masks

## Intuition
A mask is a same-shaped array of True/False that marks which elements you care about. Indexing
with a mask keeps the True positions — the vectorised version of the filtering loop from PY-12.

## Precise explanation
* `a > 3` returns a boolean array. `a[a > 3]` returns a **1-D copy** of the selected values.
* Combine masks element-wise with `&` (and), `|` (or), `~` (not). Parentheses are required:
  `(a >= lo) & (a <= hi)` — `&` binds tighter than `>=`.
* Python's `and`/`or` do **not** work on arrays (they raise "truth value is ambiguous").
* `mask.sum()` counts True values (True = 1).
* `np.where(cond, x, y)` builds a new array taking `x` where cond is True and `y` elsewhere.
  `np.minimum(a, t)` is an alternative for capping.

## Worked example
```python
a = np.array([4, -1, 9, 3, 12])
a[(a >= 0) & (a <= 9)]   # [4, 9, 3]
(a > 5).sum()            # 2
np.where(a > 5, 5, a)    # [4, -1, 5, 3, 5]
```

## Common mistakes
* `a > 0 and a < 9` → `ValueError`.
* Missing parentheses: `a >= 0 & a <= 9` evaluates `0 & a` first.
* Modifying `a[a > 5]` expecting a view: `b = a[a > 5]; b[:] = 0` does not change `a`
  (but `a[a > 5] = 0` does, because it is an assignment through the mask).

## Why this matters
Masks select rows in pandas, threshold images (CV-07), build causal attention masks (LM-08) and
apply ReLU (`np.where(z > 0, z, 0)`).

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
boolean-mask.statement:
## Task

Implement without Python loops:
* `in_range(a, lo, hi)` → 1-D array of the elements with `lo <= x <= hi` (in original order,
  row-major for 2-D).
* `count_above(a, t)` → number (Python `int`) of elements strictly greater than `t`.
* `cap(a, t)` → new array equal to `a` but with every element `> t` replaced by `t`; `a` must not
  change.

**Examples**
```python
a = np.array([4, -1, 9, 3, 12])
in_range(a, 0, 9)   # array([4, 9, 3])
count_above(a, 5)   # 2
cap(a, 5)           # array([ 4, -1,  5,  3,  5])
```
boolean-mask.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Comparisons produce masks; `&` combines them element-wise and boolean indexing extracts the
selected elements. Summing a mask counts Trues. `np.where` constructs a fresh array, leaving the
input untouched.
hints: `mask = (a >= lo) & (a <= hi)` then `a[mask]`.
`int((a > t).sum())`.
`np.where(a > t, t, a)` returns a new array.

failureFeedback.advice: Use & with parentheses: (a >= lo) & (a <= hi).
Strictly greater: a > t.
Don't assign into a; use np.where or np.minimum to build a new array.
Convert the result to a Python int.

axis-aggregations.article:
# Aggregating Along Axes

## Intuition
For a table of shape `(students, subjects)`, "average per subject" collapses the student axis;
"total per student" collapses the subject axis. The `axis` argument says **which axis
disappears**.

## Precise explanation
* `X.mean(axis=0)` → one value per column (rows collapsed), shape `(n_cols,)`.
* `X.sum(axis=1)` → one value per row, shape `(n_rows,)`.
* `keepdims=True` keeps the collapsed axis with length 1: `X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)` has
  shape `(n_rows, 1)` and broadcasts back against `X` (NP-07).
* `X.argmax(axis=1)` → index of the max in each row (first occurrence on ties).
* `X.argmax()` with no axis indexes the *flattened* array; `np.unravel_index(i, X.shape)` turns
  it back into `(row, col)`.

## Worked example
```python
X = np.array([[1, 5, 2],
              [7, 0, 3]])
X.mean(axis=0)     # [4. , 2.5, 2.5]
X.sum(axis=1)      # [ 8, 10]
X.argmax(axis=1)   # [1, 0]
np.unravel_index(X.argmax(), X.shape)   # (1, 0)
```

## Common mistakes
* Mixing up axis 0 and 1 (remember: the named axis is the one removed).
* Using flat `argmax()` and treating it as a row index.
* Forgetting `keepdims` and then failing to broadcast.

## Why this matters
Per-feature means for scaling (ML-08), per-sample predicted classes (`argmax(axis=1)`), batch
statistics in batch norm (DL-23) — all are axis reductions.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Scientific Python Lectures](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/) — Scientific Python developers (`S006`)
axis-aggregations.statement:
## Task

Write `summarize(X)` for a non-empty 2-D array, returning a dict:
* `"col_means"`: mean of each column (shape `(n_cols,)`),
* `"row_sums"`: sum of each row,
* `"row_argmax"`: index of the max in each row,
* `"max_pos"`: `(row, col)` tuple of Python ints of the overall maximum (first occurrence),
* `"row_means_keep"`: row means with shape `(n_rows, 1)`.

Raise `ValueError` if `X` is not 2-D or is empty. No Python loops.

**Example**
```python
s = summarize(np.array([[1, 5, 2], [7, 0, 3]]))
s["col_means"]   # array([4. , 2.5, 2.5])
s["max_pos"]     # (1, 0)
s["row_means_keep"].shape   # (2, 1)
```
axis-aggregations.solution:
r"""Reference solution for NP-05 Aggregations Along Axes.

Each entry is one reduction along the appropriate axis. The global maximum's flat index is
converted to a 2-D position with `unravel_index`, and `keepdims=True` preserves a column shape
for later broadcasting.
"""
import numpy as np


def summarize(X):
    X = np.asarray(X)
    if X.ndim != 2 or X.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("X must be a non-empty 2-D array")
    r, c = np.unravel_index(X.argmax(), X.shape)
    return {
        "col_means": X.mean(axis=0),
        "row_sums": X.sum(axis=1),
        "row_argmax": X.argmax(axis=1),
        "max_pos": (int(r), int(c)),
        "row_means_keep": X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True),
    }

matmul-dot.title: Matrix Products with @
matmul-dot.entryPoint: matmul_loops(A, B); matmul(A, B); batch_scores(X, w, b); gram(X)
objectives: Multiply matrices and matrix–vector pairs with the @ operator
Predict result shapes and catch mismatches before multiplying

Verify @ against the triple loop from Mathematics
matmul-dot.article:
# Matrix Products with @

## Intuition
MA-06 computed each entry of $AB$ as a dot product of a row of $A$ with a column of
$B$ using three nested loops. NumPy's `@` operator does the same in one expression and is the
most important operation in machine learning: a linear model scores a whole batch of examples
with a single `X @ w`.

## Precise explanation
For $A$ of shape $(m, n)$ and $B$ of shape $(n, p)$, $C = AB$ has shape $(m, p)$ and
$C_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik} B_{kj}$. The inner dimensions must match.

| Expression | Shapes | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `A @ B` | (m, n) @ (n, p) | (m, p) |
| `A @ v` | (m, n) @ (n,) | (m,) — each row dotted with v |
| `v @ w` | (n,) @ (n,) | scalar — the dot product |
| `X @ X.T` | (m, n) @ (n, m) | (m, m) — all pairwise dot products (the Gram matrix) |

* `A * B` is **element-wise**, not matrix multiplication.
* `np.dot` gives the same results for 1-D and 2-D arrays; `@` is the modern, clearer spelling.
* `.T` transposes a 2-D array.
* **Linear model on a batch**: rows of `X` are examples, `w` holds one weight per feature, and
  `X @ w + b` gives one score per example.

## Worked example
```python
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]); B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
A @ B        # [[19, 22], [43, 50]]
A * B        # [[ 5, 12], [21, 32]]  — different!
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.], [5., 6.]]); w = np.array([0.5, -1.0])
X @ w + 0.1  # [-1.4, -2.4, -3.4]
```

## Common mistakes
* Using `*` when you meant `@`.
* Multiplying `(3, 2) @ (3, 2)`; you probably needed a transpose.
* Confusing a 1-D vector `(n,)` with a column `(n, 1)`; `X @ w` with `w` of shape `(n, 1)` returns
  shape `(m, 1)`, not `(m,)`.

## Why this matters
Dense layers (DL-04), attention (LM-07) and least squares are all
matrix products.

## Library implementation

`@` calls `np.matmul`; `np.dot` and `np.einsum("ik,kj->ij", A, B)` are equivalent spellings for
2-D arrays. NumPy hands large products to an optimised BLAS library, which is why `@` is far
faster than the triple loop. The tests check all three spellings agree with your function.

## References

- [numpy.matmul (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.matmul.html) — NumPy Developers (`S082`)
- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Mathematics for Machine Learning](https://mml-book.github.io/) — Marc Peter Deisenroth, A. Aldo Faisal, Cheng Soon Ong (Cambridge University Press) (`S009`)
matmul-dot.statement:
## Task

Implement:

1. `matmul_loops(A, B)` — nested-list product with three loops (as in MA-06);
   raise `ValueError` if inner dimensions differ. Return a list of lists.
2. `matmul(A, B)` — `np.asarray` both and return `A @ B`; raise `ValueError` with a message
   containing both shapes if the inner dimensions differ (check before multiplying; both
   inputs are 2-D).
3. `batch_scores(X, w, b)` — scores `X @ w + b` for a 2-D `X`, 1-D `w` and a number `b`.
4. `gram(X)` — `X @ X.T`.

**Examples**
```python
matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]])   # array([[19, 22], [43, 50]])
batch_scores([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], [0.5, -1.0], 0.1)   # array([-1.4, -2.4, -3.4])
```
matmul-dot.solution:
r"""Reference solution for NP-06 Matrix Products with @.

The loop version spells out $C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}$; `@` performs the same computation in
compiled code. Checking `A.shape[1] == B.shape[0]` first produces a clear message. Scoring a batch
is one matrix–vector product plus a broadcast scalar, and the Gram matrix collects every pairwise
dot product of the rows.
"""
import numpy as np


def matmul_loops(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    if any(len(row) != n for row in A):
        raise ValueError("inner dimensions differ")
    p = len(B[0]) if B else 0
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(p)] for i in range(len(A))]


def matmul(A, B):
    A = np.asarray(A)
    B = np.asarray(B)
    if A.shape[1] != B.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot multiply {A.shape} by {B.shape}")
    return A @ B


def batch_scores(X, w, b):
    return np.asarray(X, dtype=float) @ np.asarray(w, dtype=float) + b


def gram(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return X @ X.T

broadcast-center.article:
# Broadcasting

## Intuition
Subtracting a per-column mean from every row should not need a loop: NumPy "stretches" the
smaller array across the larger one. That stretching is **broadcasting**, done without copying
memory.

## Precise explanation
Compare shapes from the **right**. Two dimensions are compatible if they are equal or one of
them is 1 (a missing leading dimension counts as 1). The result takes the larger size.
| X shape | other | result |
|---|---|---|
| (4, 3) | (3,) | (4, 3) — row vector stretched down |
| (4, 3) | (4, 1) | (4, 3) — column stretched across |
| (4, 3) | (4,) | **error** (3 vs 4) |

To scale row *i* by `w[i]` with `w.shape == (4,)`, reshape it to a column: `w[:, np.newaxis]`
(or `w[:, None]`, `w.reshape(-1, 1)`).

## Worked example
```python
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 6.]])
X - X.mean(axis=0)            # [[-1, -2], [1, 2]]
X * np.array([10, 0.5])[:, None]   # [[10, 20], [1.5, 3]]
```

## Common mistakes
* Multiplying `(4, 3)` by `(4,)` and getting a shape error — reshape to `(4, 1)`.
* Accidental broadcasting: `(n,)` minus `(n, 1)` produces an `(n, n)` matrix silently!
* Dividing by a zero standard deviation for a constant column.

## Why this matters
Standardization (ML-08), adding bias vectors in neural layers (DL-04), and pairwise distances
(NP-11) are all broadcasting.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)
- [Scientific Python Lectures](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/) — Scientific Python developers (`S006`)
broadcast-center.statement:
## Task

For a 2-D float array `X` of shape `(n, d)`, implement without loops:
* `center_columns(X)` → `X` minus its column means.
* `scale_rows(X, w)` → row `i` multiplied by `w[i]`; raise `ValueError` if `len(w) != n`.
* `standardize(X)` → `(X - mean) / std` per column (population std); columns with std 0 become
  all zeros (no division by zero, no NaN).

**Examples**
```python
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 6.]])
center_columns(X)              # [[-1., -2.], [ 1.,  2.]]
scale_rows(X, [10, 0.5])       # [[10., 20.], [ 1.5, 3.]]
standardize(np.array([[1., 5.], [3., 5.]]))   # [[-1., 0.], [1., 0.]]
```
broadcast-center.solution:
r"""Reference solution for NP-07 Centering Columns with Broadcasting.

Column statistics have shape (d,), which broadcasts across the n rows. Row weights need an
explicit column shape (n, 1). For constant columns the centred values are already zero, so
dividing by 1 instead of 0 yields zeros without NaN.
"""
import numpy as np


def center_columns(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    return X - X.mean(axis=0)


def scale_rows(X, w):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(w, dtype=float)
    if w.shape != (X.shape[0],):
        raise ValueError("w must have one weight per row")
    return X * w[:, None]


def standardize(X):
    Xc = center_columns(X)
    std = Xc.std(axis=0)
    std = np.where(std == 0, 1.0, std)
    return Xc / std

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Column statistics have shape (d,), which broadcasts across the n rows. Row weights need an
explicit column shape (n, 1). For constant columns the centred values are already zero, so
dividing by 1 instead of 0 yields zeros without NaN.
hints: `X - X.mean(axis=0)` broadcasts a (d,) vector over rows.

reshape-stack.article:
# Reshaping and Stacking

## Intuition
Reshaping reinterprets the same numbers in a different grid (12 numbers as 3×4 or 2×6), like
re-folding a strip of paper. Stacking glues arrays together along an axis.

## Precise explanation
* `a.reshape(r, c)` requires `r*c == a.size`; one dimension may be `-1` meaning "whatever fits".
  Reshape fills in **row-major (C) order** — the last axis varies fastest.
* `np.concatenate([a, b], axis=k)` joins along an existing axis; `np.stack` creates a new axis.
* `np.hstack` / `np.column_stack` join side by side; `np.vstack` on top of each other.
* A batch of images with shape `(N, H, W)` becomes a design matrix `(N, H*W)` with
  `imgs.reshape(N, -1)`.

## Worked example
```python
x = np.arange(10)
x[: (10 // 4) * 4].reshape(-1, 4)     # [[0,1,2,3],[4,5,6,7]] — remainder 8, 9 dropped
np.hstack([np.ones((2, 1)), [[3, 4], [5, 6]]])   # [[1,3,4],[1,5,6]]
```

## Common mistakes
* `reshape(4, -1)` vs `reshape(-1, 4)` — rows vs columns of size 4.
* Using reshape to transpose (it doesn't reorder data; use `.T`).
* Stacking 1-D arrays with `hstack` and getting one long vector instead of columns.

## Why this matters
Mini-batching, adding the intercept column in linear regression (ML-09), flattening images
before a dense layer (DL/CV) and splitting attention heads (LM-10) are reshapes.

## References

- [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (NumPy v2.5 Manual)](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html) — NumPy Developers (`S007`)

* `add_bias_column(X)` → `X` (shape `(n, d)`) with a column of ones prepended → `(n, d+1)`.
* `flatten_images(imgs)` → `(N, H, W)` → `(N, H*W)`, row-major per image; raise `ValueError` if
  `imgs.ndim != 3`.

**Examples**
```python
to_batches(np.arange(10), 4)          # [[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 7]]
add_bias_column(np.array([[3, 4], [5, 6]]))   # [[1., 3., 4.], [1., 5., 6.]]

```
