value-iteration.article:
# Value Iteration

## Intuition
Instead of evaluating a fixed policy, assume you will always pick the best action. Repeatedly update
each state's value with the best one-step lookahead; the values converge to the optimal ones, and
acting greedily on them is optimal.

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §4.4)
$$Q(s, a) = \sum_{(p, s', r, d)} p\,[r + \gamma(1-d)V(s')],\qquad V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a Q_k(s, a).$$
Stop when the max change < θ; then the **greedy policy** $\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)$ (ties →
lowest action) is optimal (for small enough θ).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[V_k] --> Q["Q(s,a) = Σ p[r + γV(s')]"] --> M["V_{k+1}(s) = max_a Q"] --> C{converged?}
  C -- no --> V
  C -- yes --> G["π(s) = argmax_a Q(s,a)"]
```

## Worked example
Corridor with "left" (stay, −1) and "right" (towards goal): optimal values match always-right
evaluation (RL-08); greedy policy = right everywhere.

## Common mistakes
* Taking the max over next states instead of over actions.
* Extracting the policy from stale values.
* Including terminal successors' values.

## Why this matters
Value iteration is the prototypical planning algorithm and the dynamic-programming ancestor of
Q-learning.

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
- [Dive into Deep Learning — Reinforcement Learning chapter](https://d2l.ai/chapter_reinforcement-learning/index.html) — Pratik Chaudhari, Rasool Fakoor, Kavosh Asadi (D2L) (`S034`)
value-iteration.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `q_from_v(P, V, gamma)` → array `(n_states, n_actions)` of one-step lookahead values (all states
  have the same action set).
* `value_iteration(P, gamma=0.9, theta=1e-10, max_iter=10000)` → `(V, policy)` where `policy` is an
  int array of greedy actions (ties → lowest). Synchronous updates.

**Example**
```python
g = GridWorld(["S..G", ".#.X"])     # from RL-02 (provide your own copy or use P directly)
V, pi = value_iteration(g.build_P(), gamma=0.9)
pi[0], pi[1], pi[2]                 # (1, 1, 1)  — go right towards G
```
value-iteration.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The lookahead helper computes Q from V for every state–action pair. Each sweep replaces V with the
row-wise maximum of Q; after convergence, argmax of Q gives the optimal greedy policy with the
lowest-index tie-break.
hints: `nA = len(P[0])`; `Q = np.zeros((nS, nA))`.
`Q[s, a] = sum(p * (r + gamma * (0 if d else V[s2])) for p, s2, r, d in P[s][a])`.
Loop: `Q = q_from_v(P, V, gamma); new = Q.max(axis=1)`; policy = `q_from_v(P, V, gamma).argmax(axis=1)`.

failureFeedback.advice: V(s) = max_a Σ p[r + γ(1−done)V(s')].
Sum over outcomes weighted by probability; terminal outcomes don't bootstrap.
The greedy policy uses argmax over actions of Q.
np.argmax gives the lowest action on ties.

Detect policy stability

policy-iteration.article:
# Policy Iteration

## Intuition
Start with any policy. Work out how good it is (evaluation), then switch every state to the action
that looks best given those values (improvement). Repeat until nothing changes — the policy is then
optimal. It usually needs surprisingly few rounds.

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §4.3)
1. Initialise deterministic policy π(s) = 0 for all s.
2. **Evaluate** π (RL-08) with the deterministic policy matrix.
3. **Improve:** π′(s) = argmax_a Q(s, a) from the evaluated V (ties → lowest action).
4. If π′ = π stop, else π ← π′ and repeat.
The policy improvement theorem guarantees each new policy is at least as good; with finitely many
deterministic policies the loop terminates. To avoid flip-flopping between equally good actions, the
lowest-index tie-break makes "unchanged" well defined.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P0[π0] --> E[evaluate V^π] --> I[improve: greedy w.r.t. V] --> C{π changed?}
  C -- yes --> E
  C -- no --> O[optimal π*]
```

## Worked example
Corridor with actions left/right: π₀ = all-left; evaluation gives negative values; improvement
switches the state next to the goal to right, then the others — stable after a few iterations.

## Common mistakes
* Comparing policies by values with floating-point noise instead of comparing actions.
* Forgetting to re-evaluate after improvement.
* Ties causing infinite loops.

## Why this matters
Policy iteration is the template for actor–critic methods: a critic evaluates, an actor improves.

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
- [Dive into Deep Learning — Reinforcement Learning chapter](https://d2l.ai/chapter_reinforcement-learning/index.html) — Pratik Chaudhari, Rasool Fakoor, Kavosh Asadi (D2L) (`S034`)
policy-iteration.statement:
## Task

Write `policy_iteration(P, gamma=0.9, theta=1e-10, max_iter=100)` returning `(V, policy, n_improvements)`
where `policy` is an int array and `n_improvements` the number of evaluate-improve cycles performed
(including the final one where the policy did not change). Include your own policy evaluation and
lookahead helpers. Raise `ValueError` if `gamma` not in `[0, 1)`.

**Example**
```python
V, pi, k = policy_iteration(grid_P(["S..G", ".#.X"]), gamma=0.9)
pi[:3]     # [1, 1, 1]
```
policy-iteration.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each cycle evaluates the current deterministic policy to convergence, then acts greedily with respect
to the resulting values. Because ties resolve to the lowest action, an unchanged argmax means the
policy is stable and therefore optimal.
hints: Deterministic policy matrix: `pm = np.zeros((nS, nA)); pm[np.arange(nS), pi] = 1`.
Evaluate synchronously until max change < theta; compute Q from V.
`new_pi = Q.argmax(axis=1)`; stop when `np.array_equal(new_pi, pi)`.

failureFeedback.advice: Evaluate the current policy fully before improving.
Lookahead must weight outcomes by probability and stop bootstrapping at done.
Count the final cycle in which the policy did not change.
Improvement is argmax over actions of Q computed from V^π.

mc-first-visit.article:
# Monte Carlo Prediction

## Intuition
Don't know the environment's rules? Play complete episodes, record the return that followed each
visit to a state, and average. With enough episodes the averages approach the true values.

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §5.1)
An episode is a list of `(state, reward)` pairs: the state at time t and the reward received after
acting there, $R_{t+1}$. Compute returns backwards (RL-01). **First-visit MC** averages, for each state,
only the return following its *first* occurrence in each episode; **every-visit MC** uses every
occurrence. Both converge to $V^\pi(s)$. States never visited keep value 0 (and count 0).

## Worked example
Episodes [(A, 1), (B, 0), (A, 2)] and [(B, 5)], γ = 1, states A = 0, B = 1:
episode 1 returns: t0: 3, t1: 2, t2: 2. First-visit: A ← 3, B ← 2. Episode 2: B ← 5.
V = [3, 3.5]. Every-visit: A ← {3, 2}, B ← {2, 5} → [2.5, 3.5].

## Common mistakes
* Using the *last* visit instead of the first.
* Forward return computation per visit (O(T²)).
* Averaging returns across episodes incorrectly (keep sums and counts).

## Why this matters
MC methods need no model of the environment, only experience — the foundation of model-free RL.

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
mc-first-visit.statement:
## Task

Write `mc_prediction(episodes, n_states, gamma, first_visit=True)` returning `(V, counts)` arrays
(`V[s] = 0` and `counts[s] = 0` for unvisited states). Raise `ValueError` for `gamma` outside
`[0, 1]`.

**Example**
```python
eps = [[(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, 2)], [(1, 5)]]
mc_prediction(eps, 2, 1.0)[0]                      # [3. , 3.5]
mc_prediction(eps, 2, 1.0, first_visit=False)[0]   # [2.5, 3.5]
```
mc-first-visit.solution:
r"""Reference solution for RL-11 First-Visit Monte Carlo Prediction.

A backward pass gives the return at every time step. Scanning forward, the first-visit rule skips
repeated states within an episode. Running sums and counts produce averages; unvisited states stay 0.
"""
import numpy as np


def mc_prediction(episodes, n_states, gamma, first_visit=True):
    if not 0 <= gamma <= 1:
        raise ValueError("gamma must be in [0, 1]")
    sums = np.zeros(n_states)
    counts = np.zeros(n_states, dtype=int)
    for ep in episodes:
        G = 0.0
        returns = [0.0] * len(ep)
        for t in range(len(ep) - 1, -1, -1):
            G = ep[t][1] + gamma * G
            returns[t] = G
        seen = set()
        for t, (s, _) in enumerate(ep):
            if first_visit and s in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(s)
            sums[s] += returns[t]
            counts[s] += 1
    V = np.divide(sums, counts, out=np.zeros(n_states), where=counts > 0)
    return V, counts
mc-first-visit.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

A backward pass gives the return at every time step. Scanning forward, the first-visit rule skips
repeated states within an episode. Running sums and counts produce averages; unvisited states stay 0.
hints: For each episode compute `G_t` for all t with a backward pass.
First visit: find `first = {}` mapping state → earliest t.
Keep `sums[s]` and `counts[s]`; V = sums / counts where counts > 0.

failureFeedback.advice: Only the first occurrence of each state per episode counts.
Return at t is R_{t+1} + γG_{t+1}; compute backwards.
With first_visit=False every occurrence adds its return.
Unvisited states keep V = 0 and count 0.

td0-prediction.article:
# TD(0): Learning from Every Step

## Intuition
Monte Carlo waits until the end of an episode. TD learning updates immediately after each step, using
its own current estimate of the next state's value as a stand-in for the rest of the return —
"learning a guess from a guess" (bootstrapping).

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §6.1)
For a transition $(s, r, s', d)$:
$$\delta = r + \gamma(1-d)V(s') - V(s),\qquad V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\,\delta.$$
δ is the **TD error**. Transitions are processed in order, updating V in place. With a decaying (or
small) α and enough experience, TD(0) converges to $V^\pi$; on finite batches repeated many times
(batch TD) it converges to the certainty-equivalence estimate, which can differ from the MC average.

## Worked example
V = [0, 0], transition (0, r = 1, s' = 1, not done), then (1, r = 2, terminal), α = 0.5, γ = 1:
δ₁ = 1 + 0 − 0 = 1 → V(0) = 0.5; δ₂ = 2 − 0 = 2 → V(1) = 1.

## Common mistakes
* Bootstrapping from terminal states.
* Updating with the *new* V(s) inside the same δ computation (compute δ first).
* α too large → oscillations.

## Why this matters
TD learning underlies Q-learning, SARSA, actor–critic methods and value learning in modern deep RL.

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
td0-prediction.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `td_error(V, s, r, s_next, done, gamma)` → float δ.
* `td0(episodes, n_states, alpha, gamma, sweeps=1)` → value array; `episodes` is a list of episodes,
  each a list of `(s, r, s_next, done)`; process all episodes in order, `sweeps` times, updating
  in place from `V = zeros`. Raise `ValueError` unless `0 < alpha <= 1` and `0 <= gamma <= 1`.

**Example**
```python
td0([[(0, 1.0, 1, False), (1, 2.0, 1, True)]], 2, alpha=0.5, gamma=1.0)   # [0.5, 1. ]
```
td0-prediction.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The TD error compares the one-step bootstrapped target with the current estimate; the value moves a
fraction α towards the target. Processing transitions in order with in-place updates is online TD(0).
hints: `target = r + (0 if done else gamma * V[s_next])`.
`delta = target - V[s]`; then `V[s] += alpha * delta`.
Outer loop over sweeps, then episodes, then transitions.

failureFeedback.advice: Don't bootstrap when done is True.
Update V in place, transition by transition, in order.
Repeat all episodes `sweeps` times.
Batch TD values A by bootstrapping from B (Sutton & Barto's A/B example idea).

q-learning.article:
# Q-Learning

## Intuition
Learn the value of every (state, action) pair directly from experience, always assuming you will act
optimally afterwards — even while you are still exploring. Then act greedily on those values.

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §6.5)
$$Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\big[r + \gamma(1-d)\max_{a'}Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)\big].$$
**Off-policy:** the target uses the greedy $\max_{a'}$ even though the behaviour policy is ε-greedy.
Training loop (this course's recipe, one seeded generator):
```text
for each episode:
    s = start
    for up to max_steps steps:
        a = epsilon_greedy(Q[s], epsilon, rng)      # RL-05 recipe
        s2, r, done = env_step(s, a)
        q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, done, alpha, gamma)
        s = s2; stop if done
```
The greedy policy $\arg\max_a Q(s,a)$ converges to optimal with sufficient exploration and a suitable α.

## Worked example
Q(s,·) = [0, 0], action 1 gives r = −1 to s' with max Q = 5, α = 0.5, γ = 0.9:
Q(s,1) = 0 + 0.5(−1 + 4.5 − 0) = 1.75.

## Common mistakes
* Using $Q(s', a_\text{next})$ (that's SARSA, RL-15).
* Bootstrapping from terminal states.
* Never decaying/limiting episodes → infinite loops; use max_steps.

## Why this matters
Q-learning is the basis of DQN, which learned to play Atari games from pixels.

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
- [Dive into Deep Learning — Reinforcement Learning chapter](https://d2l.ai/chapter_reinforcement-learning/index.html) — Pratik Chaudhari, Rasool Fakoor, Kavosh Asadi (D2L) (`S034`)
q-learning.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, done, alpha, gamma)` → updates `Q` in place and returns the TD error.
* `q_learning(env_step, start, n_states, n_actions, episodes, alpha, gamma, epsilon, seed, max_steps=100)`
  → `(Q, episode_returns)` following the recipe; `env_step(s, a)` returns `(s2, r, done)`;
  `episode_returns` holds the undiscounted reward sum per episode.

**Example**
```python
# 1-D corridor: states 0..3, action 1 moves right, 0 moves left; reaching 3 gives +10 and ends.
Q, rets = q_learning(corridor_step, 0, 4, 2, episodes=300, alpha=0.5, gamma=0.9, epsilon=0.1, seed=0)
Q[:3].argmax(axis=1)     # [1, 1, 1]
```
q-learning.solution:
r"""Reference solution for RL-13 Tabular Q-Learning.

The update moves Q(s, a) towards the reward plus the discounted value of the best next action
(off-policy target). The loop explores with ε-greedy behaviour from one seeded generator, applies an
update after every step, and records each episode's total reward.
"""
import numpy as np


def q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, done, alpha, gamma):
    target = r + (0.0 if done else gamma * float(np.max(Q[s2])))
    delta = target - Q[s, a]
    Q[s, a] += alpha * delta
    return float(delta)


def q_learning(env_step, start, n_states, n_actions, episodes, alpha, gamma, epsilon, seed, max_steps=100):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    returns = []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, total = start, 0.0
        for _ in range(max_steps):
            if rng.random() < epsilon:
                a = int(rng.integers(n_actions))
            else:
                a = int(np.argmax(Q[s]))
            s2, r, done = env_step(s, a)
            q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, done, alpha, gamma)
            total += r
            s = s2
            if done:
                break
        returns.append(total)
    return Q, returns

rl-frozenlake-q.article:
# Q-Learning on FrozenLake

## Intuition
FrozenLake is a 4×4 grid of ice with holes; the agent walks from the top-left to the goal at the
bottom-right and only gets reward 1 if it arrives. On slippery ice, an action may move it sideways.
Rewards are rare, so the agent must explore a lot before Q-values carry any signal.

## Precise explanation
```python
env = gym.make("FrozenLake-v1", is_slippery=True)      # 16 states, 4 actions (left, down, right, up)
Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * (0 if terminated else Q[s2].max()) - Q[s, a])
```

* This is the update of RL-13: bootstrap from the best next action **unless the episode
  terminated** (a hole or the goal). A truncated episode (100-step limit) is not terminal.
* **Decaying epsilon**: explore almost always at first, then less: ε = max(ε_min, 1 − episode/(0.7·episodes)).
* **Random tie-breaking**: at the start all Q-values are 0, and `argmax` would always choose action 0;
  pick uniformly among the actions with the maximum value instead.
* Seed both the environment (`env.reset(seed=...)`) and your own generator, so training is reproducible.
* **Evaluate** the greedy policy (no exploration) over many new episodes and report the success rate.
  On the slippery lake even the optimal policy succeeds only about three times in four.

## Worked example
On the non-slippery lake, 300 episodes are enough for a 100% success rate. On the slippery lake, 2,000
episodes give about 73%.

## Common mistakes
* Bootstrapping from the next state after falling into a hole.
* Plain `argmax` with all-zero Q-values, so the agent never leaves the first column.
* Evaluating with exploration still on.

## Why this matters
FrozenLake is the classic sanity check for tabular RL; the grid-game project idea after this step asks
you to design your own environment and train the same agent on it.

## References

- [Frozen Lake (Gymnasium docs)](https://gymnasium.farama.org/environments/toy_text/frozen_lake/) — Farama Foundation (`S141`)
- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)

   `episodes` episodes (`env.reset(seed=seed + i)`) and returns the fraction with reward 1 at the end.

rl-frozenlake-q.solution:
r"""Reference solution for RL-14 Q-Learning on FrozenLake.

Decaying epsilon spends the early episodes exploring, and random tie-breaking avoids getting stuck on
action 0 while all values are equal. The update bootstraps only from non-terminal states. Evaluation
turns exploration off and counts how often the greedy policy reaches the goal.
"""
import numpy as np


def q_learning(env, episodes, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99, eps_min=0.05, seed=0):
    if episodes < 1:
        raise ValueError("episodes must be at least 1")
    n_states, n_actions = env.observation_space.n, env.action_space.n
    Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    for ep in range(episodes):
        eps = max(eps_min, 1 - ep / (0.7 * episodes))
        obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + ep)
        done = False
        while not done:
            if rng.random() < eps:
                a = int(rng.integers(n_actions))
            else:
                q = Q[obs]
                a = int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(q == q.max())))
            next_obs, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
            target = r + (0.0 if terminated else gamma * Q[next_obs].max())
            Q[obs, a] += alpha * (target - Q[obs, a])
            obs, done = next_obs, terminated or truncated
    return Q


def success_rate(env, Q, episodes=200, seed=10000):
    wins = 0.0
    for i in range(episodes):
        obs, _ = env.reset(seed=seed + i)
        done = False
        while not done:
            obs, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(int(np.argmax(Q[obs])))
            done = terminated or truncated
        wins += r
    return wins / episodes

sarsa.article:
# SARSA: On-Policy TD Control

## Intuition
Q-learning learns values as if it will act perfectly later; SARSA learns the values of what it will
*actually* do, exploration included. Near a cliff, an exploring agent that sometimes slips should
prefer a safer path — and SARSA learns exactly that.

## Precise explanation (Sutton & Barto, §6.4; cliff-walking example 6.6)
Name from the tuple $(S, A, R, S', A')$:
$$Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\big[r + \gamma(1-d)\,Q(s', a') - Q(s,a)\big],$$
where $a'$ is the action the ε-greedy policy will take next. Loop recipe:
```text
for each episode:
    s = start; a = eps_greedy(Q[s])
    repeat up to max_steps:
        s2, r, done = env_step(s, a)
        a2 = eps_greedy(Q[s2]) if not done else 0
        sarsa_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, a2, done, ...)
        s, a = s2, a2; stop if done
```
(One shared seeded generator; ε-greedy recipe from RL-05.)

## Worked example
Q(s', ·) = [5, 2], next action a′ = 1, r = −1, α = 0.5, γ = 0.9 → target −1 + 0.9·2 = 0.8
(Q-learning would use 5).

## Common mistakes
* Choosing a′ after the update (the update must use the a′ actually taken next).
* Using max over actions (that's Q-learning).
* Forgetting to carry a′ forward as the next action.

## Why this matters
The on/off-policy distinction matters whenever exploration is costly or dangerous (robots, real
systems).

## References

- [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) — Richard S. Sutton, Andrew G. Barto (MIT Press 2018) (`S033`)
sarsa.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `sarsa_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, a2, done, alpha, gamma)` → updates in place, returns the TD error.
* `sarsa(env_step, start, n_states, n_actions, episodes, alpha, gamma, epsilon, seed, max_steps=100)`
  → `(Q, episode_returns)` following the recipe.

**Example**
```python
Q = np.zeros((2, 2)); Q[1] = [5., 2.]
sarsa_update(Q, 0, 1, -1.0, 1, 1, False, 0.5, 0.9); Q[0, 1]   # 0.4
```

## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The update bootstraps from the value of the next action actually selected by the ε-greedy policy, so
the learned values reflect the behaviour policy including its exploratory mistakes. The next action is
chosen before the update and then executed.
hints: `target = r + (0 if done else gamma * Q[s2, a2])`.
Write an inner `eps(state)` using the shared rng.
Choose `a2` before calling `sarsa_update`, then set `s, a = s2, a2`.

failureFeedback.advice: SARSA's target uses Q(s', a') for the next action actually chosen, not the max.
No bootstrapping when done.
Choose a' with ε-greedy before updating and carry it forward; SARSA should learn the safe path.
Use one seeded generator for all action choices.

tool-registry.article:
# Tools: How Agents Act

## Intuition
A language model can only produce text. To *do* things — search, calculate, read files — it emits a
request like `{"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}}`, and ordinary code runs the matching function.
The registry is the switchboard between the model and the world.

## Precise explanation
* **Register:** name → (function, schema, description). The schema lists required argument names and
  their Python types, e.g. `{"a": int, "b": int}`.
* **Dispatch:** look up the tool; check arguments (missing, unexpected, wrong type); call the function;
  wrap the outcome as `{"ok": True, "result": ...}` or `{"ok": False, "error": "..."}`.
* Errors become **data returned to the model**, not exceptions that kill the agent: the model can read
  the error and retry (AG-15).
* Clear tool names and descriptions matter: Anthropic's "Building effective agents" article
  recommends investing in well-documented, hard-to-misuse tool interfaces.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[model output: tool call] --> R{registry: known tool?}
  R -- no --> E1["error: unknown tool"]
  R -- yes --> V{args valid?}
  V -- no --> E2["error: bad args"]
  V -- yes --> F[run function] --> O["ok + result"]
```

## Worked example
dispatch({"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": "3"}}) → `{"ok": False, "error": "argument 'b' must be int"}`.

## Common mistakes
* Calling `fn(**args)` without validation (crashes or worse, silent misuse).
* Raising exceptions out of dispatch.
* Accepting `True` for an `int` parameter (bool is a subclass of int; see PY-19).

## Why this matters
Every agent framework has this layer; validation here is the first line of defence for safety
(AG-19).

## References

- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
tool-registry.statement:
## Task

Implement `class ToolRegistry` with:
* `register(name, fn, schema, description="")` — raise `ValueError` if the name is already registered.
* `dispatch(call)` — `call` is a dict with keys `"tool"` and `"args"` (dict). Return
  `{"ok": True, "result": value}` or `{"ok": False, "error": message}` for: unknown tool
  (`"unknown tool '<name>'"`), missing argument (`"missing argument '<arg>'"`), unexpected argument
  (`"unexpected argument '<arg>'"`), wrong type (`"argument '<arg>' must be <type>"`, using
  `type.__name__`; bools are not ints), or an exception raised by the tool
  (`"tool error: <ExceptionType>: <message>"`). Check in that order (args in sorted order).
* `describe()` → list of `{"name", "description", "args": {arg: type_name}}` sorted by name.

**Example**
```python
reg = ToolRegistry(); reg.register("add", lambda a, b: a + b, {"a": int, "b": int}, "Add two ints")
reg.dispatch({"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}})     # {'ok': True, 'result': 5}
reg.dispatch({"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2}})             # {'ok': False, 'error': "missing argument 'b'"}
```
tool-registry.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Dispatch validates in a fixed order — tool exists, required args present, no extras, correct types —
and only then runs the tool inside a try/except so that any failure is reported as a structured error
the model can read. Floats accept ints; bools are rejected for numeric types.
hints: Store `self._tools[name] = (fn, schema, description)`.
Check missing = sorted(schema − args), unexpected = sorted(args − schema), then types.
Wrap `fn(**args)` in `try/except Exception as e` and format `type(e).__name__`.

failureFeedback.advice: Catch exceptions from the tool and return them as an error dict.
Reject bools for int/float parameters; floats accept ints.
Check missing args before unexpected args, each in sorted order.
Return tools sorted by name with argument type names.

objectives: Extract structured tool calls from free text

parse-tool-call.article:
# Parsing What the Model Said

## Intuition
Model output is text, and text can be malformed: missing braces, extra prose, two calls at once. The
agent needs a strict parser that turns text into one of a few well-defined cases — and treats
anything else as an error to report back, not something to guess at.

## Precise explanation
Protocol used in this course (a common pattern; real APIs often return structured tool calls natively):
* A tool call is wrapped in tags: `<tool_call>{"tool": "...", "args": {...}}</tool_call>`. Exactly one
  call per message.
* A final answer starts with `FINAL:` (after optional leading whitespace).
* Anything else is invalid.
Parse with `re` to find tag contents (non-greedy, `re.DOTALL`), then `json.loads`. Validate the
structure: a JSON object with a string `"tool"` and a dict `"args"` (default `{}`).
Parsing must be **side-effect free** — never call tools here.

## Worked example
`'I will add. <tool_call>{"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}</tool_call>'` →
`{"type": "tool_call", "tool": "add", "args": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}`.
`'FINAL: 3'` → `{"type": "final", "content": "3"}`.

## Common mistakes
* Greedy regex swallowing two calls.
* `eval` on model output (arbitrary code execution!).
* Accepting both a final answer and a tool call in the same message without a rule.

## Why this matters
Robust parsing turns model unreliability into recoverable errors (AG-15) and is a security boundary.

## References

- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Shunyu Yao et al. (`S036`)

parse-tool-call.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

A non-greedy, DOTALL regex finds every tag pair. The parser enforces exactly one call, decodes it with
`json.loads` (never `eval`) and validates its shape. Without tags, only an explicit `FINAL:` prefix is
accepted; everything else becomes an error message for the agent loop.
hints: `blocks = re.findall(r'<tool_call>(.*?)</tool_call>', text, re.DOTALL)`.
If `len(blocks) > 1` → multiple; if 1 → `json.loads` in try/except `json.JSONDecodeError`.
Validate `isinstance(obj, dict)`, `isinstance(obj.get('tool'), str)`, `isinstance(obj.get('args', {}), dict)`.

failureFeedback.advice: Use a non-greedy pattern (.*?) and reject more than one block.
Pass re.DOTALL so '.' matches newlines.
Only use json.loads; never eval model output.
Accept 'FINAL:' after leading whitespace and strip the content.

ag-langchain-tools.article:
# Tools and Tool Calling with LangChain

## Intuition
In AG-01 and AG-02 you kept a dict of functions and parsed a text format for
calling them. Modern chat models do the parsing for you: you describe each tool (name, purpose,
arguments) and the model replies with **structured tool calls**. Your code runs them and sends the
results back as tool messages.

## Precise explanation
```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def word_count(text: str) -> int:
    """Count the words in a text."""
    return len(text.split())

word_count.name, word_count.description, word_count.args   # 'word_count', the docstring, a JSON schema
word_count.invoke({"text": "hello there"})                  # 2
model_with_tools = model.bind_tools([word_count])           # the model now knows the tool
```

* The **docstring becomes the description** the model reads, and the type hints become the argument
  schema — both are part of the prompt, so write them carefully.
* A model reply asking for tools is an `AIMessage` whose `tool_calls` is a list of dicts
  `{"name": ..., "args": {...}, "id": ...}`; several calls can come at once.
* Each result goes back as `ToolMessage(content=str(result), tool_call_id=call["id"])`, so the model can
  match results to calls. Use `status="error"` for failures.
* `tool.invoke(args)` validates arguments against the schema and raises an error (a `ValueError`
  subclass from Pydantic) for missing or wrongly typed arguments.

## Worked example
The model replies with two calls: `word_count({"text": "to be or not"})` and
`to_fahrenheit({"celsius": 100})`. Running them gives tool messages "4" and "212.0". A call to
`delete_files` (not registered) gets the error message "Error: unknown tool delete_files" instead of
crashing the agent.

## What the library does inside
`@tool` wraps your function in an object with a name, description and Pydantic argument schema — a
richer version of your registry — and providers convert those into their function-calling format.

## Common mistakes
* No docstring: the model has no idea when to use the tool.
* Returning the result without the matching `tool_call_id`.
* Letting a bad argument or unknown tool raise and stop the whole agent.

## Why this matters
Tool calling turns a chat model into an agent; every LangGraph agent in this topic uses this exact
message protocol.

## References

- [Tools (LangChain docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/tools) — LangChain (`S134`)
- [Messages (LangChain docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages) — LangChain (`S130`)

reflex-agent-loop.article:
# Agents and Environments

## Intuition
Strip away the LLM and an agent is still: sense the world, choose an action, change the world. Russell
and Norvig's classic two-square vacuum world makes this concrete.

## Precise explanation (AIMA, ch. 2)
* **Environment:** squares A and B, each Clean or Dirty; the agent is in one square.
* **Percept:** `(location, status)` — the agent only sees its own square (partial observability).
* **Actions:** `"Suck"`, `"Left"`, `"Right"`.
* **Simple reflex agent:** maps the current percept to an action with condition–action rules:
  if Dirty → Suck; elif at A → Right; else → Left.
* **Performance measure** (our choice): +1 for each clean square after each step, −1 per movement.
The loop: percept = env.percept(); action = agent(percept); env.execute(action); record.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[environment] -- percept --> A[agent rules]
  A -- action --> E
```

## Worked example
Start at A, both dirty: Suck (A clean, score +1), Right (−1 +1), Suck (+2), Left (−1 +2) …

## Common mistakes
* Letting the agent read the whole environment state (breaks the percept abstraction).
* Mixing up the agent function (decision) with the environment (dynamics).
* Scoring movement and cleanliness inconsistently.

## Why this matters
LLM agents are exactly this loop with a learned policy and tools as actions; AG-05 adds goals and budgets.

## References

- [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.)](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/) — Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig (`S038`)
reflex-agent-loop.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `reflex_vacuum_agent(percept)` with the rules above.
* `class VacuumWorld(dirt, location)` — `dirt` is a dict `{"A": bool, "B": bool}` (True = dirty),
  `location` "A" or "B"; methods `percept()` → `(location, "Dirty" | "Clean")` and `execute(action)`
  (unknown action → `ValueError`; Left at A / Right at B do nothing but still count as movement).
* `run(agent, env, steps)` → `(log, score)` where `log` is a list of `(percept, action)` and score
  follows the performance measure (after each action: +1 per clean square, −1 if the action was
  Left/Right).

**Example**
```python
log, score = run(reflex_vacuum_agent, VacuumWorld({"A": True, "B": True}, "A"), 4)
[a for _, a in log]   # ['Suck', 'Right', 'Suck', 'Left']
score                 # 1 + (−1 + 1) + 2 + (−1 + 2) = 4
```
reflex-agent-loop.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The agent sees only its percept and applies condition–action rules. The environment owns the state
and dynamics. The loop alternates perception, decision and execution, scoring cleanliness and
penalising movement after every step.
hints: Agent: `loc, status = percept`.
`execute`: Suck sets `dirt[loc] = False`; Left → 'A'; Right → 'B'.
Score after each step: `sum(not d for d in env.dirt.values()) - (1 if action in ('Left', 'Right') else 0)`.

failureFeedback.advice: Score after each action: clean squares minus 1 for movement.

Copy the dirt dict inside VacuumWorld.
A simple reflex agent keeps moving even when everything is clean.

goal-and-budget.article:
# Goals, Budgets and Stopping Conditions

## Intuition
An agent that never stops is a bug — and an expensive one when every step calls a paid model. Agents
need an explicit goal test and hard limits on steps and cost, plus a clear record of *why* they
stopped.

## Precise explanation
Loop:
```text
for step in 1..max_steps:
    if goal_test(state): return "success"
    action = policy(state)
    state, cost = transition(state, action)
    total += cost
    if max_cost is not None and total > max_cost: return "cost_exceeded"
check goal once more after the last step → "success" else "step_limit"
```
Return the status, final state, trajectory of actions and total cost. Checking the goal *before* acting
means an already-solved task costs nothing. Anthropic's agent guidance recommends stopping conditions
such as a maximum number of iterations to maintain control.

## Worked example
Counter from 0, goal ≥ 3, action +1 cost 1: max_steps 5 → success after 3 actions, cost 3;
max_steps 2 → step_limit with state 2; max_cost 1.5 → cost_exceeded after the second action.

## Common mistakes
* Off-by-one between steps and actions.
* Checking cost before applying it (overspend by one step).
* Returning only the final state with no reason.

## Why this matters
Budgets and termination reasons are essential for safe, debuggable agents (AG-06, AG-19).

## References

- [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.)](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/) — Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig (`S038`)
- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)

"cost": total_cost}` following the pseudocode. Raise `ValueError` if `max_steps < 0`.

**Example**
```python
r = run_with_budget(0, lambda s: "inc", lambda s, a: (s + 1, 1.0), lambda s: s >= 3, max_steps=5)
r["status"], r["state"], r["cost"]    # ('success', 3, 3.0)
```

react-loop.article:
# The ReAct Loop

## Intuition
ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) lets a language model alternate between *thinking*, *acting* (calling a tool)
and *observing* the result, so it can look things up instead of guessing. The agent code is just a
loop that shuttles messages between the model and the tools.

## Precise explanation
Transcript as a list of messages `{"role": ..., "content": ...}`:
1. Start with `{"role": "user", "content": question}`.
2. Repeat up to `max_steps`:
   * `text = model(transcript)` (our scripted model is a Python function); append
     `{"role": "assistant", "content": text}`.
   * Parse it (AG-02). Final → return the answer. Tool call → dispatch (AG-01) and append
     `{"role": "tool", "content": json.dumps(result)}`. Invalid → append
     `{"role": "tool", "content": json.dumps({"ok": False, "error": ...})}` so the model can fix itself.
3. Out of steps → status `"step_limit"`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as user
  participant M as model
  participant T as tools
  U->>M: question
  M->>T: tool_call(search, …)
  T->>M: observation
  M->>U: FINAL: answer
```

## Worked example
Scripted model: first reply calls `add(2, 3)`; after seeing `{"ok": true, "result": 5}` it replies
`FINAL: 5`. The loop returns answer "5" after 2 model calls.

## Common mistakes
* Not appending observations (the model never sees results).
* Crashing on invalid output instead of reporting the error.
* No step limit.

## Why this matters
This loop — model, tools, observations — is the core of tool-using LLM agents.

## References

- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Shunyu Yao et al. (`S036`)
- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
react-loop.statement:
## Task

Write `react_agent(model, registry, question, max_steps=5)` returning
`{"status": "final" | "step_limit", "answer": str | None, "transcript": list, "tool_calls": int}`
following the procedure above. Include your own copies of the AG-01 registry interface usage
(`registry.dispatch(call)`) and AG-02 parser (copy `parse_model_output`). `json.dumps` tool results with
default settings. `model(transcript)` receives a *copy* of the transcript list.

**Example**
```python
r = react_agent(scripted_model, reg, "What is 2 + 3?")
r["status"], r["answer"], r["tool_calls"]    # ('final', '5', 1)
```
react-loop.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each iteration asks the model for its next message, parses it, and either finishes, executes a tool,
or reports a parse error — always appending an observation so the model sees the consequence of its
action. The step limit guarantees termination.
hints: `transcript = [{'role': 'user', 'content': question}]`.
After parsing a tool call: `res = registry.dispatch({'tool': p['tool'], 'args': p['args']})`.
Append `{'role': 'tool', 'content': json.dumps(res)}`; count tool calls.

failureFeedback.advice: Append the assistant message, then a tool message with json.dumps(result).
Report parse errors to the model as {'ok': False, 'error': ...}.
Stop after max_steps model calls with status 'step_limit'.
Call the model with the transcript including previous observations.

ag-langgraph-basics.article:
# LangGraph Basics: State, Nodes and Edges

## Intuition
Your agent loops so far were `while` loops with `if`s inside. As workflows grow — retries,
approvals, several workers — that control flow becomes hard to read and test. LangGraph makes it
explicit: a **state** dict, **nodes** that read the state and return updates, and **edges** that
decide which node runs next.

## Precise explanation
```python
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
    text: str
    steps: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]      # reducer: updates are appended, not replaced

def strip(state):
    return {"text": state["text"].strip(), "steps": ["strip"]}    # return only what changes

graph = StateGraph(State)
graph.add_node("strip", strip)
graph.add_edge(START, "strip")
graph.add_conditional_edges("check", route)        # route(state) returns a node name or END
app = graph.compile()
app.invoke({"text": "  Hello ", "steps": []})      # the final state
```

* A node returns a **partial update**. Keys without a reducer are overwritten; a key annotated with a
  reducer such as `operator.add` combines the old and new values. (`operator.add(a, b)` is `a + b` as a
  function, from the standard-library `operator` module; for lists it concatenates.)
* `add_conditional_edges(node, route)` calls `route(state)` after the node and follows the returned
  name, which may point back to an earlier node to form a loop.
* `compile()` checks the graph (unknown nodes, unreachable nodes) and returns a runnable with
  `invoke`. `app.get_graph().nodes` lists the nodes; LangGraph can also draw the graph.
* A loop that never ends stops with `GraphRecursionError` after `recursion_limit` steps (default 25).

## Worked example
For "  The Quick Brown Fox Jumps  " and `max_words=3`: strip, lower, check (5 words, too long),
shorten, check (4), shorten, check (3, done). The final text is "the quick brown" and `steps` is
["strip", "lower", "shorten", "shorten"].

## Common mistakes
* Mutating `state` inside a node instead of returning an update.
* Forgetting the reducer, so each node's list replaces the previous one.
* A routing function that returns a name that is not a node.

## Why this matters
The ReAct agent, orchestrator and guardrail steps that follow are LangGraph graphs; reading and
drawing them is how you debug agents.

## References

- [Graph API (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api) — LangChain (`S136`)
- [Workflows and agents (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents) — LangChain (`S139`)

ag-langgraph-basics.solution:
r"""Reference solution for AG-07 LangGraph Basics: State, Nodes and Edges.

Each node returns only the keys it changes; the `operator.add` reducer appends step names. The
conditional edge after `check` either loops through `shorten` or ends, so the loop's condition lives
in one routing function rather than inside the nodes.
"""
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict

from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph


class CleanerState(TypedDict):
    text: str
    steps: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]


def build_cleaner(max_words):
    if max_words < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_words must be at least 1")

    def route(state):
        return "shorten" if len(state["text"].split()) > max_words else END

    graph = StateGraph(CleanerState)
    graph.add_node("strip", lambda s: {"text": s["text"].strip(), "steps": ["strip"]})
    graph.add_node("lower", lambda s: {"text": s["text"].lower(), "steps": ["lower"]})
    graph.add_node("check", lambda s: {})
    graph.add_node("shorten", lambda s: {"text": " ".join(s["text"].split()[:-1]), "steps": ["shorten"]})
    graph.add_edge(START, "strip")
    graph.add_edge("strip", "lower")
    graph.add_edge("lower", "check")
    graph.add_conditional_edges("check", route)
    graph.add_edge("shorten", "check")
    return graph.compile()

ag-langgraph-react.article:
# A ReAct Agent in LangGraph

## Intuition
The ReAct loop of AG-06 alternates thinking and acting: the model decides on a tool, the
tool runs, the model reads the result, and so on until it answers. In LangGraph that loop is two nodes
and a conditional edge — plus, for free, a step limit and saved conversation history.

## Precise explanation
```python
from langgraph.graph import START, MessagesState, StateGraph
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

bound = model.bind_tools(tools)
def agent(state):
    return {"messages": [bound.invoke(state["messages"])]}

graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)                    # {"messages": [...]} with an add_messages reducer
graph.add_node("agent", agent)
graph.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))            # runs the tool calls of the last AI message
graph.add_edge(START, "agent")
graph.add_conditional_edges("agent", tools_condition)   # "tools" if there are tool calls, else END
graph.add_edge("tools", "agent")
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
app.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage("...")]}, {"configurable": {"thread_id": "alice"}, "recursion_limit": 8})
```

* `MessagesState`'s reducer appends new messages, so the history grows: human, ai (tool calls), tool,
  ai, …
* `ToolNode` executes the calls and returns `ToolMessage`s, turning tool errors into messages.
* `recursion_limit` caps the total number of node executions; reaching it raises
  `GraphRecursionError` — the budget of AG-05.
* With a **checkpointer**, each `thread_id` keeps its own state between calls; the next `invoke` on
  the same thread continues the conversation. `app.get_state(config).values` shows it.

## Worked example
"What is 17 × 23 + 5?" The model calls `multiply(17, 23)`, reads 391, calls `add(391, 5)`, reads 396
and answers "396". The thread then holds six messages: human, ai, tool, ai, tool, ai.

## Common mistakes
* Forgetting the edge from tools back to the agent, so the model never sees the result.
* No step limit, so a confused model loops until the default limit (or your bill) stops it.
* Reusing one thread id for different users.

## Why this matters
This graph is the core of most tool-using assistants; the study-planner project idea after this step
adds real tools to it.

## References

- [Workflows and agents (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents) — LangChain (`S139`)
- [Persistence (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) — LangChain (`S137`)

   routing, and an `InMemorySaver` checkpointer.
2. `run_agent(app, question, thread_id, max_steps=8)` invokes the graph with a `HumanMessage(question)`,
   `thread_id` and `recursion_limit=max_steps`, and returns the content of the last message. If the

ag-langgraph-react.solution:
r"""Reference solution for AG-08 A ReAct Agent in LangGraph.

The agent node asks the model for its next move; `tools_condition` sends tool calls to the ToolNode
and plain answers to the end, and the tool results flow back to the model. The checkpointer stores
each thread's messages, and the recursion limit turns a runaway loop into a clear message.
"""
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.errors import GraphRecursionError
from langgraph.graph import START, MessagesState, StateGraph
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode, tools_condition


def build_agent(model, tools):
    bound = model.bind_tools(tools)

    def agent(state):
        return {"messages": [bound.invoke(state["messages"])]}

    graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
    graph.add_node("agent", agent)
    graph.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))
    graph.add_edge(START, "agent")
    graph.add_conditional_edges("agent", tools_condition)
    graph.add_edge("tools", "agent")
    return graph.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())


def run_agent(app, question, thread_id, max_steps=8):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}, "recursion_limit": max_steps}
    try:
        result = app.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(question)]}, config)
    except GraphRecursionError:
        return "Stopped: step limit reached"
    return result["messages"][-1].content

ag-message-memory.article:
# Conversation Memory with trim_messages

## Intuition
A model can only read a limited context, and every token costs time and money. Long conversations must
be cut down: keep the system instructions, keep the most recent turns, drop the oldest — without
leaving a reply whose question was dropped.

## Precise explanation
```python
from langchain_core.messages import trim_messages

trim_messages(messages, max_tokens=4, token_counter=len,       # len counts messages
              strategy="last", include_system=True, start_on="human")
```

* `strategy="last"` keeps the end of the conversation; `include_system=True` always keeps a leading
  system message (it counts towards the budget).
* `start_on="human"` drops messages from the front of the kept window until it starts with a human
  message, so the history never opens with an orphaned AI reply or tool result.
* `token_counter` is either a model (to count real tokens) or a function that receives a **list of
  messages** and returns a number. `len` counts messages; a word counter approximates tokens.
* Trimming returns a new list; the stored history is unchanged.

## Worked example
[system, human "a", ai "b", human "c", ai "d"] with a budget of 3 messages keeps system, human "c" and
ai "d". With a budget of 4, the window [ai "b", human "c", ai "d"] would start with an AI message, so
"b" is dropped too.

## What the library does inside
The sliding window of AG-10 (the optional deep dive after this step), measured in the
units you choose and aware of message roles.

## Common mistakes
* Dropping the system message and losing the instructions.
* Cutting a tool result away from the AI message that requested it.
* Counting characters when the limit is in tokens; use the model's own counter in production.

## Why this matters
Every long-running assistant needs a memory policy; trimming is the simplest, and summarising old turns
is the next step.

## References

- [Short-term memory (LangChain docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/short-term-memory) — LangChain (`S135`)
- [Messages (LangChain docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages) — LangChain (`S130`)

memory-window.title: Conversation Memory Window by Hand
objectives: Fit a conversation into a token budget
Always keep the system message and the latest messages
Replace dropped history with a summary marker
memory-window.article:
# Managing the Context Window

## Intuition
Models have a maximum context length. Long agent runs accumulate more history than fits, so the agent
must decide what to keep. A simple robust policy: always keep the instructions (system message), keep
the most recent messages, and note that older ones were dropped.

## Precise explanation
* Token counting: real tokenisers are subword-based (LM-06); we approximate with whitespace words
  (`len(text.split())`) plus a fixed overhead of 4 tokens per message (role/formatting).
* Algorithm: keep the system message (if the first message has role "system"); then walk the rest
  **from newest to oldest**, adding messages while the total stays within the budget; stop at the
  first message that doesn't fit (keeps a contiguous recent window).
* If anything was dropped, insert `{"role": "system", "content": "[N earlier messages omitted]"}` right
  after the system message — but only if it fits; if it doesn't, drop more old messages until it does,
  except that the newest kept message is never dropped for the marker (then omit the marker).
* If even the system message alone exceeds the budget → `ValueError`.

## Worked example
Budget 20; system (2 words → 6 tokens), m1 (6 words → 10), m2 (3 → 7), m3 (1 → 5): newest first:
m3 (11 total), m2 (18), m1 would be 28 → stop. Marker "[1 earlier messages omitted]" (4 words → 8)
doesn't fit (26) → drop m2 → 6 + 8 + 5 = 19 ✓. Result: system, marker, m3.

## Common mistakes
* Dropping the system message (the agent forgets its instructions and safety rules).
* Keeping a non-contiguous set (confusing the model).
* Ignoring per-message overhead.

## Why this matters
Context management is a daily engineering concern for agents that run for many steps.

## References

- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
- [LLM Course](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter1/1) — Hugging Face (`S022`)

## Task

  dropped to make room for the marker; omit the marker instead), cost of a message =
  `count_tokens(content) + 4`. The marker text is exactly `f"[{n} earlier messages omitted]"`.

**Example**
```python
msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": "be helpful"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "one two three four five six"},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "a b c"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "ok"}]
[m["content"] for m in fit_context(msgs, 20)]
# ['be helpful', '[2 earlier messages omitted]', 'ok']
```

bfs-planner.title: BFS Planner
objectives: Formulate planning as graph search
Find a shortest action sequence with breadth-first search
Reconstruct plans from parent pointers
bfs-planner.article:
# Planning with Breadth-First Search

## Intuition
Before acting, an agent can *imagine* sequences of actions and pick one that reaches the goal. When
every action costs the same, exploring plans in order of length (breadth-first) finds a shortest one.

## Precise explanation (AIMA, ch. 3)
* `successors(state)` → list of `(action, next_state)`.
* BFS: FIFO queue (`collections.deque`) starting at `start`; mark states visited when **enqueued**;
  record `parent[next] = (state, action)`; stop when a dequeued state passes `goal_test`.
* Reconstruct by following parents back to the start and reversing.
* Deterministic order: expand successors in the order given.
* Unreachable goal → `None`. Complexity O(|V| + |E|).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S((start)) --> A((a)) & B((b))
  A --> G((goal))
  B --> C((c)) --> G
```

## Worked example
Rooms: hall → kitchen, hall → study, study → garden, kitchen → garden. Shortest plan from hall to
garden has 2 actions; with successors listed kitchen first, BFS returns ["go kitchen", "go garden"].

## Common mistakes
* Marking visited on dequeue (duplicates and extra work).
* DFS instead of BFS (not shortest).
* Forgetting the start can already be a goal (empty plan).

## Why this matters
Classical planning remains useful inside LLM agents (deterministic sub-problems, verifying plans);
A* (AG-12) adds costs and heuristics.

## References

- [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.)](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/) — Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig (`S038`)
bfs-planner.statement:
## Task

Write `bfs_plan(start, goal_test, successors)` returning `{"actions": list, "states": list,
"expanded": int}` for a shortest plan (states include start and goal; `expanded` = number of states
dequeued), or `None` if no plan exists. States are hashable.

**Example**
```python
G = {"hall": [("go kitchen", "kitchen"), ("go study", "study")], "kitchen": [("go garden", "garden")],
     "study": [("go garden", "garden")], "garden": []}
bfs_plan("hall", lambda s: s == "garden", lambda s: G[s])["actions"]   # ['go kitchen', 'go garden']
```
bfs-planner.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

BFS dequeues states in order of distance from the start, so the first goal dequeued is reached by a
shortest plan. Parent pointers recorded at enqueue time make each state's discovery unique and allow
plan reconstruction.
hints: `queue = deque([start]); parent = {start: None}`.
When enqueuing `nxt` not in parent: `parent[nxt] = (state, action)`.
Rebuild: walk parents from the goal to the start, then reverse both lists.

failureFeedback.advice: Expand successors in the given order and stop when a dequeued state is a goal.
Mark states as visited when enqueued so cycles don't loop forever.
If the start is a goal, return an empty plan.
Return None when the queue empties.

a-star-planner.title: A* Planner
objectives: Search with path cost plus an admissible heuristic
Use a priority queue with deterministic tie-breaking
Compare node expansions with uniform-cost search
a-star-planner.article:
# A* Search

## Intuition
BFS explores in rings and ignores where the goal is. A* prefers states that are cheap to reach *and*
look close to the goal, guided by a heuristic — like a hiker who keeps track of distance walked and
checks the summit's bearing.

## Precise explanation (AIMA, ch. 3)
Priority $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$: g = cost so far, h = heuristic estimate to the goal.
* Pop the lowest f from a heap (ties: lower h, then insertion order via a counter).
* Skip stale entries (a cheaper g was already recorded).
* Relax neighbours: if `g + cost < best_g[nbr]`, record it and push.
* Stop when the goal is **popped** (not when first generated).
If h is **admissible** (never overestimates) and consistent, A* returns an optimal path. With h = 0 it
is uniform-cost search (Dijkstra). On a 4-connected grid with unit costs, Manhattan distance is
admissible.

## Worked example
Open 5×5 grid from (0,0) to (4,4): optimal cost 8 both ways, but A* with Manhattan expands far fewer
states than h = 0.

## Common mistakes
* Stopping when the goal is generated (can return a suboptimal path).
* Inadmissible heuristics (e.g. Manhattan × 2) losing optimality.
* Comparing non-comparable states in the heap — always include a counter.

## Why this matters
A* is the workhorse of game AI, robot navigation and route planning; heuristics are an early form of
"intuition" guiding search, a theme that returns in LLM-guided planning.

## References

- [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.)](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/) — Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig (`S038`)
a-star-planner.statement:
## Task

Write `astar(start, goal, neighbors, heuristic)` returning `{"path": list, "cost": float, "expanded": int}`
or `None`. `neighbors(s)` yields `(next_state, step_cost)` with non-negative costs; `heuristic(s)` is a
float. `expanded` counts states popped and processed (not stale entries). Heap entries:
`(f, h, counter, state)`.

**Example**
```python
r = astar((0, 0), (4, 4), grid_neighbors, lambda s: abs(s[0] - 4) + abs(s[1] - 4))
r["cost"], len(r["path"])     # (8.0, 9)
```

a-star-planner.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Entries carry their g so stale ones (superseded by a cheaper path) are skipped on pop. Neighbours are
relaxed when a strictly cheaper path is found. Stopping only when the goal is popped guarantees
optimality with an admissible, consistent heuristic; the counter makes ordering deterministic without
comparing states.
hints: `best_g = {start: 0}`, `parent = {start: None}`, `heap = [(h0, h0, next(counter), start)]`.
On pop: if `g_of_entry > best_g[state]` skip (compute g = f − h).
Rebuild the path from parents when the goal is popped.

failureFeedback.advice: Stop when the goal is popped, not when it is generated.
Order the heap by f = g + h.
Relax a neighbour only when the new g is strictly smaller; skip stale heap entries.
Popping the start counts as one expansion.

task-dag-plan.title: Dependency-Ordered Plans
objectives: Represent a plan as a dependency graph
Topologically sort tasks with Kahn's algorithm
Detect cycles and group tasks into parallel stages
task-dag-plan.article:
# Plans as Dependency Graphs

## Intuition
"Write the report" needs "collect data" and "make charts" first; charts need data. Agents (and
orchestrators, AG-17) must run sub-tasks in an order that respects dependencies — and can run
independent ones in parallel.

## Precise explanation
`deps` maps each task to the set of tasks it depends on (all tasks appear as keys).
**Kahn's algorithm:**
1. In-degree = number of unmet dependencies per task.
2. Start with all tasks of in-degree 0 (sorted, for determinism — use a heap).
3. Pop the smallest ready task, append it, decrement in-degrees of tasks that depend on it; push newly
   ready ones.
4. If fewer tasks were output than exist, there is a **cycle** → error.
**Stages:** repeatedly take *all* currently ready tasks as one stage (sorted), remove them, repeat —
each stage could run in parallel.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  data[collect data] --> charts[make charts] --> report[write report]
  data --> report
  outline[outline] --> report
```

## Worked example
deps = {data: {}, outline: {}, charts: {data}, report: {data, charts, outline}} →
order [data, charts, outline, report]; stages [[data, outline], [charts], [report]].

## Common mistakes
* Reversing edge direction (dependents vs dependencies).
* Infinite loops on cycles.
* Non-deterministic order from set iteration.

## Why this matters
Build systems, data pipelines and multi-step agent plans all schedule work this way.

## References

- [Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.)](https://aima.cs.berkeley.edu/) — Stuart Russell, Peter Norvig (`S038`)
- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
task-dag-plan.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `topo_order(deps)` → list of tasks (Kahn's algorithm, smallest ready task first using `heapq`). Raise
  `ValueError("cycle detected")` on cycles and `ValueError` if a dependency is not a key.
* `stages(deps)` → list of sorted lists of tasks that can run in parallel.

**Example**
```python
deps = {"data": set(), "outline": set(), "charts": {"data"}, "report": {"data", "charts", "outline"}}
topo_order(deps)   # ['data', 'charts', 'outline', 'report']
stages(deps)       # [['data', 'outline'], ['charts'], ['report']]
```
task-dag-plan.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Kahn's algorithm releases a task once all its dependencies are output; a min-heap picks the
alphabetically smallest ready task for a deterministic order, and leftover tasks reveal a cycle. Stages
peel off every currently-ready task at once, giving the maximum parallelism level by level.
hints: Build `dependents[d].append(t)` for each t and each d in deps[t]; `indeg[t] = len(deps[t])`.
`ready = [t for t in deps if indeg[t] == 0]; heapq.heapify(ready)`.
Stages: loop taking `sorted(t for t in remaining if all deps done)`.

failureFeedback.advice: Use a min-heap of ready tasks so the smallest ready task goes first.
If not all tasks were output, raise ValueError('cycle detected').
A stage is every task whose dependencies are all in earlier stages.
Every dependency must be a key of deps.

ag-validate-retry.article:
# Validating Tool Arguments and Retrying

## Intuition
Models make plausible mistakes: a room "101" where the format is "R101", a meeting at 8 pm when the
building closes at 5. If the tool simply runs, it does damage; if it crashes, the agent stops. The
middle way: validate the arguments, tell the model exactly what was wrong, and let it try again.

## Precise explanation
```python
class BookingArgs(BaseModel):
    room: str = Field(pattern=r"^R\d{3}$", description="Room id such as R101")
    hour: int = Field(ge=9, le=17, description="Start hour, 9 to 17")

@tool(args_schema=BookingArgs)
def book_room(room: str, hour: int) -> str:
    """Book a meeting room for one hour."""
```

* `args_schema` makes the schema (including the descriptions) visible to the model and enforces it:
  `book_room.invoke(bad_args)` raises `pydantic.ValidationError`.
* `error.errors()` lists each problem with its field (`loc`) and message (`msg`); a compact summary such
  as `room: String should match pattern '^R\d{3}$'` is what the model needs.
* Loop: invoke the model → take its first tool call → validate and run. On failure append the AI message
  and a `ToolMessage(content="Invalid arguments: ...", tool_call_id=..., status="error")`, then ask again.
  Stop after `max_attempts` and report failure instead of looping.

## Worked example
Attempt 1: `{"room": "101", "hour": 20}` → "Invalid arguments: room: String should match pattern
'^R\d{3}$'; hour: Input should be less than or equal to 17". Attempt 2: `{"room": "R101", "hour": 16}`
→ "booked R101 at 16:00".

## What the library does inside
Pydantic validation replaces the hand-written checks in AG-15 (the optional deep dive
after this step); the retry loop is the same idea with real messages.

## Common mistakes
* Retrying without the error, so the model repeats the same mistake.
* Catching all exceptions, including bugs inside the tool, as if they were bad arguments.
* Unlimited retries.

## Why this matters
Validated tools are the first line of defence for agents that act in the world — booking, paying,
editing files.

## References

- [Tools (LangChain docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/tools) — LangChain (`S134`)
- [Validators (Pydantic docs)](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validators/) — Pydantic (`S140`)
ag-validate-retry.statement:
## Task

1. `class BookingArgs(BaseModel)` with `room: str = Field(pattern=r"^R\d{3}$")` and
   `hour: int = Field(ge=9, le=17)`.
2. `book_room` — a `@tool(args_schema=BookingArgs)` with docstring `"Book a meeting room for one hour."`
   returning `f"booked {room} at {hour}:00"`.
3. `call_with_validation(model, tool, messages, max_attempts=3)` repeats up to `max_attempts` times:
   `reply = model.invoke(messages)`; if the reply has no tool calls, return `(None, attempt)`; otherwise
   invoke `tool` with the first call's args. On success return `(result, attempt)`. On
   `ValidationError`, append the reply and a `ToolMessage` with
   `content="Invalid arguments: " + "; ".join(f"{err['loc'][0]}: {err['msg']}" for err in error.errors())`,
   `status="error"` and the call's id, and continue. After the last failed attempt return
   `(None, max_attempts)`. Attempts are counted from 1; the caller's `messages` list must not be modified.

ag-validate-retry.solution:
r"""Reference solution for AG-14 Validating Tool Arguments and Retrying.

The Pydantic schema states the constraints once; the tool enforces them on every call. Each failure is
summarised field by field and sent back as an error tool message tied to the call, so the model can
correct itself; the attempt counter bounds the loop.
"""
from langchain_core.messages import ToolMessage
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError


class BookingArgs(BaseModel):
    room: str = Field(pattern=r"^R\d{3}$")
    hour: int = Field(ge=9, le=17)


@tool(args_schema=BookingArgs)
def book_room(room: str, hour: int) -> str:
    """Book a meeting room for one hour."""
    return f"booked {room} at {hour}:00"


def call_with_validation(model, tool, messages, max_attempts=3):
    history = list(messages)
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        reply = model.invoke(history)
        if not reply.tool_calls:
            return None, attempt
        call = reply.tool_calls[0]
        try:
            return tool.invoke(call["args"]), attempt
        except ValidationError as error:
            summary = "; ".join(f"{err['loc'][0]}: {err['msg']}" for err in error.errors())
            history = history + [reply, ToolMessage(content="Invalid arguments: " + summary,
                                                    tool_call_id=call["id"], status="error")]
    return None, max_attempts

## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

The Pydantic schema states the constraints once; the tool enforces them on every call. Each failure is
summarised field by field and sent back as an error tool message tied to the call, so the model can
correct itself; the attempt counter bounds the loop.
hints: Copy the conversation first: `history = list(messages)`.
Inside the loop: `call = reply.tool_calls[0]`, then `tool.invoke(call["args"])` in a try block.
On ValidationError: `history += [reply, ToolMessage(content=..., tool_call_id=call["id"], status="error")]`.

Append the reply and an error ToolMessage listing each invalid field.
Stop after max_attempts and return (None, max_attempts).

validate-and-retry.article:
# Validate and Retry

## Intuition
Models make formatting mistakes: a missing field, "5" instead of 5, a value outside the allowed list.
Instead of failing, check the output against a schema, tell the model exactly what was wrong, and let it
try again — a few times at most.

## Precise explanation
Schema format used here: dict field → spec with keys `type` (Python type), optional `required`
(default True), `enum` (allowed values), `min`/`max` (numeric bounds).
`validate` returns a **list of error strings** (empty = valid), checking in a fixed order per field
(sorted field names): missing required → type (bools are not ints) → enum → range; then unexpected
fields.
The retry loop:
```text
messages = [prompt]
for attempt in 1..max_attempts:
    text = model(messages); parse JSON; validate
    if ok: return success
    messages.append(text); messages.append("Your output was invalid: " + "; ".join(errors))
return failure with all errors
```
This is the "evaluator–optimizer" pattern in miniature (Anthropic's agent guide) and mirrors ReAct's use
of observations to correct course.

## Worked example
Schema {city: str, days: int (1..14)}; attempt 1 `{"city": "Pune", "days": "3"}` → error
"days: expected int"; attempt 2 `{"city": "Pune", "days": 3}` → success.

## Common mistakes
* Vague feedback ("invalid") — the model can't fix what it can't see.
* Unlimited retries.
* Coercing types silently ("3" → 3) and hiding real bugs.

## Why this matters
Reliable structured outputs are what let agents call real APIs safely.

## References

- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Shunyu Yao et al. (`S036`)
validate-and-retry.statement:
## Task

Implement:
* `validate(obj, schema)` → list of errors using exactly these messages:
  `"<f>: missing"`, `"<f>: expected <type>"`, `"<f>: must be one of <enum list repr>"`,
  `"<f>: must be >= <min>"`, `"<f>: must be <= <max>"`, `"<f>: unexpected field"`
  (non-dict input → `["expected a JSON object"]`). Per field only the first failing check is reported.
* `call_with_retries(model, prompt, schema, max_attempts=3)` → dict
  `{"ok": bool, "value": obj | None, "attempts": int, "errors": list_of_error_lists}`. Invalid JSON counts
  as the error list `["invalid JSON"]`. Feedback message: `"Your output was invalid: " + "; ".join(errors)`.
  `model(messages)` receives a copy of the message list (strings).

**Example**
```python
schema = {"city": {"type": str}, "days": {"type": int, "min": 1, "max": 14}}
validate({"city": "Pune", "days": "3"}, schema)    # ['days: expected int']
```
validate-and-retry.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Validation checks each field in a fixed order and stops at its first problem, producing precise,
stable messages. The retry loop gives the model its previous output plus those messages, stops at the
first valid result, and records every failed attempt's errors for debugging.
hints: Loop `for f in sorted(schema)`; use `continue` after the first error for a field.
Type check: reject bools when the type is int/float; accept ints for float.
Retry loop: on failure append the raw text and the feedback string to messages.

failureFeedback.advice: Check fields in sorted order; report only the first failing check per field; unexpected fields last.
Append the model's text and 'Your output was invalid: ' + '; '.join(errors).
Stop at the first valid attempt and report attempts used.
Give up after max_attempts and return all error lists.

ag-orchestrator-graph.article:
# Orchestrator and Workers in LangGraph

## Intuition
Some tasks split naturally: summarise each section of a report, check each file, answer each
sub-question. An **orchestrator** decides the pieces, **workers** handle one piece each (in parallel
when possible), and a **synthesiser** combines their results. How many workers are needed is known
only at run time.

## Precise explanation
```python
from langgraph.types import Send

def assign(state):                                   # a conditional edge that fans out
    return [Send("worker", {"index": i, "section": s}) for i, s in enumerate(state["sections"])]

graph.add_conditional_edges("orchestrator", assign, ["worker"])
graph.add_edge("worker", "synthesise")
```

* `Send(node, payload)` runs `node` with its own payload instead of the shared state; returning a list
  of `Send`s starts one worker per item.
* Workers write to a key with a reducer (`Annotated[list, operator.add]`), so their results are
  collected rather than overwritten. Parallel results arrive in no guaranteed order — include an index
  and sort in the synthesiser.
* The synthesiser runs once, after all workers of that step have finished.
* With zero items no worker runs, and nothing after them runs either; handle that case where it matters.

## Worked example
A document with sections "intro text", "methods text" and "results text" becomes three worker calls.
With a worker that returns the section's word count, the synthesiser writes
"1: 2 words | 2: 2 words | 3: 2 words".

## What the library does inside
The task splitting and merging of AG-17 (the optional deep dive after this step),
with LangGraph scheduling the workers and merging their state updates.

## Common mistakes
* Workers returning plain values for a key without a reducer, so only one result survives.
* Assuming results arrive in order.
* Passing the whole state to each worker when it needs only its piece.

## Why this matters
Research assistants, code reviewers and report writers use this pattern to split large jobs across
many model calls.

## References

- [Workflows and agents (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents) — LangChain (`S139`)
- [Graph API (LangGraph docs)](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api) — LangChain (`S136`)

orchestrator-workers.article:
# Orchestrator–Workers with an Evaluator

## Intuition
A lead agent breaks a job into pieces, hands each piece to a specialist, and assembles the results. A
reviewer then checks the result and may send it back with comments. Anthropic's "Building effective
agents" describes these patterns as **orchestrator–workers** and **evaluator–optimizer**.

## Precise explanation
Components (here all deterministic Python functions, stand-ins for LLM calls):
* `planner(task, feedback)` → list of subtasks `{"id", "type", "input", "deps"}` (feedback is `None`
  in round 1).
* `workers[type](input, dep_outputs)` → output (dep_outputs: dict id → output of dependencies).
* `evaluator(task, outputs)` → `(accepted: bool, feedback: str)`.
Round loop (up to `max_rounds`): plan; run subtasks in topological order (AG-13 rule: smallest id among
ready ones); collect outputs; evaluate; stop if accepted, else re-plan with the feedback. Unknown worker
types or failing workers are recorded as errors in the log and make the round fail without calling the
evaluator.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T[task] --> P[planner] --> W1[worker: research] & W2[worker: write]
  W1 --> W2 --> E{evaluator}
  E -- revise + feedback --> P
  E -- accept --> R[result]
```

## Worked example
Planner splits "brief on X" into research → write; evaluator rejects drafts shorter than 5 words with
feedback "too short"; planner then asks the writer for a long version → accepted in round 2.

## Common mistakes
* Running dependent subtasks before their inputs exist.
* Infinite revise loops (always cap rounds).
* Letting one failing worker crash the whole pipeline.

## Why this matters
Most production "multi-agent" systems are carefully structured workflows like this rather than free-form
agent chatter.

## References

- [Building effective AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic (`S037`)
orchestrator-workers.statement:
## Task

Write `orchestrate(task, planner, workers, evaluator, max_rounds=2)` returning
`{"accepted": bool, "outputs": dict, "rounds": int, "log": list}` where `log` contains strings:
`"round <r>: plan <ids in execution order>"`, `"round <r>: <id> -> <type>"` for each executed subtask,
`"round <r>: error <id>: <message>"` (unknown type: `"unknown worker '<type>'"`; exception:
`"<ExceptionType>: <msg>"`), and `"round <r>: evaluator accepted"` / `"round <r>: evaluator rejected: <feedback>"`.
`outputs` are from the last round. Cycles in a plan → `ValueError`.

**Example**
```python
r = orchestrate("brief on solar", planner, workers, evaluator)
r["accepted"], r["rounds"]   # (True, 2)
```
orchestrator-workers.solutionExplanation:
## Worked solution

The reference solution is in `solution.py`. Explanation:

Each round plans, orders subtasks by dependencies, routes each to its worker with its dependencies'
outputs, and asks the evaluator to accept or give feedback. Worker failures are logged and end the
round without evaluation; the round cap prevents endless revision loops.
hints: Topological order of subtasks by `deps` using a heap of ready ids (AG-13).
Call `workers[s['type']](s['input'], {d: outputs[d] for d in s['deps']})` inside try/except.
On a worker error, log it, mark the round failed and skip the evaluator; set `feedback` accordingly.

failureFeedback.advice: Log the plan, each executed subtask and the evaluator decision with the exact formats.
Execute subtasks in dependency order (smallest ready id first).
Pass the evaluator's feedback to the planner in the next round.
Catch worker exceptions, log them and skip evaluation for that round.

Resume it with Command(resume=...) on the same thread
